lead: Eight days after Yaldo the Church keeps the Naming of our Lord, and the civil year begins under that Name. The two readings look at it from two sides. Luke shows the Child entering the covenant of his people: circumcised on the eighth day, called Jesus, carried up to Jerusalem, and presented to the Lord with the offering of those who could not afford a lamb. Paul writes to people who already bear that Name, and tells them what it asks: “That is not the way you learned Christ!” They are to put off an old self and clothe themselves with a new one.

So the line runs from the body of a Child marked by the covenant to the life of a Christian marked by Baptism. The key words are name, law and clothing. He takes on our condition, keeping every detail of the Law, so that we may take on his.

r.h: Clothed with the new self
set: The letter carries Paul's name and speaks from prison (3:1; 4:1). The Church has always received it among his letters; many modern scholars think it may come from a close disciple writing in his name, while others defend his authorship. Its authority as Scripture does not depend on the answer.

The first three chapters speak of what God has done in Christ; from 4:1 the letter turns to how Christians should live. The readers were Gentiles by birth (2:11), so when Paul says “as the Gentiles live” he means the way of life they themselves came out of. He is describing life without knowledge of God, as they knew it from inside, and not the worth of any people.
str: vv. 17–19: the old way: an empty mind, a darkened understanding, a hard heart, and a life given over to greed and impurity.
vv. 20–21: the turn: “That is not the way you learned Christ!”
vv. 22–24: what they were taught, in three verbs: put away the old self, be renewed in mind, clothe yourselves with the new self.
¶ The order of vv. 17–19 is worth noticing. The trouble begins in the mind and the heart, and only then appears in behaviour. So the cure also begins within, in v. 23.
kw: The Greek Old Testament uses this word for the “vanity” of Ecclesiastes (1:2). A mind in futility is busy with things that cannot finally satisfy.
Literally “old man” and “new man”, as the POC keeps it. It means more than a private mood: the whole humanity of Adam, and the new humanity begun in Christ. Compare Romans 6:6 and Colossians 3:9–10.
to clothe oneself, to put on
The word for putting on a garment. Paul uses it for Baptism: “have clothed yourselves with Christ” (Galatians 3:27).
vv: That is not the way you learned Christ!
An unusual phrase. One learns a language or a trade; here Paul says one learns a Person. Christian teaching is finally an introduction to someone.
as truth is in Jesus.

Everywhere else in this letter the name comes with a title: Christ Jesus, the Lord Jesus. Only here does Jesus stand by itself. On the feast of the Naming it is good to notice this: truth has a human name and a human history.
You were taught to put away your former way of life, your old self, corrupt and deluded by its lusts,
“Deluded”: sin promises and does not deliver. The old self is not only wicked; it has been lied to.
and to be renewed in the spirit of your minds,

Between taking off and putting on stands this verb, and it is passive: to be renewed. The change is God's work in us, and in the Greek it is a continuing one. Baptism happens once; this goes on daily.
and to clothe yourselves with the new self, created according to the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness.
The Greek says simply “according to God”; the NRSV rightly brings out the echo of Genesis 1:26–27. The new self is “created”. It is a new creation, and not an improved version of the old one.
ch: The Church hears these verses as a description of Baptism. The Catechism teaches that Baptism makes the one baptised a new creature and an adopted child of God (CCC 1265), and that the white garment shows the person has put on Christ (CCC 1243). The baptismal instructions of Jerusalem linked with St Cyril explain the removal of the garment before the font as putting off the old self (in substance). St Leo the Great, in a Christmas sermon that the Catechism quotes, draws the moral: Christian, recognise your dignity, and do not go back to your former state (Sermon 21; CCC 1691).

r.h: He was called Jesus
set: Luke has just told of the birth and the shepherds. Now, in four verses, he mentions the Law of Moses or “the law of the Lord” three times. His point is simple: the Son of God was brought up by parents who did what the Law asked, as devout Jewish families did.

Three separate customs lie behind the passage. A boy was circumcised on the eighth day (Genesis 17:12; Leviticus 12:3), and in Luke's story the naming goes with it (1:59). A mother was ritually unclean for forty days after the birth of a son and then brought an offering: a lamb and a bird, or two birds if she could not afford a lamb (Leviticus 12:2–8). And every firstborn son belonged to the Lord (Exodus 13:2), and was bought back with five shekels (Numbers 18:15–16).
str: v. 21: the eighth day: circumcision and the name.
v. 22a: the purification, and the journey up to Jerusalem.
vv. 22b–23: the presentation of the firstborn to the Lord.
v. 24: the offering of two birds.
¶ The reading stops before Simeon and Anna appear (2:25–38). Today the Church holds us at the quiet start of the scene: a family keeping the Law, with nobody yet saying who the Child is.
kw: The Greek form of Yeshua, a shorter form of Yehoshua, which is also the name of Joshua. It means “the Lord saves”. Matthew gives the meaning outright (1:21). The name was common at the time; what is unique is the one who bore it.
The sign of the covenant in the flesh (Genesis 17:10–11). Paul sums up the meaning of this day: “born of a woman, born under the law” (Galatians 4:4).
The word means to place before someone. Paul uses it for what Christians do with their whole selves (Romans 12:1). In Luke 2 the first one so presented is Jesus.
vv: After eight days had passed, it was time to circumcise the child; and he was called Jesus, the name given by the angel before he was conceived in the womb.

Luke points back to Gabriel's word to Mary (1:31). The Name was not chosen by the family: it was received from heaven, and the parents obey. Circumcision is also the first shedding of his blood, a detail the Church's preachers have long noticed.
When the time came for their purification according to the law of Moses, they brought him up to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord

A note on the text. Leviticus 12 speaks of the mother only, yet the Greek here says “their”. The Latin Vulgate has eius, which does not show the gender and was long taken as “her”. The POC does not say whose. Luke seems to see the family acting together.
(as it is written in the law of the Lord, “Every firstborn male shall be designated as holy to the Lord”),
Exodus 13:2. Luke says nothing about the five shekels. He leaves us with a Child who is simply given to the Lord, somewhat as Hannah brought Samuel (1 Samuel 1:24–28).
and they offered a sacrifice according to what is stated in the law of the Lord, “a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons.”
Leviticus 12:8 allows this for one who “cannot afford a sheep”. In a single line Luke tells us about the family's means. The Son of God enters the Temple for the first time as a child of the poor.
ch: The Catechism sees in the circumcision the sign of Jesus' incorporation into Abraham's descendants and his submission to the Law, and it adds that this sign prefigures Baptism (CCC 527). It sees in the presentation the firstborn who belongs to the Lord (CCC 529). On the Name it teaches that Jesus means “God saves” (CCC 430), that this is the one name which contains everything, and that it stands at the heart of Christian prayer (CCC 435, 2666). St Bernard of Clairvaux calls the Name honey in the mouth, music in the ear and a shout of joy in the heart (Sermons on the Song of Songs 15, in substance). Peter's confession gives the reason: “There is salvation in no one else” (Acts 4:12).

qa: Why was the Son of God circumcised?

Because he truly became a son of Israel. Paul says he was “born under the law” (Galatians 4:4). He did not need the covenant sign in order to belong to God, but he took his place among his own people and kept their Law from within (CCC 527).
Did Mary need to be purified from sin?

No. The uncleanness of Leviticus 12 is ritual and concerns contact with blood and birth, the great mysteries of life. It says nothing about sin. Mary went to the Temple out of obedience, as every Jewish mother was expected to do.
Is Paul looking down on the Gentiles in Ephesians 4:17?

He is speaking to Gentile-born Christians about the life they left, and in chapter 2 he says that those who were far off have been brought near. It is not a judgment on other peoples or religions today. The Church rejects nothing that is true and holy in other religions, and she still proclaims Christ (Nostra Aetate 2).
rite: In the Syriac of the West Syriac tradition the Name is pronounced Yeshu‘, very close to what Mary and Joseph would have said in Aramaic, and close also to our Malayalam യേശു. The Malankara reader who begins the year at the Holy Qurbono begins it where the Child began his: with a family going up to God's house, bringing what it has. Today's feast also suits the home: a family could begin the year by placing its plans, debts, fears and hopes under this Name, and by asking what old clothing needs to come off this year.
study: Paul says one “learns” Christ. Who taught me Christ, and how much of my knowing him is knowledge about him rather than friendship with him?
Ephesians 4:22 calls the old self “deluded”. Which promise of sin has most often deceived me?
The Holy Family brought the offering of those who could not afford a sheep. How does this shape the way our parish receives its poorer families?
At the start of this year, what would it mean to pray the Name of Jesus each day, slowly and from the heart?

lead: The Church remembers two bishops and friends who defended faith in the Holy Trinity, Mar Baselios and Mar Gregorios, and the readings suit them well. The Epistle draws the portrait of a teacher who must hold the truth without quarrelling. In the Gospel a learned man comes by night and is told that learning is not enough: he must be born from above. Coming a few days before Denho, these words about water and Spirit also send us back to our own Baptism.

r.h: Kindly to everyone, an apt teacher
set: 2 Timothy is written as Paul's last letter, from chains (1:8; 2:9) and with death near (4:6). Many modern scholars think the Pastoral Letters come from a follower writing in Paul's name, while others hold, especially for this letter with its personal details, that Paul stands behind it. The Church receives it as inspired either way.

False teachers are troubling the community; Hymenaeus and Philetus say the resurrection has already taken place (2:17–18). Just before this reading Paul pictures a large house with vessels of gold and silver, wood and clay (2:20). How should the Lord's servant behave in such a dispute?
str: v. 21: the useful vessel, cleansed and ready.
vv. 22–23: what to run from and what to run after; no foolish controversies.
vv. 24–26: the Lord's servant: kind, patient, correcting with gentleness, hoping for the opponent's return.
kw: Literally “slave of the Lord”, a title the Old Testament gives to Moses, Joshua and David. Such a person does not fight for his own victory, since the work belongs to his Master.
A rare word in the New Testament, the opposite of “quarrelsome” in the same verse. It is the tone of a parent or nurse rather than of a debater.
A change of mind and direction. Paul says that God may grant it (v. 25). The teacher corrects, but only God converts.
vv: And the Lord’s servant must not be quarrelsome but kindly to everyone, an apt teacher, patient,
Teaching ability stands between two words about character. He must also be able to teach: kindness here does not mean silence about the truth.
correcting opponents with gentleness. God may perhaps grant that they will repent and come to know the truth,
“Perhaps”: the teacher does not control the outcome. The opponents are people to be won and not enemies to be beaten.
and that they may escape from the snare of the devil,
The real enemy is not the person across the table. The opponent is seen as someone caught in a trap, needing rescue.
ch: Mar Baselios and Mar Gregorios lived through bitter fighting over the divinity of the Son and the Holy Spirit in the fourth century. St Basil wrote On the Holy Spirit and also founded a great house of care for the poor and sick at Caesarea. St Gregory, in his funeral oration for Basil, recalls their student days at Athens, when they knew only two roads: to the church and to their teachers (Oration 43, in substance). At Constantinople in 381 Gregory gave up the see for the sake of peace. Both men show what this passage asks: firmness in truth without love of quarrel.

r.h: Born from above
set: Jesus is in Jerusalem at Passover, and many have believed because of his signs (2:23). Nicodemus is a Pharisee and “a leader of the Jews”, which in John here means a member of the ruling authorities (see 7:50). He is one person, honest and searching, and John does not make him a type of a whole people.

He comes “by night”. In John, night and light carry meaning (1:5; 13:30), yet this man will appear again: defending Jesus' right to a hearing (7:50–51), and bringing myrrh and aloes for his burial (19:39). His faith grows slowly.
str: vv. 1–2: Nicodemus comes by night, and says “we know”.
vv. 3–8: birth from above, of water and Spirit; the image of the wind.
vv. 9–12: “How can these things be?” The teacher is taught.
vv. 13–14: the Son of Man who came down must be lifted up. The sentence runs on into v. 15, where believers receive eternal life.
kw: The Greek has both meanings. Jesus means “from above”; Nicodemus hears “again” and asks about a mother's womb. The POC translates “again” (വീണ്ടും). Both are true: it is a second birth, and its source is God.

The same word means both, like the Hebrew rûaḥ and the Syriac rûḥo. So v. 8 is a play on words that a translation cannot quite carry over: the wind and the Spirit are alike, unseen, and known by what they do.
In John this means both the Cross and the glory (8:28; 12:32–33). Moses lifted the serpent on a pole for those who had been bitten (Numbers 21:8–9), and they looked and lived.
vv: Very truly, I tell you, no one can see the kingdom of God without being born from above.
Jesus does not answer the compliment; he goes straight to what Nicodemus needs. “We know,” said the teacher. To see, says Jesus, one must first be born.
Very truly, I tell you, no one can enter the kingdom of God without being born of water and Spirit.
This is the verse the Church has always linked with Baptism. Water is the sign; the Spirit is the giver of the new life.
The wind blows where it chooses, and you hear the sound of it, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes.
One cannot manage the Spirit. A person born of the Spirit becomes somewhat like the wind: moved from beyond himself.
And just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up,
The conversation that began with birth ends at the Cross. The new birth has a price, and he pays it. The word “must” belongs to God's plan.
ch: St Justin Martyr, in the second century, already quotes these words when he explains Christian Baptism (First Apology 61). The Catechism uses John 3:5 to explain why Baptism is called the washing of regeneration, “the birth of water and the Spirit” (CCC 1215), and to teach its necessity for salvation for those to whom the Gospel has been proclaimed, while God is not bound by his sacraments (CCC 1257). Some Christians speak of being “born again” as a sudden moment of feeling; the Church respects every real conversion, and she teaches that this birth is first God's gift in water and Spirit, to be lived out daily.

qa: Why does Jesus seem to mock Nicodemus in v. 10?

It is a challenge and not a sneer. The Prophets had spoken of a new heart and God's Spirit, with clean water (Ezekiel 36:25–27). A teacher of Israel could have recognised the language. Jesus goes on teaching him, and the man keeps coming back.
rite: Mar Baselios and Mar Gregorios are dear to the Syriac Churches, and their names are carried by our Catholicos and many of our bishops. Today is the name day of Moran Mor Baselios Cardinal Cleemis Catholicos: pray for him, and for all who must teach and guard the faith with the patience of 2 Timothy.
study: Think of the last argument I had about faith, in the parish or online. Was I “kindly to everyone”? What would correcting “with gentleness” have looked like?
Nicodemus came by night, and came back openly at the burial. Where is my faith still coming by night, and what would help it come out into the open?

lead: Between Yaldo and Denho the Church listens to John the Baptist. The Evening Gospel gives his plain answer to the crowds: “Bear fruits worthy of repentance” (Luke 3:8), which means sharing a coat, honest accounts, no extortion. The Old Testament lessons offer young people growing under God's eye: Joseph, loved by his father and given a long robe (Genesis 37:1–4); the boy Samuel with the little robe his mother made every year (1 Samuel 2:18–21). Psalm 45 sings of the King, and the First Letter of John asks for love “in truth and action” (see 1 John 3:18) and gives the commandment that follows from it (3:19–24).

The three readings studied here form one line about seeing what cannot yet be seen. Isaiah, whose chapter gives John the Baptist his own title of “voice” (John 1:23), tells tired exiles to lift their eyes. Hebrews shows Moses, who endured “as though he saw him who is invisible”, keeping the Passover with the blood of a lamb. In John the Baptist sees, and points: “Here is the Lamb of God”. The key words are seeing, faith and the Lamb.

r.h: Lift up your eyes on high
set: Isaiah 40–55 is addressed to the Jewish exiles in Babylon, in the years before Cyrus allowed them to go home (539 BC). Most scholars think these chapters come from a prophet of the exile in the tradition of Isaiah of Jerusalem; the Church reads the whole book together as one witness. Chapter 40 opens with “Comfort, O comfort my people” and with the voice in the wilderness (40:1, 3), the verse all four Gospels apply to John the Baptist.

The exiles live under a great empire, among splendid temples and star-gods. They have seen their own Temple burned. The question is not whether God exists, but whether God still notices them. This reading is his answer.
str: v. 25: God's challenge: “To whom then will you compare me”?
v. 26: look up: the stars are counted and called by name.
v. 27: Israel's complaint, quoted back to her.
vv. 28–31: the answer: the God who never tires gives strength to those who do.
kw: This prophet's favourite title for God, usually “the Holy One of Israel”. Holy means set apart, beyond comparison, and yet he is Israel's own.
“Their host” in v. 26 is a military word. In Babylon stars were honoured as gods; here they are a parade of soldiers, called out by name by their Commander.
those who wait for the Lord
From qāwāh, to wait with eager hope. The POC translates “those who trust in God”. Waiting and trusting are one attitude seen from two sides.
Literally “shall exchange strength”. The tired hand over their weakness and receive his strength.
vv: Lift up your eyes on high and see: Who created these?
The cure for despair begins by looking up. The One who knows every star by name will not lose track of one exile.
Why do you say, O Jacob, and speak, O Israel, “My way is hidden from the Lord, and my right is disregarded by my God”?
God quotes their prayer of complaint. He has heard even the sentence that says he does not hear.
He gives power to the faint, and strengthens the powerless.
The Creator “does not faint” (v. 28), and that is why he has strength to spare. The young, who seem to have most of it, can run out (v. 30).
but those who wait for the Lord shall renew their strength, they shall mount up with wings like eagles, they shall run and not be weary, they shall walk and not faint.

The order is surprising: flying, running, walking. The list seems to go downward, but it matches life. Flying is rare; running comes at times; walking is every day. It is for the plain daily walk that the promise matters most.
ch: All four Gospels hear Isaiah 40 in the preaching of John the Baptist (Matthew 3:3; Mark 1:3; Luke 3:4; John 1:23): the God who comforted the exiles now comes in person, and the way through the wilderness is the way of Christ. The Catechism defines hope as the virtue by which we desire the Kingdom, relying not on our own strength but on the help of the grace of the Holy Spirit (CCC 1817). Isaiah's waiting is an early school of that virtue.

r.h: By faith Moses
set: Hebrews is a sermon to Christians who are growing tired (13:22). Its author is not named; the Church has received it among the letters linked with St Paul, and the Malankara lectionary reads it as such. Chapter 11 is a long roll of honour that opens with a description of faith: “the assurance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen” (11:1).

Our passage covers Moses and the Exodus generation, and it retells Exodus 1–15 and Joshua 2–6 to show that the same faith ran through all of them. The author reads the old stories from the standpoint of Christ, whom his hearers are tempted to leave.
str: v. 23: the faith of Moses' parents.
vv. 24–26: Moses chooses God's people rather than Pharaoh's household.
v. 27: he leaves Egypt, unafraid.
v. 28: the Passover and the blood.
v. 29: the Red Sea; v. 30: Jericho; v. 31: Rahab.
¶ Seven sentences in this passage open with the same words, “By faith”. The repetition is the sermon's drumbeat, and it ends surprisingly with a foreign woman.
kw: A single Greek word, used like a refrain. Faith here is not mere opinion but a trust that acts: it hides a child, refuses a palace, walks into the sea.
“Christ” means Anointed. The phrase may echo Psalm 89:50–51, where the Lord's anointed bears insults. The author sees one pattern: those who suffer for God's people share the path of the Messiah.
Moses endured “as though he saw” the unseen God. Faith gives a kind of sight, the line that links this reading with Isaiah and with John.
Exodus 12:13 gives the promise: “when I see the blood, I will pass over you”. Hebrews mentions the blood without saying whose. The Christian reader knows where the sentence is going.
vv: choosing rather to share ill-treatment with the people of God than to enjoy the fleeting pleasures of sin.
The word “fleeting” does the work. Moses compared what lasts with what does not, and chose against his immediate comfort.
He considered abuse suffered for the Christ to be greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt, for he was looking ahead to the reward.
Faith here is a calculation done with the right scales.
By faith he left Egypt, unafraid of the king’s anger; for he persevered as though he saw him who is invisible.

Exodus 2:14 says Moses was afraid when he fled to Midian, so many commentators think this verse means the Exodus itself, while others read it as his flight seen in a different light. Either way, his strength comes from seeing the One no one can see.
By faith he kept the Passover and the sprinkling of blood, so that the destroyer of the firstborn would not touch the firstborn of Israel.
Israel's firstborn were kept safe by the blood of a lamb. This is the clearest bridge to today's Gospel.
By faith Rahab the prostitute did not perish with those who were disobedient, because she had received the spies in peace.
A Canaanite and a prostitute closes the list. Matthew names her among the ancestors of Jesus (1:5). Nobody is too far outside for faith.
ch: The Catechism says that the Old Testament is rich in witnesses to faith and points to the praise of them in Hebrews (CCC 147). The Passover lamb leads the Church to the Eucharist: at the Last Supper, in the setting of the Passover, Jesus gave it its definitive meaning (CCC 1340). St Clement of Rome, writing about the end of the first century, already sees in Rahab's scarlet cord a sign that redemption would come through the Lord's blood (1 Clement 12, in substance).

r.h: Here is the Lamb of God
set: John's Gospel opens with a sequence of days. On the first, the Baptist tells the authorities' messengers that he is not the Messiah (1:19–28). “The next day” comes this reading, and on the next the first disciples leave John and follow Jesus (1:35–39).

Unlike the other Gospels, John does not narrate the baptism of Jesus. He gives instead the testimony of the one who saw what happened there. The Baptist's whole purpose in this Gospel is to witness and then step aside (3:30).
str: v. 29: he sees Jesus and cries out.
v. 30: the one who comes after was before.
v. 31: why John baptises: so that he might be revealed to Israel.
vv. 32–33: the sign: the Spirit descends and remains.
v. 34: the climax of the testimony.
kw: Behind it stand the Passover lamb (Exodus 12) and the Servant led “like a lamb” (Isaiah 53:7). The Syriac Gospels say emreh d-Aloho. Later the first letter of Peter speaks of “the precious blood of Christ, like that of a lamb without defect or blemish” (1 Peter 1:19).
The Greek can mean both to lift up and carry, and to remove. He bears the sin and bears it away. “Sin” is singular: the whole burden of the world, not only single faults.
The Spirit does not merely touch him. In the Old Testament the Spirit often came upon people for a time; here he stays. The word returns throughout John (1:39; 15:4).
vv: The next day he saw Jesus coming toward him and declared, “Here is the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world!
Jesus says nothing in this scene. He only comes, and the Baptist names him. A shepherd's word for a young animal becomes the first title given to Jesus in public in this Gospel.
This is he of whom I said, ‘After me comes a man who ranks ahead of me because he was before me.’
Jesus is younger than John in the flesh, and comes after him in time. Yet “he was before me”: the eternal Word of the Prologue (1:1).
And John testified, “I saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove, and it remained on him.
The Spirit who was over the waters in creation (Genesis 1:2) rests on the One who will give new birth from the water.
And I myself have seen and have testified that this is the Son of God.”

A note on the text. Some ancient witnesses, including the Old Syriac Gospels, read here “the Chosen One of God”, recalling Isaiah 42:1, and the NRSV notes this in its margin. Most manuscripts read “the Son of God”, as the NRSV and the POC do. The two do not conflict: the Father's voice at the Jordan also echoes Isaiah 42:1.
ch: The Catechism joins the Baptist's cry with the Suffering Servant and the Paschal lamb (CCC 608), and sees in the baptism of Jesus his acceptance of that mission (CCC 536). St Cyril of Alexandria, commenting on this verse, says that one Lamb died for all, to gather the whole flock of humanity to the Father (Commentary on John, in substance). St Augustine, preaching on the dove, finds in it the simplicity and unity of the Spirit, who gives no room for pride or division (Tractates on John 6, in substance).

qa: John and Jesus were relatives, so how can John say, “I myself did not know him”?

Luke calls Elizabeth a relative of Mary (1:36), but the Gospels do not say how much the two men had met. John means that he did not know him as the One to come, until the sign at the Jordan showed him. Knowing a person's family is one thing; knowing his mission is another.
How could Moses suffer “for the Christ” centuries earlier?

Hebrews reads Israel's history as moving toward Christ. Moses suffered with God's people, and it is in God's people that the anointed One would come and suffer. The author is not claiming that Moses knew the name of Jesus; he is seeing one saving plan across the ages.
Why is a prostitute held up as a model?

Hebrews praises her faith and not her trade. In Joshua 2:9–11 she confesses the God of Israel, and acts on it at the risk of her life. The list teaches that faith can begin in any life. See also James 2:25.
rite: After Yaldo, the Malankara Church does not hurry past the Child; she keeps him before us and lets John tell us who he is. The feast of Denho falls this Wednesday. Each Holy Qurbono places the Baptist's words before us again, and the Lamb he pointed to is the One we receive. Families can practise the teaching of the Evening Gospel this week in one concrete act: a coat given, or an account set straight.
study: Isaiah's people thought: “My way is hidden from the Lord.” When have I said something like that? What helped me to lift my eyes?
Moses refused the palace. What comfort or status is my faith asking me to treat as “fleeting”?
John spent his life pointing away from himself. To whom have I pointed Jesus out, and how plainly?
What do the words “who takes away the sin of the world” say to me as I come forward to receive the Holy Qurbono?

lead: Hebrews begins its roll of faith at the very start of the Bible, with Abel, Enoch and Noah, who lived long before any covenant with Abraham. The Gospel gives the portrait of a life that trusts God in the same way: the Beatitudes. What Hebrews calls pleasing God, Jesus calls being blessed, and both look past what can now be seen to what God has promised.

r.h: Without faith it is impossible to please God
set: Having said what faith is (11:1) and that creation itself is known by faith (11:3), the preacher starts his list with three figures from Genesis 4–9. He has a small problem: Genesis does not use the word faith of any of them. So he reasons from what the text does say. God accepted Abel's gift; Enoch pleased God; Noah acted on a warning about what no one could yet see.
str: v. 4: Abel: an acceptable gift, a voice that still speaks.
v. 5: Enoch: taken by God, because he pleased God.
v. 6: the rule that explains them: faith believes that God is, and that he rewards.
v. 7: Noah: warned, he builds.
kw: The Hebrew of Genesis 5:24 says that Enoch “walked with God”; the Greek Old Testament, which this author reads, says he “pleased God”. To walk with God is what pleases him.
A word for reverent care. Noah's faith is not a pleasant feeling; it is fear of God that turns into many years of carpentry.
vv: he died, but through his faith he still speaks.

Genesis 4:10 says Abel's blood cried out from the ground. Later this letter says that the blood of Jesus “speaks a better word than the blood of Abel” (12:24): Abel's cries for justice, Christ's for mercy.
And without faith it is impossible to please God, for whoever would approach him must believe that he exists and that he rewards those who seek him.
Two things are the minimum: that God is, and that he is not indifferent. “Those who seek him”: a faith on the move.
By faith Noah, warned by God about events as yet unseen, respected the warning and built an ark to save his household;

A man builds a boat on dry land because of something only God has seen. The whole household is saved through the faith of one, and for this reason the Fathers and 1 Peter 3:20–21 see the ark as a figure of Baptism and the Church.
ch: The Catechism quotes Hebrews 11:6 in teaching that faith is necessary for salvation (CCC 161), and it points to the prayer and offering of these first righteous ones, Abel and Enoch among them, and to Noah (CCC 2569). It also recalls that Scripture honours great figures from among the Gentiles, Abel the just and upright Noah among them (CCC 58). Noah's ark, for its part, is listed among the Old Testament figures of Baptism (CCC 1219).

r.h: The Beatitudes
set: This is the opening of the Sermon on the Mount, the first of five great teaching blocks in Matthew. Jesus goes up a mountain and sits, the posture of a teacher, and Matthew's readers would think of Moses on Sinai. Luke has a shorter form on a level place, with four blessings and four woes (6:20–26).
str: vv. 1–2: the setting: crowds, mountain, disciples.
vv. 3–10: eight blessings. The first and the last end alike: “theirs is the kingdom of heaven”.
vv. 11–12: the blessing turns to “you”, with the prophets as models.
¶ The first and eighth are in the present tense (“theirs is”), the rest in the future. The kingdom is already given, and its fullness is coming.
kw: The word congratulates. It is the Greek for the opening of Psalm 1. It is not a command to feel happy; it is God's verdict on a condition that the world would pity.

Ptōchos is the destitute person, the beggar. In the Psalms and Zephaniah 3:12 the humble poor are those who have only God to lean on. Matthew's phrase keeps the economic picture and adds the attitude.
Psalm 37:11 is behind v. 5. It means those who do not grab or strike back, and Jesus uses the same word of himself (11:29).
vv: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
The Sermon opens with a gift and not a demand. The Kingdom belongs to those who know they cannot buy it.
“Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God.
A pure heart is an undivided one (Psalm 24:4). Hebrews spoke of those who seek God; here is what they find.
“Blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
Verses 11–12 say “on my account”. Jesus puts himself where righteousness stood. Only someone with a very high claim speaks like this.
ch: The Catechism says that the Beatitudes are at the heart of Jesus' preaching and that they depict the countenance of Jesus Christ (CCC 1716–1717); it also explains poverty of spirit (CCC 2546). St Gregory of Nyssa preached on them as steps in a climb towards God, and St Augustine, in his work on the Sermon on the Mount, reads them as a ladder of growth from humility to wisdom (both in substance). They describe Christ first, and then whoever is being formed in his likeness.

rite: The Church remembers today the Prophet Malachi, who promised that “the sun of righteousness shall rise, with healing in its wings” (Malachi 4:2), and St Kuriakose Elias Chavara (1805–1871), a priest of Kerala's Syro-Malabar Church, founder of religious communities and promoter of schools, whom Pope Francis canonised in 2014. He is a saint of our own soil, and he shows what the Beatitudes look like in everyday work.
study: Abel “still speaks”. Whose faith, now dead, still speaks to me, and what does it say?
Which Beatitude do I find hardest to believe? What would I need to see differently to take it seriously?

lead: On the eve of Denho the readings speak of growing and of being cared for. Paul describes the ascended Christ giving gifts so that the whole Body may reach maturity. Jesus tells the disciples to look at ravens and lilies. A person who has stopped being anxious about food and clothing is able to give attention to the Body; a Church built up in love is one in which the anxious are carried.

r.h: Grow up in every way into Christ
set: The letter comes to us under Paul's name from prison (on authorship, many modern scholars think of a close disciple, others defend Paul himself). Just before this reading he has listed what unites Christians: “one body and one Spirit… one Lord, one faith, one baptism” (4:4–5). Now he turns from what all share to what each receives, and shows that the differences are for the sake of the unity.
str: v. 7: to each a measure of grace.
vv. 8–10: Psalm 68 and the Christ who came down and went up.
vv. 11–12: the ministries and their purpose.
v. 13: the goal: unity and maturity.
vv. 14–16: children tossed about, or a body growing in love.
kw: The related verb is used for mending nets (Mark 1:19). Ministers exist to put the saints in working order. The “work of ministry” belongs to the whole body.
A single Greek word that means more than speech: living and dealing truly. Joined with “in love”, it rules out both soft lies and hard truths told without care.
Christ is not only the ruler of the body but also the source of its growth: “from whom the whole body” grows (v. 16).
vv: Therefore it is said, “When he ascended on high he made captivity itself a captive; he gave gifts to his people.”

Psalm 68:18 in the Hebrew and Greek says that God received gifts. Here it says “gave”. An Aramaic Jewish paraphrase of the psalm also reads “gave”, and the Conqueror who receives tribute now shares it out.
The gifts he gave were that some would be apostles, some prophets, some evangelists, some pastors and teachers,
The gifts are persons. Greek grammar joins “pastors and teachers” closely, perhaps as one ministry.
But speaking the truth in love, we must grow up in every way into him who is the head, into Christ,
The reading's central image. The Christian life is not standing still, and its direction is Christ himself.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Christ provides in his Body, the Church, the gifts and helps by which we support one another on the way of salvation (CCC 794), and it uses vv. 9–10 of the descent of Christ among the dead (CCC 631). The Second Vatican Council places all ministries inside the one people of God, for the service of the whole Body (Lumen Gentium 7, 32). St John Chrysostom, preaching on this letter, warns that nothing divides the Church as much as the love of power (Homilies on Ephesians 11, in substance).

r.h: Consider the lilies
set: “Therefore” connects these words to the parable just before: the rich man who built bigger barns and died that night (12:16–21). The rich man's sin was greed; the disciple's danger may be the same fear in a poorer form. Matthew has a parallel in the Sermon on the Mount (6:25–33).
str: vv. 22–23: the command, and the reason: life is more than food.
vv. 24–26: the ravens, and the futility of worry.
vv. 27–28: the lilies and the grass; the argument “how much more”.
¶ The reading stops just short of the positive command: “strive for his kingdom” (12:31).
kw: Anxious care that pulls the mind in many directions. Jesus does not forbid work: the birds and flowers are pictures of trust, and elsewhere his followers work and give.
Matthew says “birds”. Luke names the raven, an unclean bird in the Law (Leviticus 11:15). Yet God feeds even these (Psalm 147:9). The choice sharpens the point.
The word in v. 25 is literally a cubit, a measure of length, which the POC keeps as “മുഴം”. The NRSV takes it as a stretch of time, “a single hour”.
vv: Consider the ravens: they neither sow nor reap, they have neither storehouse nor barn, and yet God feeds them.
“Barn” echoes the rich fool. He built bigger barns and lost his life; the raven has none and is fed. The word “consider” asks for careful, patient looking.
Consider the lilies, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin; yet I tell you, even Solomon in all his glory was not clothed like one of these.
The flower cannot be identified with certainty; it may be any wild bloom of the Galilean spring. Solomon's splendour (1 Kings 10) is the highest human measure, and a weed outdoes it.
But if God so clothes the grass of the field, which is alive today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, how much more will he clothe you
Dry grass served as fuel for the clay oven. “How much more” is the logic of the kingdom, from God's care for little things to his care for you.
ch: The Catechism says that Jesus asks for childlike abandonment to the providence of the Father, who takes care of his children's smallest needs (CCC 305). On the petition “give us this day our daily bread” it explains that he is not inviting us to idleness, but wants to relieve us of nagging worry (CCC 2830). St Paul's own hard work shows that trust and labour go together (1 Thessalonians 2:9). God often feeds those who have little through those who have more.

qa: Is it wrong to plan, save, or insure one's family?

No. Jesus speaks against anxiety and greed, not against prudence; he himself speaks of counting the cost (14:28). The test is what we do with the fear: whether it drives us to trust God and care for others, or to build barns.
rite: Our Eparchy of St Mary, Queen of Peace, in the USA and Canada was erected on 4 January 2016. Many of our families live far from Kerala under heavy pressure of work and money, and the words on the ravens are spoken for them too. Tomorrow is Denho: this evening is a good time to recall the day and place of one's own Baptism.
study: Paul says that ministers are there “to equip the saints”. What is my part in “the work of ministry”, and who is equipping me for it?
What worry occupies me most this week? How would I name it to God, and what might “consider the ravens” mean for it?

lead: Denho, a Syriac word for rising or dawning, is the day the Churches of the East have long kept as the manifestation of the Lord at the Jordan. Everything today is water. The Evening Gospel tells of the baptism in Mark's plain words, with the heavens “torn apart” (Mark 1:10). The Old Testament lessons fill the day with wells and rivers: Rebekah at the well, drawing for a stranger and his camels (Genesis 24:10–20); water that fills the valley and looks to Moab as red as blood (2 Kings 3:21–27); Isaiah's joy in drawing “water from the wells of salvation” (Isaiah 12:3). In Acts, disciples who knew only John's baptism are baptised in the name of the Lord Jesus and receive the Holy Spirit (Acts 19:1–7).

The three readings studied here run as one stream. Ezekiel sees a river rising from God's house and bringing dead waters to life. Titus says what that river is for us: “the water of rebirth and renewal by the Holy Spirit”. Matthew shows the source, when the sinless Son goes down into the Jordan and the Father and the Spirit reveal him. The key words are river, appearing and righteousness.

r.h: The river flowing from the Temple
set: Ezekiel was a priest, taken to Babylon with the first group of exiles in 597 BC (1:1–3). He saw in vision the glory of the Lord leave the Temple (chapters 10–11), and the city fell in 587/586 BC. Chapters 40–48, dated about 573 BC (40:1), are his great vision of a restored Temple and land, given to people who have lost both. The glory comes back from the east (43:1–5).

A real Jerusalem has no large river; its water is a modest spring. So the geography here is that of hope. From the threshold of God's house water flows east, down the dry Judean hills and into the Dead Sea, where nothing lives. Eden's river (Genesis 2:10) stands behind the vision, as does the promise of other prophets (Joel 3:18; Zechariah 14:8).
str: vv. 1–2: the source: below the threshold, flowing east.
vv. 3–6: four measurements of a thousand cubits each: ankle, knee, waist, then a river that cannot be crossed.
vv. 7–10: trees on the banks; the sea made fresh; fish and fishermen.
v. 11: the marshes stay salt.
v. 12: trees with monthly fruit and healing leaves.
kw: The usual word for a valley stream, which runs in the rains and dries in summer. This one has no tributaries and yet grows deeper at every stage. Its source is God alone.
Literally “will be healed”. The verb is the common Hebrew word for healing. The NRSV's “fresh” is accurate about salt water, but the Hebrew tells us this is medicine for a dead sea.
“Because the water for them flows from the sanctuary” (v. 12) is the reason for everything. The life of the land is the overflow of God's dwelling.
vv: Then he brought me back to the entrance of the temple; there, water was flowing from below the threshold of the temple
It starts as a trickle, and it comes from below, on the south side of the altar. The place of sacrifice is near the source.
Again he measured one thousand, and it was a river that I could not cross, for the water had risen;
A thousand cubits is roughly half a kilometre. No one has added water, yet it rises. God's gift is measured out by steps, and at the end it is out of the prophet's depth.
Wherever the river goes, every living creature that swarms will live,

“Live” comes again and again in this verse. The lowest and deadest spot on earth becomes a place for spreading nets (v. 10). Christian readers easily think here of the disciples called to fish for people (Matthew 4:19).
But its swamps and marshes will not become fresh; they are to be left for salt.
A small realistic note. Salt was needed for sacrifice and for daily life (Leviticus 2:13). Even in the renewal, God leaves room for what has its own use.
Their fruit will be for food, and their leaves for healing.”
Revelation takes up this line for the river that flows “from the throne of God and of the Lamb” (22:1–2): “the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations”.
ch: On the last day of Tabernacles, Jesus stands up and cries, “Let anyone who is thirsty come to me” (John 7:37), and says that “rivers of living water” will flow (7:38), which John explains as the Spirit. John has already told us that the temple Jesus spoke of was his body (2:21). From his pierced side “blood and water came out” (19:34), and many Fathers saw in this the Church's sacraments. So the Church reads Ezekiel's river as the gift of the Spirit flowing from the risen Christ. The Catechism explains the symbol of water in this way: it signifies the Holy Spirit's action in Baptism (CCC 694), and it lists water as the source of life among the Old Testament signs of Baptism (CCC 1218).

r.h: The water of rebirth and renewal
set: Titus was a Greek Christian and a co-worker of Paul (Galatians 2:1–3), left in Crete to organise the communities (Titus 1:5). The letter is one of the Pastorals, which carry Paul's name. Many modern scholars think they were written by a follower of Paul after his death; others hold that Paul stands behind them. The Church receives them as inspired Scripture.

Most of the letter is about order and conduct. But twice, in the middle of ordinary advice for families and citizens, the author lifts his eyes and gives a short creed (2:11–14; 3:4–7). Both begin with the same verb: God's grace and kindness “appeared”. That is why this reading belongs to Denho.
str: 2:11–14: the grace of God has appeared: what it teaches, and what we wait for.
2:15: Titus is to teach this with authority.
3:1–2: conduct toward rulers and neighbours.
3:3: what we once were.
3:4–7: the second appearing: God saved us through the water of rebirth.
3:8–9: the saying is sure, so do good and avoid useless quarrels.
kw: This is the Greek root of “Epiphany”. It was used for the visit of a god or a ruler. Grace “appeared” in Christ's first coming (2:11; 3:4), and we wait for his “manifestation” at the end (2:13). The Syriac denḥo, the rising of a light, says the same thing.
Literally “being born again”. In the New Testament it occurs elsewhere only at Matthew 19:28, for the renewal of all things. Baptism is that coming renewal, begun in one person.
The NRSV says “water”; the Greek word means a bath or a washing. It is also used in Ephesians 5:26.
Literally “love of humankind”, a word used in Greek praise of good rulers. Here it describes God.
vv: For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all,
“To all”: on the day when the Lord is shown to the world, the reach of the grace is stated at the start.
while we wait for the blessed hope and the manifestation of the glory of our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ.

A note on the translation. One Greek article governs “God and Savior”, and the NRSV takes the phrase of one Person, Jesus Christ. The POC can be read as naming two. The NRSV reading is what most scholars today prefer, and it is a clear statement of Christ's divinity.

But when the goodness and loving kindness of God our Savior appeared, he saved us, not because of any works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his mercy, through the water of rebirth and renewal by the Holy Spirit.
The heart of the reading, set directly against v. 3. Nothing we did began this. Within three verses all three divine Persons appear: God our Savior, the Holy Spirit, and Jesus Christ (v. 6).
This Spirit he poured out on us richly through Jesus Christ our Savior,
“Richly”: the language of the river again. The Spirit is not rationed.
ch: The Catechism takes this verse as a name for Baptism: “the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit” (CCC 1215). It teaches that our justification comes from God's grace, an undeserved help (CCC 1996), and it also speaks of merit, which is itself God's gift (CCC 2006–2011). St Gregory of Nazianzus, in his oration on Baptism, calls this gift the most beautiful and magnificent of God's gifts, and speaks of it under many names, among them enlightenment and grace (Oration 40; CCC 1216; in substance).

r.h: This is my Son, the Beloved
set: John has been preaching in the wilderness and baptising people who confess their sins (3:1–6). He has warned of one more powerful who is coming, and who will baptise “with the Holy Spirit and fire” (3:11). Now the coming One stands in the line. All four Gospels treat this meeting as the start of the public ministry of Jesus. Matthew alone gives the short exchange in vv. 14–15.

The Jordan had its own memory. Israel crossed it to enter the land under Joshua, whose name is the same as that of Jesus (Joshua 3). Elijah crossed it before he was taken up (2 Kings 2:8–11). A new entry into God's promises begins at the same river.
str: v. 13: Jesus comes from Galilee.
v. 14: John tries to stop him.
v. 15: Jesus' answer, and John's consent.
v. 16: he comes up; the heavens open; the Spirit descends.
v. 17: the voice of the Father.
kw: A central word in Matthew (5:6; 6:33). It means doing what God wills, here in his plan to save. By standing with sinners, Jesus does what the Father wants.
Matthew's great verb, used for Scripture and God's plan (5:17). These are the first words Jesus speaks in this Gospel, and they say what his whole life will be.

The word used in the Greek of Genesis 22:2 for Isaac. The voice joins three texts: the royal son of Psalm 2:7, the delight of the Servant of Isaiah 42:1, and perhaps the beloved son of Abraham. At the very start the title holds the King, the Servant and the sacrifice.
vv: John would have prevented him, saying, “I need to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?”
The Greek verb suggests he kept trying to hold him back. John knows who this is, and also knows that his rite is for sinners. The early Church also felt the difficulty, and Matthew answers it here.
But Jesus answered him, “Let it be so now; for it is proper for us in this way to fulfill all righteousness.” Then he consented.
“Now”: for this moment the order is reversed. “Us”: John and Jesus together serve the plan. John's obedience is to do what seemed to him out of order.
And when Jesus had been baptized, just as he came up from the water, suddenly the heavens were opened to him and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and alighting on him.

Isaiah had begged: “O that you would tear open the heavens and come down” (64:1). They are open now. The dove recalls the Spirit over the first waters (Genesis 1:2) and the dove after the flood (Genesis 8:11).
And a voice from heaven said, “This is my Son, the Beloved, with whom I am well pleased.”

In Mark the voice speaks to Jesus: “You are my Son”. In Matthew it speaks to all who stand there: “This is”. It is a public statement, for the day of manifestation. For the first time the Father, the Son and the Spirit are shown together.
ch: The Catechism sees in this baptism Jesus' acceptance of his mission as the suffering Servant, and it calls it a manifestation (CCC 535–537). The Fathers teach in many ways that he did not need purifying, and that he went down to bless the waters. St Ignatius of Antioch, at the start of the second century, already writes that he was born and baptised so that by his suffering he might purify the water (Letter to the Ephesians 18, in substance). St Gregory of Nazianzus preaches on this day that Christ goes down into the water and we go down with him, that we may rise with him (Oration 39, in substance). The Catechism adds that the Spirit who hovered over the first waters descends now on Christ as a prelude of the new creation (CCC 1224).

qa: If Jesus had no sin, why was he baptised?

Not for his own need. He stood with sinners and took their place, as the Servant would (Isaiah 53:12), and he opened the way for us (CCC 536, 1224). The Fathers add that his touch made the waters holy, and not the other way round.
Was John's baptism the same as ours?

No. John's was a sign of repentance that pointed ahead. In Acts 19:1–7, read today, Paul finds disciples who knew only John's baptism; they are then baptised in the name of the Lord Jesus and receive the Holy Spirit. Christian Baptism gives what John's only promised: new birth and the Spirit (CCC 1265).
Does Titus 3:5 mean that good works do not matter?

No. It says that works did not earn our salvation; three verses later it says that believers should “devote themselves to good works” (3:8). Grace comes first, and it bears fruit. Catholics and Lutherans stated their common understanding of this in the Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification (1999).
rite: Denho is a day of obligation in the Malankara Church, with the Holy Qurbono for the people, and in many parishes the waters are solemnly blessed. The Syriac tradition loves to set the Jordan beside Mary's womb: St Ephrem and Mar Jacob of Serugh both speak of the water of Baptism as a womb from which the children of God are born (in substance). When the parish takes home the blessed water, it carries an echo of the river Ezekiel saw. Keep this day as a family feast of Baptism: bring out the baptismal certificate or candle, tell the children who stood for them, and renew the promises together.
study: Ezekiel's river grows from ankle-deep to too deep to cross. How deep have I let the grace of Baptism go into my life?
Titus 3:3 describes what we once were, and 3:4 begins “But”. What is the “but” in my own story?
John resisted and then consented. Where is God now asking me to do something I think is out of order?
If the Father's words are also said over each baptised person, what would change if I really believed them today?

lead: With Denho just kept, the Church turns to praise the one who baptised the Lord. In the Gospel Jesus himself gives the praise: “more than a prophet”, and no one born of woman greater. In the Epistle Paul, a prisoner, describes the same kind of service: to be a servant of a mystery larger than oneself. Both men are great because of what they point to.

r.h: A servant of the gospel
set: The letter speaks in Paul's voice from prison (on authorship, many modern scholars think of a close disciple, others defend Paul himself). Chapter 2 has just said that Gentiles and Jews are made one in Christ. Paul starts a prayer in 3:1, breaks off to explain his own mission (3:2–13), and takes up the prayer again in 3:14. This reading is the first part of that digression.
str: v. 1: the prisoner for the sake of the Gentiles.
vv. 2–4: the commission and the mystery, made known by revelation.
v. 5: hidden in the past, revealed now.
v. 6: what the mystery is.
v. 7: Paul the servant.
kw: In Paul this is not a puzzle or a secret for a few. It means God's plan, once hidden and now openly revealed. Here it has one precise content: the Gentiles belong.
Literally the managing of a household. Paul is a steward: the grace is not his own, it passes through him “for you” (v. 2).
A word for one who waits on others or carries a message. It is the root of our “deacon”. Paul, like John, defines himself by the One he serves.
vv: In former generations this mystery was not made known to humankind, as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit:
“As it has now been”: the Old Testament had already spoken of the nations coming to God (Isaiah 2:2–3), but not of this, that they would be one body with Israel in the Messiah.
that is, the Gentiles have become fellow heirs, members of the same body, and sharers in the promise in Christ Jesus through the gospel.

Three words in the Greek all begin with “together” (syn-): co-heirs, co-bodied, co-sharers. One of them, “of the same body”, may have been coined for this purpose. The Gentiles join in Israel's promises, and they do not replace Israel.
Of this gospel I have become a servant according to the gift of God’s grace that was given me by the working of his power.
Paul was a persecutor, and in the very next verse he calls himself “the very least of all the saints”. The call is a gift, and the power is God's.
ch: The Catechism sees in Israel the root onto which the Gentiles would be grafted (CCC 60; see Romans 11:17–24), and the Second Vatican Council recalls this same image when it speaks of the Church's bond with the Jewish people (Nostra Aetate 4). The readers of this passage are therefore guests of a promise made first to others, and this should make them grateful. Denho, with its manifestation to all the world, is the natural setting for this reading.

r.h: More than a prophet
set: John is in prison (3:20) and has sent messengers to ask, “Are you the one who is to come” (7:19)? Jesus answers them by pointing to his works (7:22–23). As soon as they leave, he turns to the crowd and defends John, in case anyone should think less of him for that question.
str: vv. 24–26: three questions: what did you go out to see?
v. 27: Scripture's answer (Malachi 3:1).
v. 28: the greatest, and the least.
v. 29: the people's response.
kw: Tall canes grew along the Jordan and bent in every wind. The picture means someone with no spine. Some scholars also think of the reed on the early coins of Herod Antipas, the ruler who jailed John, but this remains a suggestion.
The same word as “angel”. Malachi's messenger comes ahead to clear the road for the Lord himself.

Literally “the lesser”. Most interpreters take it of anyone in the Kingdom. Some early writers, St John Chrysostom among them, understood Jesus himself, younger than John and thought less of by people (in substance).
vv: What then did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet.
Other prophets spoke of the One to come; John saw him. He is himself foretold as the messenger, and he could point with his finger at the One the others could only announce.
I tell you, among those born of women no one is greater than John; yet the least in the kingdom of God is greater than he.”

This is not a demotion of John. It compares two moments: he stood at the door, and we have been brought in, by no merit of ours. The second half is praise of grace rather than a judgment on John, who is a saint in the Kingdom.
And all the people who heard this, including the tax collectors, acknowledged the justice of God, because they had been baptized with John’s baptism.
The ones who took John's washing seriously are able to recognise God's work. His baptism prepared hearts, and that was its purpose.
ch: The Catechism calls John the Lord's immediate forerunner (CCC 523) and says that he is “more than a prophet”, in whom the Holy Spirit concludes his speaking through the prophets (CCC 719). Here he receives the Lord's own praise. His greatness lies in the plainness of his own words: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30).

qa: Is John outside the Kingdom?

No. Jesus says elsewhere that all the prophets will be seen in the kingdom of God (Luke 13:28). The verse compares John's place in the history of salvation, before the Cross and Pentecost, with the gift of those who live after them. The Church honours him among the greatest of the saints.
rite: On the day after Denho the Syriac tradition praises the one who baptised the Lord. It is fitting that a man who always stepped aside should receive his feast right after the day of the One he pointed to. Parents, godparents and catechists share John's work: to bring someone to the river and then to let that person go to Christ.
study: “A reed shaken by the wind?” Where is my faith most easily bent by the opinion of those around me?
Paul and John both called themselves servants of something greater. Whom have I helped to come closer to Christ, and was I content to step aside?

lead: In the days of Denho the Church remembers Mar Stephanos, the first to die for Christ. The three readings fit together around him. Acts tells how he died, seeing the heavens open and praying for those who killed him. The few lines from 1 Corinthians, about a household led by a man named Stephanas, show that the word for a deacon's work, service, belongs to every faithful home. In Matthew, Jesus says that those he sends will suffer, so that Stephen's death does not take the Church by surprise.

r.h: I see the heavens opened
set: Stephen is one of the seven chosen to serve the tables of the widows in Jerusalem, “a man full of faith and the Holy Spirit” (Acts 6:5). He also preaches and works signs, and he is brought before the council (6:8–15). Chapter 7 gives his long speech, the longest in Acts, which retells the history of Israel from Abraham to Solomon. It ends with hard words that sound like the prophets of Israel themselves. Today's reading begins at the moment those words strike home.

Stephen is himself a Jew, speaking to his own people, in the name of Jesus, a Jew. Luke describes the anger of those in that room on that day. The passage says nothing against the Jewish people as such (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597).
str: v. 54: the anger of the hearers.
vv. 55–56: Stephen's vision and his words.
vv. 57–58: they rush at him, drag him out and stone him. Saul appears.
vv. 59–60: Stephen's two prayers and his death.
kw: The Greek word for a witness, one who says what he has seen. Paul later speaks of “the blood of your witness Stephen” (Acts 22:20). Because so many witnesses gave their lives, the word came to have the meaning we now give to “martyr”.
Stephen's name means a crown or a wreath, such as a winner received. The Fathers often played on the name: Stephen is crowned by the death he suffered.

The title Jesus uses for himself in the Gospels (see Daniel 7:13–14). Outside the Gospels this is the one place where a person calls Jesus by it. Jesus had told the council that the Son of Man would be seated at God's right hand (Luke 22:69).
vv: “Look,” he said, “I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God!”

Elsewhere the risen Lord is said to be seated at God's right hand (Psalm 110:1). Here he is standing. The text does not explain why. A common reading is that he rises to receive his witness, or to stand up for him before the Father, while an earthly court condemns him.
Then they dragged him out of the city and began to stone him; and the witnesses laid their coats at the feet of a young man named Saul.

Stoning outside the camp was the penalty the Law gave for blasphemy, and the witnesses were to act first (Leviticus 24:14–16; Deuteronomy 17:7). Scholars differ on whether Luke describes a formal sentence or the violence of an angry crowd. Saul appears here for the first time, as a bystander who approves (8:1).
While they were stoning Stephen, he prayed, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.”
On the Cross Jesus prayed, “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23:46). Stephen now says the same prayer to Jesus, which shows what the first Christians believed about him.
Then he knelt down and cried out in a loud voice, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” When he had said this, he died.
This echoes Jesus' own prayer of forgiveness (Luke 23:34). The Greek says literally that he “fell asleep”, the gentle Christian word for the death of the faithful.
ch: The Catechism calls martyrdom “the supreme witness given to the truth of the faith” (CCC 2473) and sees the forgiveness of enemies as a sign that love is stronger than sin, a witness the martyrs give (CCC 2843–2844). St Augustine said that if Stephen had not prayed, the Church would not have had Paul (in substance). The prayer of the dying man bore fruit in the young man holding the coats.

r.h: Devoted to the service of the saints
set: These verses come from the closing lines of the letter, among Paul's travel plans and greetings. A small party from Corinth has reached him at Ephesus (16:8). Paul had baptized the household of Stephanas himself (1:16). In a Church torn by rival groups (1:10–12), he asks the Corinthians to respect those who serve. The likely reason the verses are read today is the likeness of the names, Stephanas and Stephanos, and the word “service”.
str: v. 15: the household of Stephanas, the first in Achaia to believe.
v. 16: put yourselves at the service of such people.
vv. 17–18: Paul's joy at the three visitors; give them recognition.
kw: The word for the first part of a harvest, offered to God. Achaia was the Roman province of southern Greece, with Corinth as its chief city. The POC keeps the image: “ആദ്യഫലങ്ങൾ”.
The word from which “deacon” comes. Here it describes what a whole household has chosen to do for the believers. Nobody appointed them; Paul says literally that they “appointed themselves” to it.
vv: members of the household of Stephanas were the first converts in Achaia, and they have devoted themselves to the service of the saints;
A family can be a ministry. In the New Testament “the saints” are all the baptized, not only those the Church later canonised.
for they refreshed my spirit as well as yours. So give recognition to such persons.
Paul, who has written so strongly in this letter, is honest about needing his friends. Quiet people who refresh the spirits of others deserve honour.
ch: The Second Vatican Council calls the Christian family a domestic Church (Lumen Gentium 11; CCC 1656–1657). The tradition sees in the seven of Acts 6 the beginnings of the diaconate, and Stephen as the first among deacons; the service Paul praises here in one household shows the same spirit in the home.

r.h: I send you prophets, sages, and scribes
set: Jesus is in Jerusalem, in the Temple, in the last days before his Passion. In chapter 23 he speaks a series of “woes” to the scribes and Pharisees. These are prophetic warnings, of a kind Israel's own prophets spoke to their own people (see Isaiah 5:8–23). They are addressed to particular leaders (23:29), and Jesus speaks as a Jew within his people. The verses of today close that speech.
str: v. 34: Jesus sends messengers, and foretells what they will suffer.
v. 35: all innocent blood, from Abel to Zechariah.
v. 36: “this generation”.
kw: The names of Israel's teachers, now used of those Jesus himself sends. Matthew's Gospel knows of Christian scribes (13:52). Note who speaks: “I send you”. In Luke's parallel the sender is “the Wisdom of God” (Luke 11:49).

Blood of the innocent, which in the Bible cries out to God, as Abel's did (Genesis 4:10). The Letter to the Hebrews says that Jesus' blood “speaks a better word than the blood of Abel” (Hebrews 12:24).
vv: some of whom you will kill and crucify, and some you will flog in your synagogues and pursue from town to town,
Jesus has said the same thing to the Twelve (10:17–23). Stephen, stoned in Jerusalem, is the first of these witnesses whose death Acts records.
from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, whom you murdered between the sanctuary and the altar.

Abel is the first innocent man killed in the Bible. A Zechariah son of Jehoiada was stoned in the Temple court (2 Chronicles 24:20–22), and Chronicles stands last in the Hebrew Bible, so the phrase may mean “from the first to the last”. The name “son of Barachiah” belongs to the prophet of Zechariah 1:1; Luke's parallel leaves it out (Luke 11:51), and commentators explain the difference in several ways, with no agreed answer.
ch: The Church firmly reads these words as a prophetic warning, not as a sentence on a people. The Jews “should not be presented as rejected or accursed by God, as if this followed from the Holy Scriptures” (Nostra Aetate 4), and the Catechism refuses to lay the guilt of Christ's death on Jews as a whole (CCC 597–598). The Catechism adds that all sinners were the authors of Christ's Passion (CCC 598). The same warning stands over any Christian who silences a messenger of God.

qa: Do words like “upon you may come all the righteous blood” mean that the Jewish people carry a curse?

No. The Church teaches the opposite (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597). Jesus speaks in the manner of Israel's prophets to the leaders before him. Stephen himself, dying at the hands of an angry crowd, prays that the sin not be held against them; Christians can do no less.
rite: The Syriac Churches honour Mar Stephanos in the days of Denho, close to the Lord's Baptism. What was seen at the Jordan, the open heavens, Stephen sees at his death. A deacon serving at the Holy Qurbono stands in his line: he serves at the altar and among the people, and the two belong together.
study: Stephen's last prayer was for those who were killing him. Who is the person I find it hardest to pray for?
Who in my parish quietly “refreshes the spirit” of others, as Stephanas did, and how could I honour that person?
What does it cost today to be a witness to Christ where I live?

lead: Both readings ask what it means to belong to God. Paul insists that God stays faithful to Israel even when people fail, for his word does not depend on us. In Mark, Jesus warns that outward observance means little when the heart is far away. God's faithfulness and our sincerity are the two sides of today's lesson, and both are for Christians to hear first.

r.h: The faithfulness of God
set: Paul has just said that true circumcision is a matter of the heart (2:28–29). An objection follows at once: then what is the use of being a Jew? He answers in the manner of a teacher arguing with an imagined questioner, a common style of the ancient schools. Quick questions and short answers follow. The argument is dense here, and Paul takes it up fully in chapters 9–11.
str: vv. 1–2: what advantage has the Jew? Much: God's words were entrusted to them.
vv. 3–4: human unfaithfulness cannot cancel God's faithfulness.
vv. 5–6: is God then unjust to judge? By no means.
vv. 7–8: a false conclusion, “let us do evil so that good may come”, is rejected.
kw: God's own spoken words, here above all his promises and the Scriptures. Paul calls this a treasure, and Christians received these same Scriptures from Israel.
Pistis usually means faith, but of God it means fidelity, the fact that he can be relied on. Paul sets it against apistia, faithlessness, in the same verse.
Literally “may it not be”. This strong refusal is one of Paul's habits in Romans, and it stands twice in today's short passage (vv. 4, 6).
vv: Much, in every way. For in the first place the Jews were entrusted with the oracles of God.
After the sharp words of chapter 2, Paul does not say “none”. He says “much”. He will later list what belongs to Israel (9:4–5).
What if some were unfaithful? Will their faithlessness nullify the faithfulness of God?
Note the word “some”. The heart of the verse is about God: what he has promised, he does not take back. Paul later says it plainly: “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (11:29).
And why not say (as some people slander us by saying that we say), “Let us do evil so that good may come”?
Some people twisted Paul's teaching on grace into this, and he rejects it. Grace is never a licence for sin.
ch: The Council, following Paul, teaches that God holds the Jews most dear for the sake of their fathers, and that he does not repent of the gifts he makes or the calls he issues (Nostra Aetate 4). The Catechism says that the Old Covenant has never been revoked (CCC 121) and gives Romans 9:4–5 when it speaks of the Jewish people (CCC 839). Verse 8 has also become a rule of Christian morals: one may never do evil so that good may result from it (CCC 1756, 1789).

r.h: Their hearts are far from me
set: Jesus has been healing crowds around Gennesaret (6:53–56). Teachers come from Jerusalem and see some of his disciples eating without the ritual washing of hands. This was about religious purity, not hygiene. Many scholars think that the Pharisees wished to bring the holiness that the Law asked of priests (Exodus 30:17–21) into ordinary homes and meals. They were devout people who took God seriously, which is why the debate matters.
Verses 3–4 are an aside by Mark, who seems to be writing for readers who do not know these customs. “All the Jews” is his own summary; many scholars think that practice varied.
str: vv. 1–2: the visitors see what the disciples do.
vv. 3–4: Mark explains the custom.
v. 5: the question.
vv. 6–7: Jesus answers from Isaiah 29:13.
v. 8: the charge.
kw: Koinos means “common”, the opposite of “set apart” for God. Mark explains the word for his readers: “that is, without washing them”.
The teachings handed down alongside the written Law. The word paradosis is neutral in itself; Paul uses the word and its verb for the teaching he hands on to the Church (1 Corinthians 11:2, 23).
In Greek, first of all a stage actor who speaks behind a mask. Here it means a person whose outward piety does not match the heart.
vv: “Why do your disciples not live according to the tradition of the elders, but eat with defiled hands?”
The question is about how a disciple should live. It is a real question among people who care about the Law.
‘This people honors me with their lips, but their hearts are far from me;
Jesus quotes Israel's own prophet, who said this to his own people. The word is for every worshipper. Anyone can say all the right prayers with a distant heart.
You abandon the commandment of God and hold to human tradition.”
The contrast is between God's command and what people have added. In the next verses, beyond today's reading, Jesus gives an example: a custom used to avoid caring for one's parents (7:9–13).
ch: The Catechism distinguishes the Apostolic Tradition, which comes from the Lord, from the many theological, disciplinary, liturgical and devotional traditions that grow in local Churches and may be changed under the guidance of the Magisterium (CCC 83). It also teaches that Jesus takes us to the heart, from which comes what truly defiles (CCC 582). Mark's scene is about the heart, not a judgment on Jewish piety; Jesus was himself a faithful Jew (CCC 577–582).

qa: If Jesus criticises tradition, why do we keep so many traditions?

Jesus does not reject tradition as such. He rejects any human custom that takes the place of God's command. Apostolic Tradition hands on the faith itself (CCC 81–83). Our liturgical customs are precious when they lead the heart to God, and they turn empty when only the lips take part.
study: When is my prayer most in danger of being “lips” without “heart”, and what helps me at those times?
God stays faithful even when people fail. Where do I need to hear that today?

lead: On this first Sunday after Denho, the light that shone at the Jordan begins to move among people, and it calls them by name. God calls in the middle of ordinary work. Moses is keeping his father-in-law's sheep when the bush burns. Simon and Andrew are casting a net and James and John are mending theirs when Jesus walks by. The Evening Gospel (Mark 1:14–20) has already told that same call the night before. Jacob the shepherd (Genesis 30:25–43) shows God blessing the work of a man's hands, Psalm 147:1–11 praises the Lord who heals the brokenhearted, and Isaiah 49:7–13 tells of a God who comforts his people.

The readings treated below are the three that carry the day. In Exodus, God calls Moses and reveals his name. In Ephesians, Paul looks behind every call, to the choice God made “before the foundation of the world”. In Matthew, Jesus calls the first disciples, and Acts 2:37–47 shows where that call leads: to a community gathered for teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread and prayer. The key words are call, name and follow.

r.h: The bush that was not consumed
set: Moses, raised in Pharaoh's house, has fled Egypt after killing an Egyptian (Exodus 2:11–15). He has settled in Midian, married and become a shepherd. “After a long time” the king of Egypt dies, the Israelites cry out, and God hears them and remembers his covenant (2:23–25). The reader knows that God is about to act; Moses, out with the flock, does not.
Horeb is another name for the mountain elsewhere called Sinai. The place where God calls Moses is the place to which he will one day bring the whole people (v. 12).
str: vv. 1–3: the flock, the mountain, the strange sight.
vv. 4–6: God calls, “Moses, Moses!”, and names himself the God of the fathers.
vv. 7–10: God has seen and heard, and he sends Moses.
vv. 11–12: “Who am I?” “I will be with you.”
vv. 13–15: “What is his name?” The name is given.

¶ The pattern is one that recurs in the Bible's stories of a call: God comes, gives a task, the person objects, God promises to be with him, and a sign is given (compare Gideon, Judges 6; Jeremiah 1).
kw: A thorny desert shrub. The word is rare, and it sounds like “Sinai”, as many commentators note. God chooses a plain thorn bush, and it is not consumed.

From the verb “to be”. The Hebrew tense can also mean “I will be who I will be”. The name is a promise and also a mystery: God is the One who is, and he does not hand himself over to be controlled. The Greek Old Testament reads “I am the One who is”.

The four letters of the divine name, linked here with the verb “to be”. Out of reverence the people of Israel do not pronounce it, and read “Adonai”, Lord, in its place. The Greek Old Testament and the New Testament follow with Kyrios, and the NRSV prints “the Lord” (CCC 209).
vv: he looked, and the bush was blazing, yet it was not consumed.

Fire in the Bible often marks God's presence (Exodus 19:18). God's fire does not destroy what it fills. The text says “the angel of the Lord” appeared, and then that “the Lord” and “God” spoke: the angel is God's own presence made visible.
Then he said, “Come no closer! Remove the sandals from your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground.”
God comes near, and yet he says, “Come no closer”. Holiness is the distance within the nearness. Moses's working day, on a desert hill, has become sacred ground.
“I have observed the misery of my people who are in Egypt; I have heard their cry on account of their taskmasters. Indeed, I know their sufferings,
The verbs pile up: observed, heard, know, and next, “I have come down” (v. 8). This God is not far above human pain. Note “my people”, said while they are still slaves.
But Moses said to God, “Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh,
Moses's question about himself gets an answer about God.
He said, “I will be with you;

In Hebrew “I will be” is ’ehyeh, the same word as in v. 14. So the name God gives in v. 14 is first of all a promise of company. Matthew's Gospel will end on the same note: “I am with you always” (Matthew 28:20).
“I am who I am” … “Thus you shall say to the Israelites, ‘I am has sent me to you.’”
The Catechism says that this is a name both revealed and, in a way, refused: God tells who he is, and remains the hidden God (CCC 206).
ch: The Catechism treats this passage at length: God calls Moses from the bush, reveals himself as the living God who is faithful to the fathers, and sends him (CCC 204–209). The event remains “one of the primordial images of prayer” for Jews and Christians alike (CCC 2575). Jesus himself reads the bush for the resurrection: the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob “is God not of the dead, but of the living” (Matthew 22:32).
