St Gregory of Nyssa, in his Life of Moses, sees in the bush burning without being consumed a figure of the Virgin who gave birth and was not harmed; and he reads the sandals as what is dead and earthly, which a person lays aside to stand in the light (in substance). The Malankara calendar remembers him tomorrow, 11 January.

r.h: Chosen in Christ before the foundation of the world
set: The letter opens with a hymn of blessing in the form familiar from Jewish prayer: “Blessed be God, who...”. In Greek, vv. 3–14 are one very long sentence that rolls forward like praise and does not stop to draw breath.

The letter bears Paul's name, and the Church has always received it as Scripture. Many scholars think a disciple wrote it in Paul's name after his death, while others hold that Paul is the author. The doubt does not touch its authority. Some of the oldest manuscripts lack the words “in Ephesus” in v. 1, and so many think the letter was meant to go round several Churches.
str: v. 3: the blessing.
vv. 4–6: the Father has chosen us and destined us to be his children.
vv. 7–12: in the Son, redemption, the plan revealed, and an inheritance.
vv. 13–14: the Holy Spirit is the seal and the pledge.
¶ The Trinity gives the outline, and a refrain marks each part: “to the praise of his glory” (vv. 6, 12, 14, with small differences).
kw: The same root twice in v. 3. God has blessed us, and so we bless God. This is the movement of Christian prayer (CCC 2626–2627).
This phrase, with “in him” and “in the Beloved”, runs through the whole passage. Everything God gives us, he gives by placing us in his Son.
A term from Greek and Roman law, by which a person was made a son with full rights of inheritance. We become by grace what Christ is by nature.
To sum up under one head (v. 10). St Irenaeus built his teaching of recapitulation on this word: Christ takes up all things and restores them in himself.
A word from commerce for the first payment that guarantees the rest. The POC's “അച്ചാരം” is a very good Malayalam match. The Spirit is the advance on what is still to come.
vv: just as he chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world to be holy and blameless before him in love.
God's choice is older than the world, and its purpose is holiness. Before we did anything, we were already loved. Matthew's fishermen did not know it, but their call on the shore began here.
He destined us for adoption as his children through Jesus Christ,
“Destined” is a word of love, not of fate. In this passage it is always for something good, adoption and praise.
In him we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses,
Redemption is the word for buying back a slave or a captive. It recalls the Exodus, Israel brought out of slavery.
as a plan for the fullness of time, to gather up all things in him, things in heaven and things on earth.
Christ is the goal not only of the Church but of creation. Nothing good in heaven or on earth is left outside.
were marked with the seal of the promised Holy Spirit;
A seal showed ownership and protected what it marked. The Catechism connects this word with Baptism and Chrismation (CCC 1295–1296).
ch: The Catechism opens its treatment of the liturgy with these very verses (CCC 1077–1079): the liturgy is the Father's blessing received and returned. It also applies the passage to Mary, blessed “in Christ with every spiritual blessing” and chosen before the world began (CCC 492). St Irenaeus, in Against Heresies, makes the gathering up of all things in Christ a key to the whole of salvation (in substance).

r.h: Follow me
set: Jesus has been baptized (3:13–17) and tempted (4:1–11). John's arrest, told later in full (14:3–12), is the signal. Jesus leaves Nazareth and moves to Capernaum, a fishing town on the north-west shore of the lake.

Zebulun and Naphtali were the northern tribal lands that Assyria took in the eighth century before Christ (2 Kings 15:29). Galilee had a mixed population, and Isaiah called it “Galilee of the nations” (Isaiah 9:1). That is the very place where Isaiah promised light, and so that is where Matthew shows the light beginning.
str: vv. 12–16: Jesus settles in Galilee, and Isaiah 9:1–2 is fulfilled.
v. 17: his first preaching.
vv. 18–20: Simon and Andrew.
vv. 21–22: James and John.
kw: Literally “change your mind”: a turning of the whole person. In the Hebrew Scriptures the matching idea is shuv, “to return” to God. John preached the same words (3:2).
Matthew's usual phrase. “Heaven” is a reverent Jewish way of saying “God”. It means God's reign drawing near in Jesus, not a place we go to only after death.
Literally “come behind me”. A disciple walks behind his teacher. Pupils in that world usually sought out a teacher; here the teacher goes out and calls.
The word stands in both scenes (vv. 20, 22). Matthew tells no long inner debate. The story is shaped to show that the word of Jesus has authority.
vv: the people who sat in darkness have seen a great light, and for those who sat in the region and shadow of death light has dawned.
In the season of Denho this verse is at home, for the name of the season speaks of light rising. The first to see it are those farthest from the centre.
From that time Jesus began to proclaim, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has come near.”
The whole preaching of Jesus is here in seed. The order matters: the Kingdom comes near first, and repentance is the response.
And he said to them, “Follow me, and I will make you fish for people.”

The call has a promise inside it: “I will make you”. Jesus uses their own trade to describe their new work. Jeremiah spoke of God sending “many fishermen” (Jeremiah 16:16); here the fishing is for rescue.
Immediately they left their nets and followed him.
Nets were their living. Mark adds that the sons of Zebedee left their father “with the hired men” (Mark 1:20), so they were not destitute, and they had something to leave.
Immediately they left the boat and their father, and followed him.
This is the second and harder step: first the nets, now the family and the family business. Nothing here tells us to neglect our parents (compare 15:4–6); the call means that Jesus now comes first.
ch: The Catechism sees this preaching as the coming of the Kingdom (CCC 541) and the call to conversion as the first work of grace (CCC 1427, 1989). St Gregory the Great asks what Peter and Andrew really left, having only a few nets, and answers that one leaves much who keeps nothing for himself (in substance). Every baptized person is called in this way, each in a different state of life, and not all are asked to leave home (CCC 1533, 2013).

qa: What does God's name “I am who I am” mean?

It says that God is the One who truly is, the source of all being, and that he will be with his people. He does not give a label that people can use to control him. The Catechism says the name both reveals and keeps God's mystery (CCC 206, 213). Jesus' own “I am” sayings in John's Gospel (for example John 8:58) stand in this light.
Does “destined” in Ephesians mean that God decides beforehand who goes to heaven and who to hell?
No. God “predestines no one to go to hell” (CCC 1037). Ephesians speaks of being destined for adoption and holiness. In God's eternal plan, each person's response in freedom is included (CCC 600).
Did the fishermen really leave everything at once, without knowing Jesus?

Matthew tells the story in the shortest form, to show the power of Jesus' word. John's Gospel tells of an earlier meeting of Andrew and Peter with Jesus near the Jordan (John 1:35–42), and many commentators think the two accounts can stand together. Either way, the point stands: the disciple's life begins with Jesus' call.
rite: In the Malankara tradition the liturgical day begins with the evening, so the first disciples were already heard from Mark on Saturday night before Matthew tells of them at the morning Qurbono. Denho means the rising or dawning of light, and it has its own Sundays: the light of the Jordan now comes to the shore of Galilee. In many of our churches, footwear is left at the door, and the words to Moses can be remembered there: “the place on which you are standing is holy ground.” At the Holy Qurbono the call is renewed. For an hour we leave our nets behind, and we come to the One who calls us by name, as the first community did in the breaking of bread (Acts 2:42).
study: God called Moses, and Jesus called the fishermen, in the middle of ordinary work. What might God be saying to me in the place where I work?
Moses asked, “Who am I?”, and God answered, “I will be with you.” Which task do I fear, and how would that answer change it?
Ephesians says that I was chosen before the foundation of the world. How does that change the way I see myself and others?
What are my “nets”, the good things that might keep me from following more closely?

lead: Paul begins with a blessing that comes out of real suffering: the God of all consolation comforts us so that we can comfort others. The Gospel speaks of a gift with no limit: the Spirit is given “without measure”. Consolation that passes from person to person, and a Spirit that never runs out, make a fitting pair for the memory of Mar Gregorios of Nyssa, who taught that the soul never stops growing toward God.

r.h: The God of all consolation
set: Paul's relations with the Corinthians have been painful. He has written them a letter “with many tears” (2:4), and has been waiting anxiously for news. His letters usually open with a thanksgiving; here he opens with a blessing of God, in the form of Jewish prayer. He writes as a man who has lately been close to death.
str: vv. 3–4: God consoles us so that we can console others.
vv. 5–7: suffering and consolation are shared between Paul and the Church.
vv. 8–9: the affliction in Asia, and what it taught him.
vv. 10–11: God will rescue again, and your prayers help.
kw: Comfort that also strengthens, from a word meaning to call someone to one's side. The word and its verb come again and again in these verses, as the English “console” and “consolation” show. John's Gospel calls the Holy Spirit by a related name, the Paraclete (John 14:16).
Literally pressure, being pressed or crushed. Paul uses the same picture in v. 8: “crushed”.
An official verdict. What happened to Paul in the Roman province of Asia, whose chief city was Ephesus, he does not say, and scholars can only guess.
vv: Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and the God of all consolation,
“Father of mercies” is a phrase at home in Jewish prayer. A man who has just despaired of life begins by praising God.
who consoles us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to console those who are in any affliction
Consolation is not for keeping. A wound that God has healed can become a way of helping others. Those who have suffered often know what to say, and when to say nothing.
so that we would rely not on ourselves but on God who raises the dead.
Paul sees a purpose in the worst of it. When every human support is gone, only the God of the Resurrection remains.
as you also join in helping us by your prayers,
The great apostle says that he needs the prayers of the Church he has quarrelled with. Prayer binds the Church together even when relations are hard.
ch: The Catechism says that blessing is the basic movement of Christian prayer (CCC 2626) and points to Paul's own life as an example of intercession in the first Christian communities (CCC 2636). It teaches that suffering united with Christ becomes a sharing in his saving work (CCC 1521). The Church's anointing of the sick is one sign that God's consolation comes through the hands of others.

r.h: He gives the Spirit without measure
set: John the Baptist has just said of Jesus, “He must increase, but I must decrease” (3:30). The verses that follow could be the Baptist still speaking, or the evangelist reflecting on the scene. The Greek has no quotation marks, and commentators differ. Either way, they sum up the whole of chapter 3, with its themes of being born from above, testimony and life.
str: v. 31: the one from above and the one from the earth.
vv. 32–33: his testimony, and those who accept it.
vv. 34–35: God's words, the Spirit, and all things in the Son's hands.
v. 36: the choice between life and wrath.
kw: The same word Jesus used to Nicodemus (3:3, 7), where it also means “again”. The one who comes from above is the one who gives birth from above.

Literally “not from a measure”, as one measures out grain. The Greek of v. 34 does not state the subject: God gives the Spirit to the Son, or the Son gives the Spirit to us. The POC names God as the giver: “ദൈവം അളന്നല്ല ആത്മാവിനെ കൊടുക്കുന്നത്”.
Verse 33 uses the word for setting one's seal on a document: whoever accepts the testimony puts his own signature to the truth of God.
vv: Whoever has accepted his testimony has certified this, that God is true.
Faith is not a guess. It is a personal signature, a word of trust in the God who speaks.
He whom God has sent speaks the words of God, for he gives the Spirit without measure.
The prophets each received a gift for a task. Jesus has the Spirit in fullness, and from that fullness he gives.
Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever disobeys the Son will not see life, but must endure God’s wrath.

In John eternal life begins now, as a present gift: “has”. God's “wrath” is not a fit of temper; it describes the state of one who refuses life. The verse is a warning given so that a person may turn.
ch: The Catechism quotes this Gospel when it teaches that from the moment of his conception the humanity of Christ is filled with the Holy Spirit, for God gives him the Spirit without measure (CCC 504). It adds that from his fullness we have all received. It also cites this passage when it speaks of the need of faith for salvation (CCC 161).

rite: Mar Gregorios of Nyssa (fourth century) was the younger brother of Mar Baselios, and one of the great Cappadocian Fathers. As a bishop he defended the faith of Nicaea on the Trinity. In his Life of Moses he taught that the soul, drawn on by God who has no limit, never reaches an end of its growth, and that each discovery opens a greater longing (in substance). A Spirit given “without measure” is the Gospel root of that teaching.
study: Whom has God placed near me who needs the consolation I once received?
Where has God's gift to me become smaller only because my longing has become smaller?

lead: In the season of Denho, Paul tells us where to look for God's glory: “in the face of Jesus Christ”. In the Gospel that same face turns to a man with a withered hand, on the sabbath, in a synagogue. The glory of God and care for a suffering human being are not two subjects. Mar Thevodosios, remembered today, joined the two in his monastic life.

r.h: The light in the face of Christ
set: In 2:14–7:4 Paul defends his ministry to a Church that doubts him. He has just compared the new covenant with the old, using the veil on Moses' face (3:12–18). Now he carries the picture on: unveiled truth, the light of the gospel, and a face that shines.
str: vv. 1–2: no cunning; the open statement of the truth.
vv. 3–4: why some do not see.
vv. 5–6: not ourselves, but Christ; the light of creation shines again.
kw: Christ is “the image of God” (v. 4; see Colossians 1:15). The first human beings were made in God's image (Genesis 1:27); Christ is that image in its fullness.
In Greek, as with the Hebrew kābôd, the weight and radiance of God's presence. Moses saw it and his face shone (Exodus 34:29–35). Paul's readers see it in Christ.
Paul's word for himself in v. 5. It is the opposite of a religious leader who promotes himself.
vv: We have renounced the shameful things that one hides;
A word for preachers and teachers. There is no trick in the gospel, nor any need to bend the word to win people.
In their case the god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelievers,

“The god of this world” is the Evil One (compare John 12:31), and Paul is not speaking of a second god. He gives no list of who these people are. The verse teaches that the failure to see can have a cause greater than a person's own mind.
For we do not proclaim ourselves; we proclaim Jesus Christ as Lord and ourselves as your slaves for Jesus’ sake.
“Jesus is Lord” is the Church's oldest creed (see 1 Corinthians 12:3).
it is the God who said, “Let light shine out of darkness,” who has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.
Paul recalls Genesis 1:3. Baptism and faith are a new creation, the first day over again. Many scholars also hear an echo of Paul's own experience on the road to Damascus (Acts 9:3).
ch: The Catechism begins its teaching on human dignity from Christ, the image of the invisible God, in whom we see who we are (CCC 1701, citing this verse). It describes the ministry of the Church as service: those who are ordained are “slaves of Christ”, in the image of him who freely took the form of a slave for us (CCC 876).

r.h: It is lawful to do good on the sabbath
set: This is the second sabbath dispute in a row. Just before this the disciples plucked grain (12:1–8). The sabbath was a great gift to Israel, a day of rest and joy kept by God's command (Exodus 20:8–11). Jewish teachers of the time discussed in earnest what it allowed, and later rabbinic law held that saving a life overrides the sabbath (Mishnah Yoma 8:6). So this is a debate within Judaism, among people who loved the sabbath, Jesus among them.
str: vv. 9–10: the synagogue, the man and the question.
vv. 11–12: the sheep in the pit, and Jesus' teaching.
v. 13: the healing.
v. 14: some plan against him.
kw: The word that links both sabbath stories (12:2, 10, 12). The question is what God's Law really wants.
Literally “dried up”. The hand cannot work, and for a labouring man that may mean no bread.
so that they might accuse him
The question is asked as a test, and the man himself seems to matter little to those who ask it. Any religious person can fall into this danger.
vv: “Suppose one of you has only one sheep and it falls into a pit on the sabbath; will you not lay hold of it and lift it out?

Jesus appeals to the plain sense of his hearers. Not everyone agreed: the Qumran community's Damascus Document forbids lifting an animal from a pit on the sabbath, which shows that such cases were really discussed.
How much more valuable is a human being than a sheep! So it is lawful to do good on the sabbath.”
Jesus changes the question from “what may I not do?” to “what good can I do?”.
Then he said to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” He stretched it out, and it was restored, as sound as the other.

He does no work with his hands, not even a touch. A word, and the man's obedience. St Jerome records that a Gospel used by Jewish Christians of his time called this man a mason who begged for healing so that he need not beg for bread (in substance).
But the Pharisees went out and conspired against him, how to destroy him.
Matthew speaks of those present on that day, not of all Pharisees and certainly not of the Jewish people. Nicodemus, himself a Pharisee, became a disciple in secret (CCC 595).
ch: The Catechism says that Jesus never fails to respect the holiness of the sabbath, gives it its authentic interpretation, and declares it a day for doing good (CCC 2173). The Christian Sunday carries on that spirit: works of mercy and care for the sick and the poor are part of keeping it (CCC 2184–2186). On the disputes of Jesus with some teachers of the Law, the Church warns against blaming the Jewish people (CCC 595–597).

rite: Today we remember Mar Thevodosios the Abbot, who built a great monastery near Bethlehem, with houses beside it for the sick, the old and the poor. Prayer and care for the suffering stood side by side, just as they do in today's readings. The man with the withered hand was healed in a house of prayer.
study: Whose face has shown me something of the glory of God?
Sunday is coming. What good could I do on the Lord's day for someone who cannot return it?

lead: Today's readings take in two directions of the heart. Paul asks that prayer be made “for everyone”, since God “desires everyone to be saved”. Jesus says, “Do not judge.” The two go well together. A person cannot go on condemning those for whom he is truly praying.

r.h: Prayer for everyone; one mediator
set: The letter is addressed to Timothy, left at Ephesus to care for the Church there (1:3). It gives instructions for Church life, and prayer comes first. It bears Paul's name. Many scholars think a later disciple wrote the Pastoral Letters in his name, while others hold that Paul is the author in some way. The Church reads it as inspired Scripture in either case.

The kings and rulers in view were not Christians. The Church was small, and could suffer at their hands. Even so she is told to pray for them, as Jeremiah had told the exiles to pray for the city of their exile (Jeremiah 29:7).
str: vv. 1–2: pray for everyone, and for those in authority.
vv. 3–4: God wants everyone to be saved.
vv. 5–6: one God, one mediator, a ransom for all.
v. 7: Paul's own mission to the Gentiles.
kw: Four words that together cover the whole of prayer. The text hardly means four separate kinds. The last is the word from which “Eucharist” comes.
One who stands between two parties to bring them together. Christ can do this because he is God and also “himself human”.
A strengthened form of lytron, the price of release, with an echo of Jesus' own word: “to give his life a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45).
vv: First of all, then, I urge that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for everyone,
The word “everyone” or “all” keeps returning in the passage (vv. 1, 2, 4, 6). The Church's prayer is meant to be as wide as God's will to save.
who desires everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.
The verse sets out God's own desire. Truth and salvation go together here.
For there is one God; there is also one mediator between God and humankind, Christ Jesus, himself human,
Note the stress on his humanity. The one who brings us to God has walked in our condition.
ch: The Catechism quotes these verses to show that God wills the salvation of all and that the Church is sent because of it (CCC 74, 851). It also applies them to our duty of prayer for those in authority (CCC 2240), and to Christ's unique mediation in his sacrifice (CCC 618). The Holy Qurbono obeys this command in the intercessions it makes for the whole Church and the world.

r.h: Do not judge
set: We are near the end of the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5–7). Jesus has spoken of the Law, of prayer and of trust in the Father. He now turns to the way disciples treat one another. Luke gives a related saying in his Sermon on the Plain (Luke 6:37–42).
str: vv. 1–2: do not judge, and why.
vv. 3–5: the speck and the log.
v. 6: what is holy and the dogs: a saying that seems to stand alone, on discernment.
kw: It can mean to discern, or to condemn. Here it means condemning a person. Jesus cannot be forbidding all moral discernment, since a few verses later he tells disciples to know false prophets by their fruits (7:15–16).
A chip of wood against a beam. The picture is deliberately funny, and Jesus' hearers may well have smiled. A carpenter's son knows both.
The same word as for the actor behind a mask. This time it is said to every disciple who corrects others without looking at himself.
vv: “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged.
The passive “be judged” is a reverent way of saying “God will judge you”. The final verdict on a person belongs to God.
Why do you see the speck in your neighbor’s eye, but do not notice the log in your own eye?
The fault that we most easily see in others is often our own.
You hypocrite, first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your neighbor’s eye.
Jesus does not say the speck should stay. Correction is a work of love (compare 18:15), but it can only be done after looking at oneself first, and with clear sight.
“Do not give what is holy to dogs; and do not throw your pearls before swine,

The verse is hard. It does not license calling people animals. It asks for care with holy things. The Didache, a very early Christian writing, applies it to the Eucharist, which is for the baptized (Didache 9:5).
ch: The Catechism warns against rash judgment, and asks everyone to put the most favourable interpretation on another's words and actions (CCC 2477–2478). It distinguishes the act from the person: we may judge that an act is grave, but we must entrust the judgment of persons to the justice and mercy of God (CCC 1861). St Augustine, on this very passage, says that deeds whose motive is uncertain should be taken in the better sense (in substance).

qa: “One mediator”: then why do we ask Mary and the saints to pray for us?

Their prayer does not compete with Christ's mediation; it depends entirely on it. The Council teaches that Mary's role “in no way obscures or diminishes this unique mediation of Christ, but rather shows its power” (Lumen Gentium 60; CCC 970). Paul himself, in this very passage, asks Christians to pray for one another. All such prayer is a sharing in the one prayer of Christ (CCC 2634–2635).
study: For whom have I stopped praying because I have already judged them?
Which “log” do I need to look at before speaking to anyone about a “speck”?

lead: Paul gives the heart of the Gospel: all have sinned, and all are justified by God's grace as a gift. Jesus tells his friends not to fear those who can kill only the body, because even the hairs of their heads are counted. Those who know they are held by grace are able to be fearless. Today's martyrs, the monks of Sinai and St Devasahayam of Travancore, lived that out.

r.h: Justified by his grace as a gift
set: From 1:18 to 3:20 Paul has shown that Jews and Gentiles alike stand in need of God's mercy. Now he turns with “But now”. Many consider these few verses to be the heart of the letter. The sentences are dense and full of words from the law court, the slave market and the Temple.
str: vv. 21–22a: God's righteousness is revealed, attested by the Law and the prophets, through faith.
vv. 22b–23: there is no distinction; all have sinned.
v. 24: justified by grace, through redemption.
vv. 25–26: Christ's blood shows that God is righteous and makes righteous.
kw: Not only a quality God has, but his saving faithfulness in action, by which he makes people right with himself. The same phrase is found in 1:17. Compare Isaiah 51:5–6.
This is the word that excludes payment. No one can buy or earn this.

The Greek Old Testament uses this word for the mercy seat on the ark, sprinkled with blood on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:14–15; compare Hebrews 9:5). Paul may mean that Christ is the place where God and sinners meet in mercy.
vv: But now, apart from law, the righteousness of God has been disclosed, and is attested by the law and the prophets,
“Apart from law” and “attested by the law” stand in one verse. The Law of Israel is not despised; it bears witness (see 3:31).
the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe.

A note on the Greek: The phrase pistis Iēsou Christou can mean “faith in Jesus Christ” or “the faith (faithfulness) of Jesus Christ”; the NRSV notes the second in its margin. Scholars discuss it to this day. Both are true: Christ's fidelity saves, and we receive it by faith.
since all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God;

Paul's “all” leaves no room for pride, whatever one's origin. The Church, for her part, confesses Mary preserved by a singular grace from her first moment, which is itself a gift of that same redemption (CCC 491–492).
they are now justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus,
Three words explain each other: grace, gift, redemption. Nothing we do comes first.
ch: The Catechism quotes these verses in full to teach that justification is merited by Christ's Passion and given through Baptism (CCC 1987–1992), and it links v. 25 with the mercy seat (CCC 433). The Council of Trent also taught that nothing which comes before justification, whether faith or works, merits the grace of justification. In 1999 Catholics and Lutherans signed a Joint Declaration confessing together that “by grace alone” we are accepted by God, and not because of any merit of ours. Grace then bears fruit in love (Galatians 5:6; CCC 2008–2011).

r.h: Do not fear those who kill the body
set: A crowd of thousands has gathered, and Jesus speaks “first to his disciples” (12:1). He is on his way to Jerusalem (9:51), and he knows what awaits him and them. His words are close to those sent out to the Twelve in Matthew (Matthew 10:28–31).
str: v. 4: do not fear those who can kill only the body.
v. 5: fear the one who has final authority.
vv. 6–7: sparrows and hairs: do not be afraid.
kw: A rare word from Jesus in the first three Gospels. He says these hard words as a friend. Compare John 15:15.
From the Hebrew for the Valley of Hinnom, south of Jerusalem, a place of evil memory (Jeremiah 7:31). In the New Testament it is the name of final loss (CCC 1034).
The cheapest food in the market. Matthew has two for a penny (Matthew 10:29); Luke has five for two pennies, as if the fifth had no price at all. That very bird is not forgotten.
vv: “I tell you, my friends, do not fear those who kill the body, and after that can do nothing more.
Human power stops at death. This is the courage of every martyr.
fear him who, after he has killed, has authority to cast into hell.
Most commentators take this to mean God, not the devil, since only God has that authority. It is the holy fear of the Bible, the fear of losing him. The next verses show that it is not terror.
Are not five sparrows sold for two pennies? Yet not one of them is forgotten in God’s sight.
The argument runs from small to great, as Jesus so often does. God's care reaches even what the market values least.
But even the hairs of your head are all counted. Do not be afraid; you are of more value than many sparrows.
Being counted does not mean being spared: the martyrs' lives were counted, and still they died. The promise is that nothing of them was lost to God.
ch: The Catechism teaches God's providence from words like these (CCC 302–305), and calls martyrdom the supreme witness to the truth of the faith (CCC 2473). The early Christians kept the records of the martyrs with great care, as “the archives of truth written in letters of blood” (CCC 2474). Holy fear of God is itself a gift of the Holy Spirit (CCC 1831).

qa: Do Catholics believe in justification by faith or by works?

We are justified by God's grace, received in faith and Baptism; no work of ours earns it (CCC 1992, 2010). Works done in love are the fruit of that grace, and by it they have real value (CCC 2008–2011). Catholics and Lutherans stated this common understanding in their Joint Declaration of 1999.
rite: The Syriac tradition remembers today the Forty Martyrs of Sinai, monks killed by raiders in the desert of Sinai. The Church in India honours St Devasahayam (Lazarus), a married layman of Travancore, baptised as an adult, who gave his life for Christ in 1752 and was canonised by Pope Francis in 2022. May those who suffer for their faith in many lands today, and those who wrong them, be remembered in our prayer.
study: Which fear, more than any other, keeps me from living the Gospel openly?
If I truly believed that salvation is a gift, how would that change the way I look at my failures, and at the failures of others?

lead: Our calendar today remembers Mary, the Mother of God, for the seeds, at the time of sowing. Both readings speak of seed. Paul uses the farmer's work to teach generous giving: God gives the seed, and we sow it. In the Gospel the word about the Child is sown in the shepherds and in all who hear them, and in Mary it goes deep. The key words are sow and treasure.

r.h: God supplies seed to the sower
set: Chapters 8 and 9 of this letter are about a collection. Paul was gathering money among his Gentile churches for the poor Christians of Jerusalem (compare Romans 15:25–28; 1 Corinthians 16:1–4). It mattered to him as a sign that Jews and Gentiles in Christ are one family. He does not command the Corinthians. He reasons with them, and in these verses he turns to the farm.
str: v. 6: the rule of the field: as you sow, so you reap.
v. 7: give from the heart, cheerfully.
vv. 8–9: God is able to provide, as Psalm 112 says of the just man.
vv. 10–11: God supplies the seed, and the harvest ends in thanksgiving.
kw: Our word “hilarious” comes from it, but here it means glad and willing. Paul is echoing the Greek text of Proverbs 22:8, which speaks of God blessing a cheerful giver.
The verb goes back to the rich citizen in a Greek city who paid for a chorus at the festival. So it came to mean supplying generously. Paul's picture is of God as the great sponsor of every harvest.

In v. 6 “bountifully” is literally “with blessings”. The same word stands behind “bountiful gift” and “voluntary gift” in v. 5; the “blessing” of v. 8 is another Greek word, charis, grace. A gift to the poor is itself a blessing, for the one who gives and for the one who receives.
vv: the one who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and the one who sows bountifully will also reap bountifully.
Every farmer knows that seed thrown on the field looks like a loss for a time. Paul is not promising riches to donors. In v. 10 the harvest he names is righteousness.
God loves a cheerful giver.
God looks at the heart of the one who gives more than at the size of the gift.
He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your seed for sowing and increase the harvest of your righteousness.
The first half echoes Isaiah 55:10, where God's rain gives “seed to the sower and bread to the eater”. Even what we sow was first given to us.
ch: From the beginning Christians brought gifts for those in need along with the bread and wine for the Eucharist, and the Catechism cites Paul's collection in this connection (CCC 1351). What Paul asks of the Corinthians therefore stays close to the altar. In the Holy Qurbono we offer what the earth has given and human hands have made, and we are sent out to share.

r.h: Mary treasured all these words
set: The angels have announced the birth to shepherds in the fields near Bethlehem (2:8–14). David was once a shepherd in these same parts (1 Samuel 16:11). The Catechism sees meaning in the fact that simple shepherds were the first witnesses (CCC 525). The angels now leave, and the shepherds have only a word to go on.
str: v. 15: the shepherds decide to go.
v. 16: they go in haste and find the family.
vv. 17–18: they tell what they were told, and all are amazed.
v. 19: Mary keeps it all in her heart.
kw: In vv. 15, 17 and 19 Luke uses the same Greek word. “This thing that has taken place” is literally “this word”. Like the Hebrew dābār, it means both a word and an event. In the Bible, what God says happens.
To hold something carefully so that it is not lost. Luke says the same of Mary after the finding in the Temple (2:51, with a related verb).
Literally “to throw together”: to set things side by side and compare them. Mary lays the angel's promise beside the manger and the shepherds' story, and she thinks them through.
vv: “Let us go now to Bethlehem and see this thing that has taken place, which the Lord has made known to us.”
The shepherds have heard a word, and they go to see it. Faith starts with hearing and moves on to seeing.
So they went with haste and found Mary and Joseph, and the child lying in the manger.
Luke used the same note of haste for Mary going to Elizabeth (1:39). The sign the angel gave them was a very ordinary one: a baby in a feeding trough.
But Mary treasured all these words and pondered them in her heart.
“All who heard” were amazed (v. 18), but amazement soon fades. Mary does something else. She keeps the word and works at it. Luke does not say that she understood everything at once.
ch: The Catechism says that Jesus learned to pray from his mother, who kept in her heart and meditated on all the great things done by the Almighty (CCC 2599). The Council of Ephesus (431) confessed Mary as Mother of God, because the Child in the manger is the eternal Son (CCC 466, 495). Our Syriac word for her is Yoldath Aloho, she who gave birth to God. The Word was sown in her heart before and after it took flesh in her womb, and she is the model of the good soil, those who “hold it fast in an honest and good heart” (Luke 8:15).

qa: Is it a superstition to bring seed to church or to ask Mary's prayers for a harvest?

No, if it is done with faith. Blessings of the fruits of the earth are among the Church's sacramentals (CCC 1667, 1671). We do not treat a blessing as a guarantee of a crop. We confess that the seed, the rain and the growth come from God, and we ask the Mother of God to pray with us. The Gospel adds that the farmer's own heart must also become good soil.
rite: Our calendar speaks today of the Mother of God “for the seeds”, a day that belongs to the sowing season. It lets us pray for farmers and all who work the land, for a good harvest and a fair price. Today also recalls the founding of the Eparchy of Muvattupuzha in 2003, a day to give thanks for those who sowed the faith there.
study: What gift of mine do I give “reluctantly or under compulsion”? How could it become cheerful?
Mary set the events of her life side by side and pondered them. What in my life this year do I need to lay before God in that way?

lead: Today the calendar recalls the chains of St Peter and a shepherd of our own Church, Bishop Geevarghese Mar Divannasios (2018). Hebrews tells us to remember our leaders and to imitate their faith, and then points past them to the One who does not change. In the Gospel Jesus asks what kind of servant a leader is when the master seems to be away. The key words are remember, outside the camp and faithful.

r.h: The same yesterday and today and forever
set: This is the closing chapter of the sermon we call the Letter to the Hebrews, written for Christians who were tired and tempted to drift back. The author, who is not named, has argued that Christ's sacrifice fulfils the worship of the old covenant. Now he draws practical conclusions. Chapter 13 gives short commands about love, marriage, money and leaders.
str: vv. 7–8: remember your leaders; Christ does not change.
v. 9: do not be carried away by strange teachings.
vv. 10–12: the altar, and Jesus who suffered outside the gate.
vv. 13–14: let us go to him; we have no lasting city.
vv. 15–16: the sacrifices that remain: praise and sharing.
kw: Literally “those who go ahead”. The word here (vv. 7, 17, 24) describes what they do, leading the way, more than any rank.
The way out or end of something. The readers are to look at how those leaders' lives ended, perhaps in martyrdom, and to copy their faith.
A phrase from the Psalms (for example Psalm 50:14 in the Greek). The Catechism lists “sacrifice of praise” among the names of the Eucharist (CCC 1330).
vv: Remember your leaders, those who spoke the word of God to you; consider the outcome of their way of life, and imitate their faith.
The verb “spoke” is in the past tense, and many think these leaders had already died. The Church's memorial days do what this verse asks.
Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.
Leaders pass away. This is why the verse comes straight after the one about them. Christ, who taught them, is the one who stays.
Therefore Jesus also suffered outside the city gate in order to sanctify the people by his own blood.
On the Day of Atonement the bodies of the sacrificed animals were burned outside the camp (Leviticus 16:27). The author sees in this a sign of Calvary, which lay outside the walls.
For here we have no lasting city, but we are looking for the city that is to come.
Christians are at home among people, but they are always on a journey.
ch: “We have an altar” (v. 10) has been read in two ways. Many scholars see the Cross here; some Catholic interpreters also hear the Eucharist, and the two are not far apart, since the Eucharist makes present the one sacrifice of the Cross (CCC 1366–1367). The verses are about Christian worship and not a judgement on the Jewish people, whose covenant God has not revoked (CCC 121). Verse 16 keeps worship and charity together: praise on the lips and sharing with the poor are both called sacrifices.

r.h: The faithful and wise servant
set: Jesus is giving his last great discourse, on the end of the age, on the Mount of Olives (Matthew 24–25). He has just said that the Son of Man will come at an unexpected hour (24:44). This parable applies that warning to people who are in charge of others. Luke has the same parable, and there Peter asks whether it is meant for everyone (Luke 12:41–46).
str: v. 45: the question: who is the faithful and wise slave?
vv. 46–47: the blessing on the one found at work.
vv. 48–49: the wicked slave who says the master is delayed.
vv. 50–51: the master comes without warning.
kw: The Greek word means a slave. A trusted slave in a large household could manage all its affairs. His authority is only lent to him.
Practically wise. It is the same word as for the man who built on rock (7:24) and the bridesmaids with oil (25:2).
In Matthew, one who plays a part. The wicked servant wears the master's authority while serving himself.
vv: “Who then is the faithful and wise slave, whom his master has put in charge of his household, to give the other slaves their allowance of food at the proper time?
The job is plain: feed the others on time. Authority in the Church exists for this.
Blessed is that slave whom his master will find at work when he arrives.
What matters is that he is found doing his ordinary duty.
But if that wicked slave says to himself, ‘My master is delayed,’
The trouble starts in a thought. When a leader stops expecting to give an account, the fellow slaves soon suffer for it.
He will cut him in pieces and put him with the hypocrites, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.
The Greek is as harsh as the English, and the POC softens it to “punish”. It is a parable's strong way of saying how seriously God takes the abuse of those in our care.
ch: St Augustine preached on the day of his own ordination anniversary with such service in mind: for you I am a bishop, with you I am a Christian (Sermon 340, in substance). The Catechism reminds us that the Lord's coming is always near, though we are not told the time (CCC 673). The parable speaks first to bishops and priests, and then to every parent, teacher and employer, to all who have others in their charge.

rite: The chains of St Peter recall the night when an angel led him out of Herod's prison (Acts 12:1–11), while “the church prayed fervently to God for him” (12:5). Peter's chains remind us that a leader in the Church may be bound, but the word is not. Today we also remember Bishop Geevarghese Mar Divannasios, who served our Church, and we follow Hebrews 13:7 by giving thanks for him.
study: Whose faith, among those who taught me the Gospel, should I imitate? Have I thanked God for that person?
Who depends on me for their “food at the proper time”, in the home, at work or in the parish?

lead: On this Second Sunday after Denho the Gospel gives us one sentence that explains all the other readings. Philip says, “We have found him about whom Moses in the law and also the prophets wrote”. The lessons today are chosen from those very books. Leviticus (22:26–33) gives the law's word, “I am the Lord; I sanctify you”, and the First Letter of Peter (1:13–25) draws the conclusion: “You shall be holy, for I am holy”. Proverbs (8:22–36) shows Wisdom at God's side at the beginning, which the Fathers read of the eternal Son. Isaiah (51:1–8) tells a tired people, “Look to the rock from which you were hewn”. Micah (5:1–8) points to a small town and a coming shepherd. In the Evening Gospel (Luke 4:14–15) Jesus returns to Galilee “filled with the power of the Spirit”.

We study three readings closely: Micah 5:1–8, the Old Testament lesson closest to the Gospel, since it asks what good can come from a small place; Romans 3:1–8, on God's faithfulness to the people to whom he entrusted these Scriptures; and John 1:43–51, where one man's doubt meets an invitation. The key words are little, faithfulness and come and see.

r.h: From you shall come forth one who is to rule
set: Micah came from Moresheth, a village of Judah (1:1), and he preached in the eighth century BC, in the same years as Isaiah. It was the age of the Assyrian empire. Its armies destroyed the northern kingdom of Israel and later overran the towns of Judah, Micah's own countryside among them.

A note on numbers. In the Hebrew Bible, verse 1 of this chapter is the last verse of chapter 4, and the Bethlehem verse is 5:1. The NRSV and the POC number it 5:2, and we follow them here. Verse 1 is hard to translate, but its sense is plain: the city is under siege and its ruler has been humiliated.
str: v. 1: Jerusalem besieged; its ruler struck on the cheek.
v. 2: Bethlehem, the small town, and the ruler from of old.
v. 3: a time of waiting until “she who is in labor has brought forth”.
vv. 4–5a: the shepherd, and peace.
vv. 5b–6: shepherds raised against Assyria.
vv. 7–8: the remnant among the nations, like dew and like a lion.
kw: Small, the youngest, of no account. God's habit in the Bible is to choose such people: David himself was the youngest son of Jesse, left with the sheep (1 Samuel 16:11).

Literally “his goings forth”. It comes from the same verb as “shall come forth” earlier in the verse. In its first sense it may point to the ancient line of David. The Church sees in it more than the prophet could have seen.
“Feed his flock” is one Hebrew idea: to shepherd. A true king of Israel is a shepherd (Ezekiel 34:23). Jesus will take this up: “I am the good shepherd” (John 10:11).
vv: But you, O Bethlehem of Ephrathah, who are one of the little clans of Judah, from you shall come forth for me one who is to rule in Israel, whose origin is from of old, from ancient days.

Jerusalem is besieged and its king humiliated, and the prophet looks away from the capital to the village where David was born. God starts again from the small place. Matthew has the chief priests and scribes quote this verse to Herod (Matthew 2:5–6).
until the time when she who is in labor has brought forth;
A mother stands unnamed at the centre of the promise, as in Isaiah 7:14; Isaiah was Micah's contemporary. The Second Vatican Council reads both prophecies of Mary (Lumen Gentium 55).
And he shall stand and feed his flock in the strength of the Lord, in the majesty of the name of the Lord his God.
He rules by God's strength, not his own. That is the opposite of the Assyrian kings, who boasted of their power.
and he shall be the one of peace.

Hebrew: zeh šālôm, “this one shall be peace”. Compare Ephesians 2:14: “he is our peace”. The next lines still speak of war and of a lion among sheep (v. 8), the language of a people under attack. Christians read them in the light of the shepherd who laid down his life.
ch: Micah 5:2 was among the first prophecies Christians quoted for the birth of Jesus; St Justin Martyr uses it in his Dialogue with Trypho (in substance). Lumen Gentium 55 places it with Isaiah 7:14 among the texts that gradually bring the Mother of the Redeemer into clearer light. The Catechism says the Lord's coming was prepared over long centuries (CCC 522). We read such texts with respect, knowing that Jewish readers hold them too and that their first meaning belonged to Micah's own day.

r.h: The faithfulness of God
set: Paul wrote to the Christians of Rome around AD 57, probably from Corinth, to a community he had not founded. In chapter 2 he has argued that Jews and Gentiles alike will answer to God, and that the outward sign means little without obedience of the heart. Any listener would object: then has God's choice of Israel meant nothing? Paul takes up the objection in the lively style of a teacher arguing with an imagined questioner. He gives a short answer here and the full one in chapters 9–11.
str: vv. 1–2: what advantage has the Jew? “Much, in every way.”
vv. 3–4: human faithlessness does not cancel God's faithfulness.
vv. 5–6: is God unjust to judge? By no means.
vv. 7–8: “Let us do evil so that good may come” is rejected.
kw: God's own sayings, the Scriptures. This is Israel's first privilege. Every Christian who reads the Psalms or Isaiah receives them from the hand of the people who were “entrusted” with them.
Pistis means both faith and faithfulness. Here it describes God himself: he keeps his word. Behind it stand the Hebrew words for God's steadfast truth.
Literally “may it not be”. This is Paul's strongest denial, heard in vv. 4 and 6 and repeatedly in this letter.
vv: Much, in every way. For in the first place the Jews were entrusted with the oracles of God.
Paul will give the longer list at 9:4–5. Today's Old Testament lessons are themselves the proof of what he says here.
What if some were unfaithful? Will their faithlessness nullify the faithfulness of God?
Paul says “some”. He is not condemning a people. The point applies to the Church too: our failures do not cancel the promises of God.
By no means! Although everyone is a liar, let God be proved true,
The quotation that follows is from Psalm 51:4 in its Greek form, David's psalm of repentance. A sinner who confesses says that God is right.
And why not say (as some people slander us by saying that we say), “Let us do evil so that good may come”? Their condemnation is deserved!
Paul's preaching on grace was being twisted into a licence to sin. He treats this as slander. This verse lies behind a basic rule of Christian morals.
ch: The Church hears this reading together with Romans 11:29, “the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable”, which Nostra Aetate 4 and the Catechism (CCC 839) take up in speaking of the Jewish people. From verse 8 the Catechism draws the moral rule: one may not do evil so that good may result from it (CCC 1756, 1789). No good end makes an evil act right. The same God who is faithful to Israel is faithful to us.

r.h: Come and see
set: John's opening chapter moves day by day. John the Baptist has pointed to Jesus and told of the Spirit coming down on him (1:29–34), the mystery of Denho. Two of his disciples have followed Jesus, heard “Come and see” (1:39), and Andrew has found his brother Simon (1:40–42). Today is “the next day”, and the chain goes on.

Philip's name is Greek, and his town Bethsaida lay at the north of the Lake of Galilee. Nathanael, whose name means “God has given”, was from Cana (21:2). He does not appear in the other Gospels under this name, and a long tradition identifies him with Bartholomew, whom the lists place beside Philip. This cannot be proved.
str: vv. 43–44: Jesus finds Philip: “Follow me.”
v. 45: Philip finds Nathanael.
v. 46: the objection and the invitation.
vv. 47–49: Jesus knows him; Nathanael confesses.
vv. 50–51: the promise of greater things.
kw: Andrew “found” Simon (1:41), Jesus “found” Philip (1:43), and Philip “found” Nathanael (1:45). Philip says “we have found”, but the verse before shows who found whom first.

Jesus calls Nathanael “truly an Israelite in whom there is no deceit”. In Genesis 27:35 Jacob, who later receives the name Israel, took the blessing “deceitfully”, and the Greek Bible has this word there. Verse 51 then recalls Jacob's ladder. Many commentators see a deliberate play on his story.
Jesus himself said much the same to the first two disciples (1:39). In John, “to see” often means to believe. Those who have been invited pass on the invitation.
vv: “We have found him about whom Moses in the law and also the prophets wrote, Jesus son of Joseph from Nazareth.”
The first half of Philip's sentence is the high claim; the second half sounds ordinary. John's readers know that there is much more to say about the “son of Joseph” (1:1–18).
“Can anything good come out of Nazareth?” Philip said to him, “Come and see.”
Nazareth was a small village, and the Old Testament never names it. Micah said the same kind of thing of Bethlehem. Philip does not argue. He has no answer except an invitation, and it is enough.
“I saw you under the fig tree before Philip called you.”

John does not tell us what happened under the tree, and guesses remain guesses. Micah's vision of peace has everyone sitting under their own fig trees (Micah 4:4), and some have heard an echo of it. What is clear is that Nathanael feels fully known, and that this opens him.
“Rabbi, you are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel!”
The doubter makes the fullest confession of the chapter so far.
“Very truly, I tell you, you will see heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of Man.”

The “you” here is plural in Greek: the promise is for all the disciples. Genesis 28:12 had the angels on a ladder at Bethel, the “gate of heaven”. Now Jesus himself is the meeting place of heaven and earth.
ch: St Augustine read the fig tree as the shade of sin under which Christ saw us before grace called us (Tractates on John 7, in substance). Pope Francis, in Evangelii Gaudium 127–129, describes this person-to-person sharing of the Gospel, which begins in a friendly conversation. Philip is the model: he tells what he has found and invites a friend to meet Jesus. At every Holy Qurbono the heavens are opened in this sense, for Christ is there as the meeting place of God and people.

qa: Philip calls Jesus “son of Joseph from Nazareth”. Does this go against Bethlehem and the virgin birth?

No. Philip is saying what people knew. Joseph was the legal father of Jesus, and that is how Jesus belongs to David's house. John knows the Bethlehem question well: later the crowd objects that the Messiah should come from David's town (7:41–42), and John leaves the irony for his readers to enjoy. The Church confesses the virginal conception (CCC 496–497) along with the honoured place of St Joseph.
Proverbs 8:22 says the Lord “created” Wisdom. Is the Son a creature?

This was the verse Arius's followers used. St Athanasius answered them in his Discourses Against the Arians (Book II): the Son is the eternal Wisdom of the Father, and the word “created” is to be understood of the Son's becoming man for us (in substance). The Nicene Creed confesses him “begotten, not made”. Proverbs itself is poetry about God's Wisdom, and the Fathers saw it reach its fullness in Christ.
Does Romans 3 mean that God has finished with the Jewish people?

It says the reverse. “Will their faithlessness nullify the faithfulness of God? By no means!” Paul's argument ends in chapter 11 with the promise that the gifts and calling of God are irrevocable. The Church today speaks with respect of the people to whom God first spoke (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 839).
rite: In our West Syriac tradition, Denho (the “rising” or “dawning”) celebrates the Lord's baptism and his showing to the world. The Sundays after Denho follow that light as it reaches one person after another; today it reaches Philip and Nathanael. Today's date also recalls Mar Antonios of Egypt. St Athanasius tells in his Life of Antony that the young man heard the Gospel in church and took it as spoken to himself. Tomorrow the fast of the Ninevites begins, and Micah gives a small preparation: the land of Assyria and “the land of Nimrod” (5:6) were the great enemy, and Genesis 10:11 says Nineveh was built from that land. In the Book of Jonah God sends his prophet to that very city.
study: Bethlehem and Nazareth were places of no account. Whom or what have I written off because it seems too small for God to use?
Have I ever said “Come and see” to someone? What would it mean for me to do so this week?
Paul says that our faithlessness does not cancel God's faithfulness. When have I found this to be true?
Jesus knew Nathanael before they met. How does it change my prayer to know that he saw me “under the fig tree”?

lead: The three days of the fast of the Ninevites begin with a prophet running away. Jonah hears God's call and goes the other way, and the pagan sailors pray while he sleeps. The Epistle (Philippians 2:1–11) shows the opposite road: Christ “humbled himself and became obedient”. In the Gospel Jesus takes Jonah as the only sign he will give. The key words are go down and sign.

r.h: Jonah flees from the presence of the Lord
set: Jonah son of Amittai is named in 2 Kings 14:25 as a prophet in the reign of Jeroboam II, in the eighth century BC. The book that bears his name is different from the other prophets. It is a short story about a prophet, with hardly any oracles. Nineveh, on the Tigris opposite modern Mosul, was a great city of Assyria, and it became the empire's capital. Assyria had destroyed the northern kingdom of Israel, and to an Israelite ear the name meant cruelty (see Nahum 3). Nineveh fell in 612 BC. God sends the prophet to the enemy's own city.
str: vv. 1–2: God's command: “Go at once to Nineveh”.
v. 3: Jonah goes down to Joppa and takes a ship for Tarshish.
vv. 4–6: the storm; the sailors pray; Jonah sleeps; the captain wakes him.
v. 7: the lots fall on Jonah.
kw: Jonah goes down to Joppa (1:3), down into the ship (1:3), down into the hold (1:5), and his psalm will say “I went down” (2:6). The storyteller lets us watch him sink step by step, long before he is in the water.
“The Lord hurled a great wind” (1:4). The sailors hurl the cargo (1:5), and later they hurl Jonah himself (1:12, 15). The NRSV uses “threw” for these. One verb binds the scene together.
The same Hebrew word is Nineveh's “wickedness” (1:2) and the “calamity” in the storm (1:7). This word will keep returning through the book (3:8, 10; 4:1), so it is worth watching.
vv: “Go at once to Nineveh, that great city, and cry out against it; for their wickedness has come up before me.”
God is concerned with the sin of a people who are not Israel. From its first lines the book says he is the God of all nations.
But Jonah set out to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the Lord.
Nineveh lay to the east. Tarshish, perhaps in Spain, stood for the far end of the western sea. The storyteller does not yet say why Jonah runs. We learn that only in 4:2.
Jonah, meanwhile, had gone down into the hold of the ship and had lain down, and was fast asleep.
Everyone on board is praying to some god, and the one man who knows the true God is asleep.
“What are you doing sound asleep? Get up, call on your god! Perhaps the god will spare us a thought so that we do not perish.”

A pagan captain speaks the words a prophet should be saying. His “Get up” is the same word God used in v. 2 (“Go at once” is literally “Get up, go”). God's call comes back to Jonah on a stranger's lips.
ch: Centuries later, at this same port of Joppa, God told another Jewish preacher, Peter, to go to the Gentiles (Acts 10:5–23). Peter also resisted at first, and then he went. The Syriac Churches have loved this book; a long verse homily on the repentance of Nineveh has come down under the name of Mar Aprem (Ephrem). The Catechism names the seasons of penance as intense moments of the Church's penitential practice (CCC 1438). The fast begins with the honest question whether I too am running.

r.h: The sign of Jonah
set: Jesus has healed a man who was blind and mute, and his opponents have said that he does this by the power of demons (12:22–37). Now “some of the scribes and Pharisees” ask for a sign. Matthew says “some”. Jesus, a Jew speaking to his fellow Jews as the prophets did, is addressing those who are refusing him at that moment. Jonah's home was Gath-hepher (2 Kings 14:25), generally placed in Galilee, not far from Nazareth.
str: v. 38: the request for a sign.
vv. 39–40: the only sign: Jonah, three days and three nights.
v. 41: the people of Nineveh will rise at the judgment.
v. 42: so will the queen of the South.
kw: Here it means a proof on demand. Jesus refuses to perform on request, but he names the one sign that will be given: his death and rising.
The prophets called unfaithfulness to the covenant adultery (for example Hosea 2). Jesus speaks in their voice. It is a word about faithfulness, and it has nothing to do with a whole people's worth.

The word the Greek Bible uses in Jonah. The Hebrew of Jonah says only “a large fish” (1:17). The POC here says “തിമിംഗലം”, whale, while in Jonah it says “മത്സ്യം”, fish. No one needs to worry about the species.
vv: “An evil and adulterous generation asks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah.
They already have many signs in front of them. What is lacking is the will to believe.
so for three days and three nights the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth.
Jesus rose on the third day, and in Jewish reckoning part of a day could count as a whole day and night. This is how Matthew explains the sign: a man goes down into death and comes back.
The people of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, because they repented at the proclamation of Jonah, and see, something greater than Jonah is here!
The verse lets Gentiles stand as witnesses in the judgment. These are the people of the fast we are beginning: they had less and they did more.
ch: The Catechism lists the sign of Jonah among the ways Jesus linked faith in the resurrection to his own person (CCC 994), and teaches that he truly went down into the realm of the dead (CCC 632–635). In the Roman catacombs Jonah is one of the most frequently painted figures. Early Christians, burying their dead, drew the man thrown up alive from the fish. For them he was a picture of Christ's Pasch and of their own hope.

qa: Did a fish really swallow Jonah?

Catholics may read this question calmly. Many Fathers took the story as history. Many Catholic scholars today, and notes such as those of the Jerusalem Bible, read the book as an inspired teaching story, since it has the marks of one; the Church asks us to attend to the literary form of each book (Dei Verbum 12) and has not defined this point. Jesus' comparison holds either way, for the point of both is God's mercy and the resurrection. What we may not do is argue about the fish and miss the call to repent.
rite: Baooutho d'Ninwoye, the supplication of the Ninevites, is an old fast of the Syriac Churches. Accounts of its beginning differ. East Syriac memory links it with a plague in sixth-century Mesopotamia, and West Syriac tradition credits Mar Marutha of Tikrit (seventh century) with spreading it. The Thomas Christians of Kerala have long kept it as Moonnu Nombu, and the Coptic Church keeps a Fast of Nineveh too. Today our calendar also remembers Moran Mor Cyril Baselios Catholicos (+2007), first Major Archbishop of our Church, and Joseph Mar Severios (+1955), with Mar Cyril and Mar Athanasius of Alexandria. The Church Unity Octave begins today.
study: What is my “Tarshish”, the place I go so that I need not do what God has asked?
Who outside my own circle has reminded me of God, as the captain reminded Jonah?

lead: On the second day the prophet obeys, and a whole city turns. Our calendar reads chapter 3 today and Jonah's prayer of chapter 2 tomorrow, so the story's order is changed here. Keep in mind that in the story the fish has already given Jonah back. The Gospel warns against living as if nothing could interrupt us, and the Epistle (Romans 12:9–15) says how the watchful live. The key words are overthrown, turned and keep awake.

r.h: Nineveh believes and repents
set: This is the middle of the story. After the storm, the fish and the prayer, God does not choose another prophet. “The word of the Lord came to Jonah a second time”. The storyteller paints Nineveh in big colours: a three days' walk across, and a fast that takes in even the animals. The picture is deliberately larger than life, and it smiles a little as it teaches.
str: vv. 1–3: the second call; this time Jonah goes.
v. 4: Jonah's short sermon.
v. 5: the people believe and fast, great and small.
vv. 6–9: the king's response and decree.
v. 10: God sees and changes his mind.
kw: The Hebrew of Jonah's sermon has only five words, ending with this one. The verb hāpak is used of Sodom being overthrown (Genesis 19:25), but it can also mean to be turned around or changed. Nineveh was indeed “overturned”, though not as Jonah expected: its heart was turned.
The great Old Testament word for repentance. “All shall turn from their evil ways” (3:8), and God “saw... how they turned” (3:10). The hands must turn along with the heart.
to relent, to change one's mind

Said here of God (3:9, 10). This is the language of the Bible, which speaks of God in human terms. God's warning was a call meant to be answered (see Jeremiah 18:7–8). He has not changed; it is Nineveh that has changed.
vv: And he cried out, “Forty days more, and Nineveh shall be overthrown!”

Jonah goes only a day's walk into a city three days across, and he does not mention God or mercy. The ancient Greek Bible reads “three days” here, while the Hebrew, the NRSV and the POC have “forty”. Forty is the Bible's number for testing and for penance.
And the people of Nineveh believed God; they proclaimed a fast, and everyone, great and small, put on sackcloth.
The people act before the king hears. It is one of the finest sentences in the prophets, said of Israel's enemies. Compare what Genesis 15:6 says of Abraham.
All shall turn from their evil ways and from the violence that is in their hands.
The animals in sackcloth may make us smile. The serious note is in the word “violence”. A fast that leaves violence in the hands is not the fast God wants (Isaiah 58:3–7).
Who knows? God may relent and change his mind;
The pagan king presumes nothing. Joel 2:14 has the same “Who knows?” Humility does not demand mercy; it hopes for it.
When God saw what they did, how they turned from their evil ways, God changed his mind
God sees their works, and the text names their turning, not their fasting, as what he saw.
ch: The Catechism says that Jesus' call to conversion, like that of the prophets before him, does not aim first at outward works, “sackcloth and ashes,” fasting and mortification, but at the conversion of the heart (CCC 1430). Those outward works then give it expression (CCC 1430–1431, 1434). St John Chrysostom, preaching on the Statues in a frightened Antioch, pointed to this verse: God did not say that he saw their fasting, but that they turned from evil ways (in substance). Mar Aphrahat, in his Demonstration on Fasting, also holds up the fast of the Ninevites as a true fast (in substance).

r.h: Keep awake
set: Still in the final discourse on the Mount of Olives, Jesus has said that no one knows the day or the hour except the Father (24:36). These verses work that out with two pictures, the days of Noah and the thief at night, and they lead on to the faithful servant (24:45–51).
str: vv. 37–39: as in the days of Noah.
vv. 40–41: two in the field, two at the mill.
v. 42: keep awake.
vv. 43–44: the thief at night; be ready.
kw: “Presence” or “arrival”, used of a king's visit to a city. Matthew uses it in vv. 37 and 39 for the Lord's return in glory. The POC says “ആഗമനം”.
An imperative of watching. The Christian name Gregory comes from this root, “the watchful one”. It means being alert to the Lord and does not mean a nervous fear.
“One will be taken.” The verb in v. 40 often means to take someone to oneself (compare 1:20; 17:1). Scholars differ whether “taken” here means rescued or carried off in judgment. See below.
vv: they were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the day Noah entered the ark,
There is nothing wrong with any of these things. The danger is to live wholly inside them, as if nothing else could happen.
Then two will be in the field; one will be taken and one will be left.
The two look alike and do the same work. The difference is inward and cannot be seen from outside.
Keep awake therefore, for you do not know on what day your Lord is coming.
Notice the word “your”. The one who is coming is our Lord, and it is his servants who wait for him.
Therefore you also must be ready, for the Son of Man is coming at an unexpected hour.
Jonah's sermon gave Nineveh forty days. We are given no number, so the time to turn is today.
ch: The Catechism teaches that since the Ascension Christ's coming has been imminent, even though it is not for us to know the times (CCC 673), and that we must therefore watch constantly (CCC 1036, quoting Lumen Gentium 48). It warns against any claim to calculate the end. The first fruit of a fast is the clear head it gives, and Paul's list in today's Epistle shows what a person awake actually does: love without pretence, patience, prayer and hospitality.

qa: Does “one will be taken” mean the “rapture” some preachers speak of?

No. The idea of a secret rapture of believers before the end is a modern teaching, and the Catholic Church does not hold it. Jesus is speaking of the one coming of the Son of Man in glory, and he uses these pictures to say: be ready.
rite: Mar Macarios the Great, whom we remember today, was a monk of the Egyptian desert in the fourth century, long remembered for his gentleness. The watchfulness of the desert is what the Gospel asks of us. It is also the name day of Geevarghese Mar Makarios. Pray for him, and pray in this Unity Octave for the oneness of all Christians.
study: What in my own life is “the violence that is in [my] hands”, at home or at work, and how can this fast turn it?
What keeps me from being awake to God: not sins only, but “eating and drinking”, the ordinary busy days?

lead: On the third day of the fast we go down with Jonah to the bottom of the sea and hear him pray. In the Gospel Jesus refuses to treat other people's disasters as proof of their sin, and he turns the question back on us. The Epistle (1 Thessalonians 5:1–11) calls us “children of light”. Today we also honour St Sebastian. The key words are belly of Sheol, remember and repent.

r.h: Jonah's prayer from the belly of the fish
set: Jonah has been thrown into the sea, and “the Lord provided a large fish” (1:17; in the Hebrew Bible this verse is 2:1, so that the verse numbers of the psalm are one higher there). The chapter is a psalm of thanksgiving with a sentence of narrative on either side. Its language is close to the Book of Psalms throughout. Many scholars think that the storyteller placed here a psalm that was known in Israel, or composed it in that familiar style.
str: v. 1: Jonah prays from the fish.
v. 2: the summary: I called, and he answered.
vv. 3–6a: the descent: waters, weeds, the bars of the deep.
vv. 6b–7: “yet you brought up my life”.
vv. 8–9: vows and thanksgiving.
v. 10: the fish gives him back.
kw: The Hebrew name for the place of the dead. The POC says “പാതാളം”. “The belly of Sheol” joins the belly of the fish with the realm of death. To the Old Testament, death's deepest pain was to be cut off from God's presence.

The great word for covenant love, usually “steadfast love”. In v. 8 idol worshippers abandon their true source of it. Jonah will quote the same word about God in 4:2, and it is exactly what angers him.
The closing cry of the psalm (v. 9), from the same root as the name Yeshua, Jesus. Psalm 3:8 has the same cry.
vv: “I called to the Lord out of my distress, and he answered me; out of the belly of Sheol I cried, and you heard my voice.
He speaks in the past tense while still inside the fish. It is a song of thanks before the rescue is complete. Faith gives thanks from the dark.
all your waves and your billows passed over me.
These words echo Psalm 42:7. Jonah in his worst hour prays in the words he learned in Israel's worship. Those who learn the psalms have words when they cannot find any.
As my life was ebbing away, I remembered the Lord; and my prayer came to you, into your holy temple.
Jonah ran from God's presence (1:3), and here he finds that even from the depths his prayer reaches it. No depth is beyond God's hearing.
But I with the voice of thanksgiving will sacrifice to you; what I have vowed I will pay. Deliverance belongs to the Lord!”
The sailors have already offered sacrifice and made vows (1:16). Now the prophet catches up with them.
Then the Lord spoke to the fish, and it spewed Jonah out upon the dry land.
God has spoken to the prophet and been disobeyed. He speaks to the fish, and it obeys at once. The storyteller's humour is at work even here.
ch: The Fathers saw in this chapter Christ's descent among the dead and his rising. St Cyril of Jerusalem compares the two in his Catechetical Lectures (14, in substance): Jonah was cast into the fish, and Christ of his own will went down into death. The Catechism teaches that Jesus, like all people, experienced death and went down to the realm of the dead as Saviour (CCC 632–633). The Fathers also read the chapter of Baptism, a going down into water and a coming up to new life (Romans 6:4; CCC 1214).

r.h: Unless you repent
set: Jesus is on the road to Jerusalem, and he has just told the crowd to read the signs of the present time and settle their accounts while there is still time (12:54–59). Some people bring him news of a killing. Luke is our only source for this incident, but what we know of Pilate from Josephus and other writers makes it easy to believe. The tower of Siloam stood near the pool of that name in the south of Jerusalem, and we know nothing more of its fall. The parable of the barren fig tree, given one more year, comes straight after (13:6–9).
str: v. 1: the news about the Galileans and Pilate.
vv. 2–3: were they worse sinners? No. Repent.
vv. 4–5: the tower of Siloam: the same question, the same answer.
kw: Used in v. 2. The common assumption was that great suffering points to great sin. The friends of Job argue this, and the Book of Job rejects it.
In v. 4, literally “debtors”. The word recalls the unsettled account in 12:58–59. Everyone has a debt before God.
A change of mind, a turning of the whole person, which the Hebrew calls šûb.
vv: At that very time there were some present who told him about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices.
The killing happened at worship, probably in the Temple. The tellers may have expected Jesus, a Galilean, to condemn Pilate or to comment on the victims. He does neither.
“Do you think that because these Galileans suffered in this way they were worse sinners than all other Galileans?
Jesus takes away a comfortable idea: that disaster falls on others because they deserve it. Compare John 9:3.
No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all perish as they did.
The question is turned around. The real issue is not their sins but ours. Every news report is a reminder that life is short and that today is the time to turn.
those eighteen who were killed when the tower of Siloam fell on them
The first case was a crime and this one an accident. Together they cover all the sudden deaths we can imagine.
ch: The Catechism says that no quick answer will suffice to the question of evil (CCC 309), and that it is the whole of the Christian faith that answers it. It describes interior repentance as a radical reorientation of our whole life, a return to God with all our heart (CCC 1431). So Jesus does not explain disasters here, and he forbids us to make them a judgement on the victims. He uses them as a call: to turn while there is time, and to help those who suffer.

qa: When a flood or an earthquake comes, is God punishing the people there?

Jesus says plainly that we may not draw this conclusion about those who suffer. God does not will the evil of innocent suffering for its own sake, and our answer to such disasters is prayer and help for those who suffer in many lands. We may each ask what the event says to my own life. That is the question Jesus asks here.
rite: The Church honours St Sebastian today. Rome remembered him as a martyr from an early date. The story of the arrows, and of how he survived them to die later under clubs, comes from a later account of his passion, which historians read with caution. His story and Jonah's meet at this point: both teach that no depth or danger puts us beyond God's care. The Unity Octave continues. This is the third day of the fast, and the fast concludes tomorrow.
study: Which psalm or prayer have I learned so well that it would come to me “from the depths”?
When I hear of a disaster, what is my first thought about those who suffered, and how would Jesus change it?

lead: The fast ends with a surprise: the prophet is angry that God has been merciful. Around this reading the calendar gathers others. The Evening Gospel (Luke 12:54–59) asks us to read the present time. Abraham pleads for Sodom and Joshua falls before the ark (Genesis 18:22–33; Joshua 7:6–13). Psalm 13 asks “How long, O Lord?”. Saul the persecutor is thrown down and called (Acts 9:1–9), and he tells of it in Galatians 1:13–24. We study Jonah 4:1–11 and Luke 11:29–32. The key words are concern and something greater.

r.h: Should I not be concerned about Nineveh?
set: Nineveh has repented and been spared (3:10). Now, at last, we learn why Jonah ran in chapter 1. He was never afraid of failing. He was afraid of succeeding. This is the last chapter of the book. It is entirely a conversation between God and an angry man, set outside the city under a booth and a bush.
str: vv. 1–3: Jonah's anger and his prayer: “I knew”.
v. 4: God's first question.
vv. 5–6: the booth and the bush.
vv. 7–9: the worm, the wind, and God's second question.
vv. 10–11: God's last question, and the end of the book.
kw: “Is it right for you to be angry?” is literally, “Is it good that it burns in you?” God treats anger as something to be looked at. He does not scold.

The plant is unknown, though many think of the castor-oil plant. When St Jerome rendered it “ivy” in place of the older Latin “gourd”, St Augustine reported an uproar over the reading in an African congregation, and the two exchanged letters about it (in substance).
The closing word of the book's argument (vv. 10, 11). It means the feeling of one who is moved to spare. The POC says “അനുകമ്പ”.
vv: for I knew that you are a gracious God and merciful, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love, and ready to relent from punishing.

This is Israel's great creed from Exodus 34:6, which Joel 2:13 also quotes. Jonah says it as a complaint. The verse is the key to the whole book: a person can know the creed perfectly and still resent it when it is applied to an enemy.
And the Lord said, “Is it right for you to be angry?”
Jonah does not answer. God does not end the conversation with him either.
But God said to Jonah, “Is it right for you to be angry about the bush?” And he said, “Yes, angry enough to die.”
The prophet has grown more attached to his shade than to a hundred and twenty thousand lives. The storyteller wants us to laugh, then to be silent.

And should I not be concerned about Nineveh, that great city, in which there are more than a hundred and twenty thousand persons who do not know their right hand from their left, and also many animals?”

“Do not know their right hand from their left” may mean small children, or those without moral understanding. The “many animals” are a last, tender touch. The book stops here, with God's question unanswered. The answer is left to the reader.
