ch: The Catechism takes the words of Exodus 34:6 as God's self-revelation (CCC 210), and Jonah 4 shows how demanding they are. It is wrong to make Jonah a caricature of the Jewish people. This book is Israel's own Scripture, and the synagogue reads it on the afternoon of Yom Kippur, the holiest day of the year. It holds a mirror to every believer, Christian and Jew, who is glad of mercy for himself and slow to want it for others. Jesus asks the same of us in the parable of the elder brother (Luke 15:25–32).

r.h: Something greater than Jonah is here
set: The crowds are growing, and some have been asking Jesus for “a sign from heaven” (11:16). Matthew tells of the same saying (Matthew 12:38–42). Luke's version has its own emphasis: the sign is Jonah himself, the man who came from far with a word of God, as the Son of Man now stands before the crowd. Jesus speaks these hard words to his own contemporaries, as the prophets did; they are not a judgement on a people.
str: v. 29: this generation asks for a sign.
v. 30: Jonah was a sign to Nineveh; the Son of Man to this generation.
v. 31: the queen of the South.
v. 32: the people of Nineveh.
kw: The word for a herald's announcement, used in the Greek of Jonah 3:2. The same word later names the Church's first preaching of the Gospel.
The Greek is neuter, “something more”, not “someone”. It points to all that has arrived in Jesus: God's Kingdom, in person. The POC's “വലിയവൻ”, “a greater one”, says directly who that is.
The Queen of Sheba (1 Kings 10:1–13), who came from a far country to hear Solomon. She and the people of Nineveh are both Gentiles, a theme close to Luke's heart.
vv: it asks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah.

We read Matthew's account three days ago. There the sign was three days in the sea monster. Here Luke does not mention them. The two evangelists show the same sign from two sides, the rising and the preaching.
For just as Jonah became a sign to the people of Nineveh, so the Son of Man will be to this generation.
Nineveh saw no miracle in the Book of Jonah. It only heard a man speak, and it turned.
The people of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, because they repented at the proclamation of Jonah, and see, something greater than Jonah is here!
Luke ends on this note, and today the fast ends on it too. The Ninevites believed a reluctant prophet who gave them five words. We have the Son of God, the whole Gospel and the Holy Qurbono.
ch: St Paul is the great example in today's other readings. Saul, on his own account a zealous persecutor, is stopped on the road, and he can write that God “was pleased to reveal his Son to me, so that I might proclaim him among the Gentiles” (Galatians 1:15–16). Like Nineveh, he turned. The Catechism names conversion as a continuing task of the whole Church: an uninterrupted task, for she is “at once holy and always in need of purification” (CCC 1428, quoting Lumen Gentium 8). The fast ends, but the turning does not.

qa: Why does the Book of Jonah end with a question and no answer?

Because the reader must give it. We are not told whether Jonah came round. The only other prophetic book that ends on a question is Nahum (3:19), which also concerns Nineveh, and it speaks of her cruelty. Scripture lets both stand: the crimes of Nineveh are real, and God's mercy reaches even them.
rite: Moonnu Nombu concludes today. It is a small fast before the Great Fast, a rehearsal for repentance. Today we also remember St Agnes, the young Roman virgin and martyr (died about the year 304). St Ambrose, in his work on virgins, speaks of her as a girl of about twelve. She reminds us that the response to Christ can be total at any age. The Church Unity Octave continues, and all the readings about Nineveh make a fitting prayer for it: God's concern is wider than our circle.
study: Whom would I secretly rather God did not forgive? What might God ask me, as he asked Jonah?
This fast is ending. What one “turning” will I carry forward from these days into the Great Fast?

lead: On the day the Church remembers Mar Timotheos, both readings speak of keeping faithfully what has been handed on. Paul charges his young co-worker to fight the good fight and to keep the commandment until the Lord appears. In the Gospel Jesus says that he has come not to abolish the law and the prophets but to fulfil them. Timothy knew both sides of this: he learned the sacred writings from childhood (2 Timothy 1:5; 3:15) and then learned from Paul to read them in the light of Christ.

r.h: The man of God and the King of kings
set: Timothy came from Lystra, the son of a Jewish mother and a Greek father (Acts 16:1), and became Paul's constant companion. Paul left him at Ephesus to guard the Church from false teaching (1 Timothy 1:3), and the historian Eusebius records him as the first bishop of Ephesus. The verses just before today's reading warn against the love of money, so “shun all this” points to greed and the quarrels that surround it.

A note on authorship: the Church has always received this letter as inspired and as coming under Paul's name. Many scholars today think the letters to Timothy and Titus were written by a disciple carrying on Paul's teaching; others defend Paul as their author. The question does not change the letter's authority.
str: v. 11: what to flee and what to pursue.
v. 12: the fight, and the good confession already made.
vv. 13–14: a solemn charge before God and Christ.
vv. 15–16: a hymn of praise. Many scholars think the letter is using words already sung or prayed in the Church.
kw: The word comes from the athletic contest as well as from battle. It is a present command: keep on struggling. The prize is not a human honour but eternal life.

To say the same thing, to declare publicly. Timothy made his confession before many witnesses, which many take to mean his baptism and others his ordination (compare 1 Timothy 4:14). Jesus made his before Pilate. The disciple stands where the Master stood.
The shining forth of the Lord at his coming. Timothy's whole ministry is lived between Christ's first witness and this final appearing.
vv: But as for you, man of God, shun all this; pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, endurance, gentleness.
“Man of God” is the old title of Moses, Elijah and the prophets. The list ends with endurance and gentleness: strength that does not turn harsh.
In the presence of God, who gives life to all things, and of Christ Jesus, who in his testimony before Pontius Pilate made the good confession, I charge you
The Creed we pray still names Pontius Pilate, because our faith rests on what happened at a real time and place. Timothy's courage is measured by Christ's own courage on trial.
It is he alone who has immortality and dwells in unapproachable light, whom no one has ever seen or can see; to him be honor and eternal dominion. Amen.
Earthly lords looked very large in the Roman world. This hymn reminds a young pastor who is truly King.
ch: In its teaching on revelation the Catechism uses this verse: God, who “dwells in unapproachable light”, wants to share his own divine life with us (CCC 52). It also teaches that a Christian must profess the faith without equivocation when witness is required (CCC 2471). These two go together in the reading: adoration of the God beyond all sight, and courage in plain daylight before the powers of this world.

r.h: Not to abolish but to fulfil
set: These verses come early in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5–7), after the Beatitudes and the words about salt and light. They open the section where Jesus says “You have heard that it was said” and goes deeper into the commandments (5:21–48). “The law or the prophets” is a way of naming the Scriptures of Israel. Many scholars think Matthew wrote for a community with a strong Jewish Christian background, for whom this question mattered greatly.
str: v. 17: the principle: not abolish but fulfil.
v. 18: the law stands until all is accomplished.
v. 19: doing and teaching belong together.
v. 20: a righteousness that goes further.
kw: Katalyein means to tear down or dissolve, as one pulls down a building. Plēroun means to fill up, to bring to its full measure. Jesus does not replace the house; he brings to completion what it was built for.
The iota stands for the smallest Hebrew letter, yod. The keraia, literally a little horn, is a tiny mark on a letter. The POC has the Malayalam idiom for the same thing.
A key word in Matthew: a life that is right before God. It is not a longer list of duties but a fidelity that reaches the heart, as vv. 21–48 go on to show.
vv: Do not think that I have come to abolish the law or the prophets; I have come not to abolish but to fulfill.
For truly I tell you, until heaven and earth pass away, not one letter, not one stroke of a letter, will pass from the law until all is accomplished.
Nothing God has said falls to the ground. In Matthew the phrase “until all is accomplished” looks toward what God brings to completion in Jesus.
For I tell you, unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven.

This is not contempt for the Pharisees, whose love of the law was real. The Catechism notes that integral observance of the law in letter and spirit was dear to them (CCC 579). Jesus asks his disciples for more, not for less.
ch: The Catechism takes these verses as the key to Jesus' relation to the law (CCC 577–582), and teaches that the Law of the Gospel fulfils, refines, surpasses and leads the Old Law to its perfection (CCC 1967). St Augustine gave the Church its classic saying: the New Testament lies hidden in the Old, and the Old is made plain in the New (CCC 129). This is why the Holy Qurbono reads from both, and why a Christian never treats the Scriptures of Israel as something left behind.

qa: If Jesus did not abolish the law, why do Christians not keep all its food rules and rites?

Theologians such as St Thomas Aquinas distinguish the moral commands, which remain for ever, from the rites and civil rules of ancient Israel, which pointed ahead to Christ and reach their goal in him. The Council of Jerusalem already settled this for Gentile believers (Acts 15). The moral law is not lessened but deepened (CCC 1968).
rite: The title “Apostle” for Mar Timotheos is used in the wider sense: he was not one of the Twelve, but a man sent with Paul, who may include him when he writes “apostles of Christ” (1 Thessalonians 1:1; 2:7). He was young for his task (1 Timothy 4:12) and often unwell (5:23). His memory encourages catechists, parents and young priests: faith passed on by a grandmother and a mother (2 Timothy 1:5) can go on to feed a whole Church.
study: Paul tells Timothy both to flee and to pursue. What must I flee, and what must I pursue, in this season of my life?
How does the faith of our family help the children to love the Old Testament and find Christ in it?

lead: Hebrews points beyond every earthly priesthood to Christ, seated at the Father's right hand as the one high priest. Matthew shows that same Christ among the crowds, giving speech back to a man who could not speak. The priest in heaven and the healer on earth are one Lord. The crowd sees and is amazed, others see and suspect: the same Lord calls for a decision.

r.h: The main point: such a high priest
set: Hebrews calls itself a “word of exhortation” (13:22): a sermon for tired Christians, probably of Jewish background. Its author is not named, and from early times the Church has linked it with Paul's letters. Chapters 7–10 are the heart of the argument, and here the preacher stops to gather up what he has said about Christ's priesthood.
str: vv. 1–2: the summary: a high priest seated in heaven, serving in the true tent.
vv. 3–5: he too must offer; the earthly sanctuary is a sketch and shadow.
v. 6: a more excellent ministry and a better covenant.
kw: The chief thing, the sum of the matter. The preacher tells his hearers exactly what they must take home.
One who performs a public service, and in the Greek Bible a minister of worship. Our word liturgy comes from the same root: Christ himself is the chief minister of the Church's worship.
One who stands between two parties and brings them together. Christ can do this because he is both God and man (1 Timothy 2:5).
vv: we have such a high priest, one who is seated at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in the heavens,
Priests stood to serve (10:11). Christ sits, because his one offering is complete. Psalm 110 stands behind this image.
They offer worship in a sanctuary that is a sketch and shadow of the heavenly one;
The quotation that follows is Exodus 25:40: Moses was shown a pattern on the mountain. A shadow is not nothing. It is real and points to what casts it.
But Jesus has now obtained a more excellent ministry, and to that degree he is the mediator of a better covenant, which has been enacted through better promises.

Hebrews goes on to quote the “new covenant” of Jeremiah 31 (Hebrews 8:8–12). “Better” belongs to the fulfilment God himself promised to Israel; it gives no ground for despising the people to whom he promised it. The Church teaches that the Old Covenant has never been revoked (CCC 121).
ch: The Catechism teaches that everything the priesthood of the Old Covenant prefigured is fulfilled in Christ, the one mediator (CCC 1544). His priesthood is unique, and it is made present through the ministerial priesthood without being lessened. It quotes St Thomas Aquinas: only Christ is the true priest, the others being only his ministers (CCC 1545). Every kohno who stands at the altar stands there as servant of the one High Priest.

r.h: A mouth opened, and two responses
set: Matthew gathers a series of Jesus' mighty works in chapters 8–9. This short scene closes the series, straight after the healing of two blind men, the “they” of v. 32 (9:27–31). A fuller version of the same kind of event comes in 12:22–24, where the charge is answered at length. In the ancient world, as in the Gospels, an affliction like muteness could be attributed to a demon, and Jesus' healing is shown as a victory over evil.
str: v. 32: the mute man is brought.
v. 33: the demon is cast out, he speaks, and the crowds wonder.
v. 34: the Pharisees give another explanation.
kw: The word can mean mute, deaf or both. Isaiah promised that in the day of God's coming “the tongue of the speechless” would sing for joy (Isaiah 35:6).
A title for the chief of the evil spirits. Matthew 12:24 gives the name Beelzebul.
vv: After they had gone away, a demoniac who was mute was brought to him.
The man cannot ask for himself, so others bring him. A family or a parish can be the voice of those who cannot speak.
And when the demon had been cast out, the one who had been mute spoke; and the crowds were amazed and said, “Never has anything like this been seen in Israel.”
The crowds are the people of Israel themselves, and their wonder is an honest beginning of faith.
But the Pharisees said, “By the ruler of the demons he casts out the demons.”

The fact is not denied, only its meaning. The Gospel does not ask us to condemn a group of people; it warns any religious person, ourselves included, that seeing good done can harden rather than open the heart.
ch: The Catechism says just this of Jesus' signs: they attest that the Father has sent him and invite faith, but they can also be occasions for offence, and despite his evident miracles some reject him and even accuse him of acting by the power of demons (CCC 548). His exorcisms show the coming of the Kingdom and the defeat of Satan's reign (CCC 550).

rite: Tomorrow is Kohne Sunday, the commemoration of the departed priests. Today's epistle prepares for it well: priests die, but the priesthood of Christ does not. It is a good evening to pray by name for the priests who baptised us, absolved us and taught us.
study: Hebrews gives one “main point”. If I had to give the main point of my faith in one sentence, what would it be?
Whom do I know who has no voice, and how can I bring that person to Christ?

lead: Before the Great Fast the Malankara Church keeps two Sundays of remembrance: today the departed priests (kohne), and next Sunday, Aneede, the departed faithful. The readings stand at the graveside of God's servants and ask what remains when a priest dies. Aaron dies on Mount Hor and his vestments pass to his son (Numbers). The preacher of Hebrews tells us to remember our leaders and imitate their faith, because “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever”. Jesus asks who is the faithful and wise servant whom the master finds at work when he arrives.

The other readings of the day circle the same theme. The evening Gospel gives the parable of the pounds, entrusted and accounted for (Luke 19:11–27). Joshua's death closes the story of the land (Joshua 24:29–33). Sirach praises Aaron, anointed for an everlasting covenant (Sirach 45:15–22). Isaiah promises joy to God's servants (Isaiah 65:13–16). Paul takes leave of the elders of Ephesus and tells them to keep watch over the flock (Acts 20:25–38). The key words today are handing on, remembering and being found faithful.

r.h: Aaron's vestments pass to Eleazar
set: Israel is near the end of the forty years. This same chapter has just told of the waters of Meribah, where Moses and Aaron failed to show God's holiness before the people (20:2–13), and of Edom refusing them passage (20:14–21). Now the generation of the Exodus begins to pass away: Miriam has died at Kadesh (20:1), Aaron dies here, and Moses will die in sight of the land (Deuteronomy 34).

Aaron was the first high priest, consecrated with his sons in Leviticus 8 and clothed in the vestments described in Exodus 28. Numbers 33:38–39 dates his death to the fortieth year after the Exodus, at the age of one hundred and twenty-three. The place of Mount Hor is not known for certain; an old tradition points to a peak near Petra called Jebel Harun, “Aaron's mountain”. Deuteronomy 10:6 places his death at Moserah, a different stage of the journey, which suggests that Israel kept more than one record of the route.
str: vv. 22–23: the people arrive at Mount Hor, on the border of Edom.
v. 24: God's word: Aaron will not enter the land.
vv. 25–26: the command: go up, strip, clothe.
vv. 27–28: it is done, in the sight of all; Aaron dies on the top.
v. 29: thirty days of mourning.
¶ The scene has very few words and no speech from Aaron. The whole weight falls on the single action with the vestments.
kw: A Hebrew idiom for death, used also of Abraham and Isaac (Genesis 25:8; 35:29). Death is pictured as joining those who went before, not as vanishing. The POC renders it “shall join his fathers”.
The same priestly garments that made Aaron high priest are taken off him and placed on Eleazar. The office does not belong to the man. It is received, carried, and handed on.
The Hebrew word for priest. The Syriac kohno, plural kohne, which gives today's Sunday its name, is from the same family of words.
vv: “Let Aaron be gathered to his people. For he shall not enter the land that I have given to the Israelites, because you rebelled against my command at the waters of Meribah.
The high priest who has interceded for Israel for forty years also needs mercy. The Bible does not make its priests into idols, and neither should we.
Moses stripped Aaron of his vestments, and put them on his son Eleazar; and Aaron died there on the top of the mountain.

Aaron's brother does this for him on the mountain, while the people watch from below (v. 27). It must have been one of the hardest things Moses ever did, and the text says only that he did it. Aaron gives up everything before he dies, and the service of God does not stop for a single day.
When all the congregation saw that Aaron had died, all the house of Israel mourned for Aaron thirty days.
They see Eleazar come down in Aaron's vestments, and they understand. Israel will mourn Moses for the same thirty days (Deuteronomy 34:8). Grief for a priest is a true part of faith.
ch: Hebrews gives the Christian reading of this scene: “the former priests were many in number, because they were prevented by death from continuing in office; but he holds his priesthood permanently, because he continues forever” (Hebrews 7:23–24). Aaron's vestments had to pass from one body to the next. Christ's priesthood does not pass away. The Catechism sees the priesthood of Aaron as a sign that prepares for Christ's (CCC 1539–1544), and teaches that those ordained share in his one priesthood (CCC 1545). When a bishop or priest dies, the Church mourns the man, and the one Priest goes on serving at the altar through another.

r.h: Remember your leaders; go to him outside the camp
set: The last chapter of Hebrews turns from high argument to practical counsel. The hearers are weary, and their first teachers seem to have died. The author is not named. The Church's tradition counts it among the epistles of St Paul, and today's lectionary lists it so; many scholars today, Catholics included, think that a companion or disciple of Paul wrote it. Either way the Church receives it as inspired Scripture.

The section is framed by the word about “leaders” (vv. 7 and 17). Behind vv. 11–13 stands the Day of Atonement, when the bodies of the sacrificed animals were burned outside the camp (Leviticus 16:27).
str: v. 7: remember your leaders and imitate their faith.
v. 8: the unchanging Christ.
vv. 9–10: not strange teachings; we have an altar.
vv. 11–13: Jesus suffered outside the gate; let us go to him.
v. 14: no lasting city here.
vv. 15–16: the sacrifices that please God: praise and sharing.
kw: Those who go ahead and guide. The word is general and does not yet name a fixed office, but it is about those who preached the word and led the community.
The way out, the end of a course. Many read it here as the way their lives ended: they kept faith to the last. Look at how they finished, and imitate that.
A phrase from the Greek Old Testament for the thank-offering (compare Psalm 50:14). “The fruit of lips” echoes the Greek text of Hosea 14:2. Praise itself is an offering to God.
Translated here “share what you have”. The same word means fellowship and communion. Sharing with those in need is called a sacrifice alongside praise.
vv: Remember your leaders, those who spoke the word of God to you; consider the outcome of their way of life, and imitate their faith.

This verse is today's commemoration in one line. We remember, we look at the end of their road, and we imitate. It is their faith that we are told to imitate, because a priest, like all of us, may have faults.
Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.
Set straight after v. 7, this verse gives the reason for hope. Leaders die, and Christ remains. The Lord whom our departed priests preached yesterday is the one we receive today.
We have an altar from which those who officiate in the tent have no right to eat.

The meaning is debated. Some interpreters think of the Cross, the place of Christ's sacrifice; many Catholic interpreters also hear in it the Eucharistic table, where that sacrifice is received. The two belong together in the Church's faith.
Therefore Jesus also suffered outside the city gate in order to sanctify the people by his own blood. Let us then go to him outside the camp and bear the abuse he endured.

Golgotha lay outside the walls. To follow Jesus is to leave security for his sake. This is an exhortation to Christians to share his shame. It does not condemn the people of Israel, who are not to blame as a people for his death (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597).
Through him, then, let us continually offer a sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips that confess his name.
Do not neglect to do good and to share what you have, for such sacrifices are pleasing to God.
Altar and alms belong together.
ch: The Catechism lists “sacrifice of praise” among the names of the Eucharist, with this verse behind it (CCC 1330). The Holy Qurbono is exactly that: through Christ, an offering of praise, joined to the sharing of what we have. The Church's care to honour those who taught the faith also goes back to very early times; the commemoration of the departed priests within the liturgy expresses Hebrews 13:7 in prayer.

r.h: The servant found at work
set: This parable belongs to Jesus' last great discourse, about the end of the age (Matthew 24–25). It comes right after the warning “you also must be ready” (24:44). Luke gives a parallel in which Peter asks whom the parable is for (Luke 12:41–46); the answer there points especially to those given charge over others. On Kohne Sunday the Church hears it with its priests in mind, and every one of us has some household to care for.
In a large household of that time a trusted slave could be placed over the others and manage the master's goods. When the owner was away for a long time, his character was tested.
str: v. 45: the question: who is the faithful and wise servant?
vv. 46–47: the master finds him at work and raises him.
vv. 48–49: the other way: “My master is delayed”.
vv. 50–51: the unexpected return and the judgment.
kw: The NRSV says “slave”; the POC says ഭൃത്യൻ, servant. The word is harsh to our ears, but Paul and others took it as a title of honour for a minister of Christ (Romans 1:1).
Trustworthy with what was given, and clear-sighted about what time it is. Matthew uses phronimos for the wise builder (7:24) and the wise bridesmaids (25:2).
The servant's whole task is ordinary: food, on time, for others. Pastoral holiness is mostly this.
Literally cut in two, a harsh image of final judgment. Many interpreters take it as a figure of utter punishment and separation; the POC renders it as to punish.
vv: “Who then is the faithful and wise slave, whom his master has put in charge of his household, to give the other slaves their allowance of food at the proper time?
The servant is put in charge of his fellow servants, not raised out of their number. For a priest, the food is the word and the Holy Qurbono, given on time and every time.
Blessed is that slave whom his master will find at work when he arrives.
The beatitude is for being found at work, not for knowing the date.
But if that wicked slave says to himself, ‘My master is delayed,’
The danger begins in a thought said to oneself. Delay tempts leaders to treat the household as their own.
and he begins to beat his fellow slaves, and eats and drinks with drunkards,
Two failures: harshness toward the people in his care and self-indulgence. The Lord takes the abuse of those in one's care very seriously.
He will cut him in pieces and put him with the hypocrites, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.
Matthew's strongest language is kept for those who misuse a trust. It is a warning to every person with authority, and also the Lord's protection of the little ones.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the ordained priesthood is ministerial, “in the strict sense of the term a service” (CCC 1551). St Augustine said to his people, in words that the Second Vatican Council quotes: for you I am a bishop, with you I am a Christian (Sermon 340; Lumen Gentium 32). St Gregory the Great opens his Pastoral Rule by calling the care of souls the art of arts (in substance). Every one of them knew that he too would give an account.

qa: Why do we pray for priests who have died? Were they not holy men?

They were men who served God, and they were also sinners who needed mercy, like Aaron. From the earliest times the Church has prayed for the dead, trusting that they may be fully purified before they see God (2 Maccabees 12:45; CCC 958, 1032), and she offers the Eucharistic sacrifice for them (CCC 1371). Our prayer is also a debt of thanks.
If a priest has sinned, are the sacraments he celebrated still real?

Yes. The Church teaches that the sacraments act by the power of Christ, not by the personal holiness of the minister (CCC 1128), and that the unworthiness of the minister does not prevent Christ from acting (CCC 1584). The minister is not preserved from all human weakness, and his faults can harm the Church (CCC 1550), so the warning of today's Gospel remains. But the people of God are not left without grace.
Does “outside the camp” mean that Christians have left Judaism behind as worthless?

No. Hebrews is calling Christians to share Christ's shame, and the argument about the old sanctuary is about fulfilment. The Church honours the covenant with Israel, which God has never revoked (CCC 121, 839), and rejects blaming the Jewish people for the death of Jesus (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597).
rite: Kohne Sunday, in the West Syriac tradition of the Malankara Church, is an act of gratitude and intercession before the Great Fast begins. The Church remembers those who stood at the altar, baptised and absolved, and buried our dead. It is a day to name the priests of our parish and family, to visit their graves where we can, and to offer the Holy Qurbono for them. Then the same Sunday asks us to pray for our living priests, who carry today what those others carried before them, and to encourage the young men who may hear the same call.
study: Which priest brought me closest to God? What in his faith can I imitate this week?
Aaron's vestments passed on in one action. How do we hand on responsibility in our parish and family without clinging to it?
Hebrews joins praise and sharing as sacrifices. How do the two go together in my Holy Qurbono and in my week?
What “household” has the Lord put in my care, and in what way am I giving them food at the proper time?

lead: Three readings tell one story from three sides. Acts gives the event: a man on a road, a light, a voice, and blindness. Galatians gives Paul's own telling, years later, without excuses: God “was pleased to reveal his Son to me”. John gives the prayer of Jesus the night before he died, “that they may all be one”. The man who tried to tear the Church apart became a builder of her unity, and the voice he heard on the road already told him why: to hurt Christ's disciples is to hurt Christ. The key words are call, revelation and one.

r.h: Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?
set: Saul first appears at the stoning of Stephen, where the witnesses lay their coats at his feet (Acts 7:58), and he then goes after the believers in Jerusalem (8:1–3). When many of them scatter, he goes further. Damascus lay several days' journey to the north and had a substantial Jewish community. Many scholars place this event in the mid-thirties of the first century.

Saul acts out of zeal for God as he understands it, not out of cynicism (compare Galatians 1:14; Philippians 3:6). Saul, the disciples and the synagogues he names were all Jewish, so this is a struggle inside the Jewish community of that time. It is not a contest between Jews and Christians as we use those names today, and it gives no ground for blaming the Jewish people.
str: vv. 1–2: Saul's mission, with letters from the high priest.
vv. 3–4: the light, the fall, and the voice.
vv. 5–6: “Who are you, Lord?” and the answer.
v. 7: his companions hear, but see no one.
vv. 8–9: three days without sight, food or drink.
¶ Luke tells this story three times (Acts 9, 22, 26), which shows how much it mattered to him. Today's reading stops before Ananias comes. Saul is left in the dark, waiting.
kw: An early name for the followers of Jesus (Acts 19:9, 23; 22:4; 24:14), a Jewish way of speaking of a life walked with God. The POC gives its sense as “the way of Christ”.

The name is doubled, as when God called Abraham (Genesis 22:11), Jacob (46:2), Moses (Exodus 3:4) and Samuel (1 Samuel 3:10). The call comes in the form Israel's great ones heard. Luke uses the Hebrew form of the name here.
To pursue, to hunt down. The Lord uses this verb twice (vv. 4–5), and each time its object is himself.
vv: Meanwhile Saul, still breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord, went to the high priest
“Breathing” is almost literal: this is the air he lives in. Grace meets him at the height of his sin, not after a slow improvement.
He fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to him, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?”
The voice does not say “my disciples”. It says “me”. This is the seed of what Paul later teaches about the Body of Christ (1 Corinthians 12:12, 27).
He asked, “Who are you, Lord?” The reply came, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.

“Lord” may be only a respectful address at first, but it becomes the truth. For Saul, a crucified man he took for a false Messiah is alive and speaks from heaven. Everything he thought he knew must be rebuilt.
Saul got up from the ground, and though his eyes were open, he could see nothing; so they led him by the hand and brought him into Damascus.
The man who came to lead others away bound is now led by the hand.
For three days he was without sight, and neither ate nor drank.
Many readers hear a passage through death to life in the three days, and a preparation for the baptism he receives from Ananias (9:18). Fasting before baptism is an ancient Christian practice.
ch: St Augustine, preaching on the Ascension, says that Christ, though seated in heaven, still suffers on earth in his members; that is why the Head cried out, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (in substance). The Catechism points to Paul's conversion as the moment he proclaimed Jesus as Son of God (CCC 442, quoting Galatians 1:15–16 and Acts 9:20). The same teaching on the Church as Christ's Body is set out in CCC 787–795. Whatever is done to the least of his people is done to him (compare Matthew 25:40).

r.h: God was pleased to reveal his Son to me
set: Paul writes to Churches in Galatia that are troubled by teachers who question his authority and his Gospel. He answers with his own story. He wants to show that his Gospel did not come from a human source: he received it by “a revelation of Jesus Christ” (1:12). So he is careful about who he saw, where, and when. This is the only first-hand account of his calling apart from brief mentions, and he gives it for a purpose, not as autobiography.
str: vv. 13–14: his earlier life: persecutor and zealot.
vv. 15–16a: God's act: set apart, called, revealed.
vv. 16b–17: no human consultation; Arabia and Damascus.
vv. 18–20: after three years, fifteen days with Cephas; an oath.
vv. 21–24: Syria and Cilicia, and the Churches of Judea glorify God.
kw: God set Paul apart before he was born. Paul uses the language of the call of Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1:5) and of the Servant (Isaiah 49:1). He understands his calling as a prophetic call within Israel's story.
Literally “in me”. The revelation is both a vision of the risen Lord and a work within him. The Son is shown to Paul so that he can be shown through Paul.

The verb means to visit in order to get to know, to inquire; our word history comes from the same root. Fifteen days with Peter must have included much talk about Jesus. Kepha is the Aramaic and Syriac word for rock, the name Jesus gave Simon.
vv: You have heard, no doubt, of my earlier life in Judaism. I was violently persecuting the church of God and was trying to destroy it.

Paul does not hide this. For this reason he calls himself the least of the apostles (1 Corinthians 15:9). He says it with shame about his own actions; it is not a judgement against Israel, whom he never stopped calling his own (Romans 9:3–5; 11:1).

But when God, who had set me apart before I was born and called me through his grace, was pleased to reveal his Son to me, so that I might proclaim him among the Gentiles, I did not confer with any human being,
In this one sentence God is the one who acts: he sets apart, calls and reveals, and Paul receives. Mission is part of the call from the first moment.
but I did not see any other apostle except James the Lord’s brother.
On the word “brother”, see the question below.
they only heard it said, “The one who formerly was persecuting us is now proclaiming the faith he once tried to destroy.”
The Churches he had harmed do not hold on to the grudge.
And they glorified God because of me.
This may be the most beautiful line of the passage. The people he wounded give God the glory for him.
ch: The Catechism quotes these very verses when it speaks of faith in Jesus as Son of God: Paul's preaching begins from this revelation (CCC 442). St John Chrysostom, who preached seven homilies in praise of Paul, loved to show how fully grace had transformed this man (in substance). For the Church, Paul's past is a permanent lesson: no sinner is beyond the reach of God's call.

r.h: That they may all be one
set: John 17 is the prayer of Jesus at the end of the Last Supper, as he goes to his Passion. Christian tradition calls it his “priestly” prayer (CCC 2747). In vv. 1–5 he prays for his own glorification and in vv. 6–19 for the disciples at the table. Today's verses reach beyond the table to every believer, ourselves included.
str: v. 20: he prays for those who will believe through the disciples' word.
v. 21: that they may be one, as the Father and the Son.
v. 22: the gift of glory, for the sake of unity.
v. 23: “completely one”, so that the world may know.
kw: The Greek is neuter: one reality, as Jesus says “The Father and I are one” (10:30). The model of Christian unity is the communion of the Father and the Son, which is far more than agreement or good manners.
In John, the glory of God is seen in the Son, above all on the Cross. Jesus gives it to believers, so that love and self-giving become the mark of their unity.
From the verb meaning to bring to completion, the same family as Jesus' last word on the Cross in John, “It is finished” (19:30). Unity is a work brought to its end by God.
vv: “I ask not only on behalf of these, but also on behalf of those who will believe in me through their word,
You and I are named in this prayer. Faith comes down to us through a chain of living witnesses.
that they may all be one. As you, Father, are in me and I am in you, may they also be in us, so that the world may believe that you have sent me.
Unity is not only for our own comfort. It is the sign by which the world comes to believe, so division among Christians hides Christ.
I in them and you in me, that they may become completely one, so that the world may know that you have sent me and have loved them even as you have loved me.
The last surprise of the passage: the Father loves believers as he loves the Son.
ch: The Second Vatican Council begins its decree on ecumenism with this thought: division among Christians openly contradicts the will of Christ and scandalises the world (Unitatis Redintegratio 1), and it recalls this prayer in the next section (UR 2). St John Paul II took the words as the title of his encyclical Ut Unum Sint (1995). The Catechism says that Christ always gives his Church the gift of unity, and that the Church must always pray and work for it (CCC 820). The final goal of God's whole plan is our entry into the unity of the Blessed Trinity (CCC 260). St Cyril of Alexandria, commenting on this chapter, saw the one Eucharistic Body as the bond that makes believers one with Christ and one another (in substance).

qa: Did Paul change his religion on the road to Damascus?

He met Jesus as the Messiah of Israel, and that changed everything. But he never stopped worshipping the God of Israel or calling himself an Israelite (Romans 11:1). For this reason many scholars prefer to speak of a call as well as a conversion, and Paul himself uses the language of a prophet's call. The word conversion remains true in the deepest sense: he turned from his sin and his former life to Christ.
Acts 9:7 says his companions heard the voice; Acts 22:9 says they did not. Is this a contradiction?

Acts 9:7 says they “heard the voice but saw no one”; Acts 22:9 says they “saw the light but did not hear the voice”. Luke kept both tellings in one book and saw no problem. A common explanation is that they knew something was happening, a sound and a light, but only Saul understood the message and saw the Lord.
Galatians calls James “the Lord's brother”. Did Mary have other children?

No. The Church teaches Mary's perpetual virginity. In the languages of the Bible the word for brother can include close relatives. The Catechism explains that James and Joseph, called brothers of Jesus, are sons of another Mary, and that they are close relations of Jesus (CCC 500). Some Eastern Fathers thought of them as Joseph's children by an earlier marriage. All agree on Mary's virginity.
rite: This reading speaks closely to Malankara Catholics. Syria and Cilicia (Galatians 1:21) are the home ground of Paul's early mission, and at Antioch the disciples were first called Christians (Acts 11:25–26). The West Syriac tradition we inherit traces its roots to that city, and the chief Anaphora of our Holy Qurbono bears the name of Mar Yakob, the James of today's epistle. On 20 September 1930 the bishops Geevarghese Mar Ivanios and Jacob Mar Theophilos entered into full communion with the Bishop of Rome, so our Church has its own reason to treasure this prayer of Jesus. We pray it with love for our sister Churches, and with humility about our own part in the wounds of division. The Week of Prayer for Christian Unity closes today.
study: Saul was stopped at the height of his certainty. When has God stopped me, and what did I learn in the dark before the light returned?
“They glorified God because of me.” Is there anyone who has given God thanks for what has changed in me? Is there someone whose past I still hold against him?
What can our parish do this year to live Jesus' prayer for unity with Christians of other Churches near us?

lead: On India's Republic Day the two readings speak of what is written and of what is owed. Paul says the Corinthians themselves are a letter of Christ, written on human hearts. Jesus looks at a coin with an emperor's head on it and says: give to the emperor what is his, and to God what is God's. A Christian is a loyal citizen whose deepest belonging is to God, in whose image each person is made.

r.h: A letter of Christ
set: Paul founded the Church at Corinth (Acts 18:1–11), but rival teachers have since arrived, it seems with written recommendations, and questioned his standing. Such letters were a normal and good practice in the early Church (Acts 18:27; Romans 16:1–2). Paul's point is not to despise them but to say that he has something better: the Corinthians themselves.
str: v. 1: do we need letters of recommendation?
vv. 2–3: you are our letter, a letter of Christ, written by the Spirit.
vv. 4–5: our confidence and competence are from God.
kw: A common kind of ancient letter that introduced the bearer to a host or a community. Paul turns the idea round: the living community is the recommendation.
en plaxin lithinais / en plaxin kardiais sarkinais
tablets of stone / tablets of human hearts
Literally “hearts of flesh”. Paul draws together the tablets of Sinai (Exodus 31:18) with God's promises to write the law on the heart (Jeremiah 31:33) and to give a heart of flesh (Ezekiel 36:26).
Sufficiency, being equal to a task. Paul says plainly that it does not come from himself. The same root appears three times in vv. 5–6.
vv: You yourselves are our letter, written on our hearts, to be known and read by all;

A note on the text: most manuscripts read “our hearts”, which the NRSV and the POC follow; a few read “your hearts”. Either way the point stands: people read the Gospel in the life of a community before they read it in a book.
and you show that you are a letter of Christ, prepared by us, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts.
Christ is the author, the Spirit the ink, Paul the hand or courier, the people the page.
Not that we are competent of ourselves to claim anything as coming from us; our competence is from God,
ch: The Catechism uses this very verse: if God's law was written on tablets of stone by the finger of God, then the letter from Christ, entrusted to the care of the apostles, is written with the Spirit of the living God on the hearts of men (CCC 700). The New Law is written by the Holy Spirit on the heart (CCC 1965–1966). The Church does not read this as setting aside Israel's law as worthless. She reads it as the fulfilment of what the prophets foretold.

r.h: Give to the emperor, and to God
set: Jesus is in Jerusalem in his last days, teaching in the Temple. Some Pharisees and Herodians, who did not normally share a cause, come together to test him. The question was painful: since AD 6 Judea had paid a direct tax to Rome, and Judas the Galilean had raised a revolt against it (Acts 5:37). To answer “Yes” would look like betraying his people's hopes; to answer “No” could be reported to the Romans as sedition. This is one group's test of Jesus, not a judgement on a people.
str: vv. 15–17: the trap, with flattery first.
vv. 18–19: “Show me the coin.”
vv. 20–21: the question and the answer.
v. 22: they are amazed and go away.
kw: The NRSV has “head”, the literal sense is “image”, and the POC has “രൂപം”. A denarius of the emperor Tiberius bore his head and a title calling him son of the divine Augustus. The same word is used in the Greek Bible for the image of God in humanity (Genesis 1:26–27).
Not simply “give”, but to pay what is owed. The word assumes a real debt to the state, and a far greater debt to God.
A word from the theatre: actors behind a mask. The questioners' flattery hides their purpose, and the fact that they can produce such a coin shows that they already use it.
vv: Show me the coin used for the tax.” And they brought him a denarius.
Jesus seems to have none himself.
Then he said to them, “Whose head is this, and whose title?”
They answered, “The emperor’s.” Then he said to them, “Give therefore to the emperor the things that are the emperor’s, and to God the things that are God’s.”

The answer is neither revolt nor worship of the state. It gives the state its proper place, and thereby limits it. The second half is the larger: the coin bears Caesar's image; what bears God's image?
ch: Early Christians read the saying this way: the coin with Caesar's image goes to Caesar, and the human being, who bears God's image, goes to God; so Tertullian and St Augustine (in substance). The Catechism teaches that citizens have a duty to contribute to the good of society, that it is morally obligatory to pay taxes, to vote and to defend one's country (CCC 2238–2240), and it quotes this verse to teach that one must refuse obedience when civil commands are contrary to the moral order (CCC 2242). The early Letter to Diognetus, quoted in CCC 2240, says that Christians live in their own lands as resident aliens, sharing everything as citizens (in substance).

qa: Does this saying mean that religion should keep out of public life?

No. Jesus does not divide life into two separate rooms, because everything belongs finally to God. The Council teaches that the Church and the political community are independent in their own fields, and that both serve the same human persons (Gaudium et Spes 76). Christians take part in public life as citizens, guided by conscience.
rite: The Constitution of India came into force on 26 January 1950 and, among much else, protects liberty of conscience and of religion for all persons (Article 25). Today Malankara Catholics give thanks for the land we love. We pray for those who govern and those who are governed (1 Timothy 2:1–2), for justice, and for all who suffer. We serve the nation best as a “letter of Christ”, in honest work, in paying what we owe, in care for the poor, and in peace with all.
study: If someone read my family's life as a letter, what would it say about Christ?
What do I owe my country as a citizen, and what do I owe God alone? Where do I find it hard to keep the two in order?

lead: Both readings today are about marriage, and both refuse to treat it as a merely private arrangement. Ephesians measures the love of husband and wife by the love of Christ for the Church. In Matthew, Jesus takes a permission in the Law and leads his hearers back to what God wanted from the beginning. Together they say that marriage is a promise on which God himself has staked something.

r.h: As Christ loved the Church
set: This passage belongs to a “household code”, a common form of moral teaching in the Greek and Roman world that set out the duties of wives and husbands, children and parents, slaves and masters. Other examples in the New Testament are Colossians 3:18–4:1 and 1 Peter 2:18–3:7. The letter names Paul as its author, though many scholars think a disciple wrote it in his name; the Church receives it as inspired Scripture either way.

The verse just before the reading governs everything: “Be subject to one another out of reverence for Christ” (5:21). In Greek, verse 22 has no verb of its own and borrows it from verse 21, so the instruction to wives is one case of a duty laid on all. What is new is not the form but what fills it. The code of that time told husbands to rule; this one tells them to love, and to give themselves up.
str: vv. 22–24: wives and the Church's response to Christ.
vv. 25–27: husbands and Christ's self-giving, with its echo of washing and of a bride made ready.
vv. 28–30: one flesh: to love one's wife is to love one's own body.
vv. 31–33: Genesis 2:24 quoted, the “great mystery” named, and a closing word to both.
kw: A word of ordered belonging, taken from the language of arrangement. It does not excuse any harm. St John Paul II taught that in Christ this subjection is to be understood as mutual (Mulieris Dignitatem 24). No one can read this passage as permission to dominate or to hurt a wife or husband.
The word the New Testament uses above all for God's love and for the love that gives itself. Household codes of the time did not normally give this command to husbands. Its measure here is the Cross.

In Paul's letters, God's plan once hidden and now revealed in Christ. The Latin Bible renders it sacramentum here. The verse alone does not set out the Church's later teaching on the seven sacraments, but the Church finds in it the root of her understanding of marriage as a sacrament (CCC 1616–1617).
vv: Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her,

The authority a husband may claim is the authority of the one who died for the other. St John Chrysostom, preaching on this verse, tells a husband that he should be ready to give his life for his wife, as Christ did for the Church (in substance).
In the same way, husbands should love their wives as they do their own bodies.
The argument turns on Genesis: the two are one flesh. Care for the other is not an extra virtue; it is care for one's own life.
This is a great mystery, and I am applying it to Christ and the church.
The writer reads Genesis 2:24 on two levels. Human marriage is real and good in itself, and it is also a sign of something larger: God's marriage with his people.
ch: The Catechism quotes this passage when it teaches that the whole Christian life bears the mark of the spousal love of Christ and the Church, and it calls Baptism a kind of nuptial bath that comes before the wedding feast, the Eucharist (CCC 1616–1617). Christ is the source of the grace by which couples can live this love (CCC 1642). St John Paul II, in Mulieris Dignitatem 24, says that the newness of the Gospel lies in this mutual subjection, even though the wording of the time remains in the text.

r.h: Back to the beginning
set: These two verses are one of the six sayings in the Sermon on the Mount that run “You have heard... but I say to you” (5:21–48). Jesus has just said that he came not to abolish the Law but to fulfil it (5:17). Each saying goes to the root of a commandment, and this one follows the saying on adultery in the heart (5:27–30).

The certificate comes from Deuteronomy 24:1–4. It gave a dismissed wife some protection, because it showed that she was able to marry again. Later Jewish writings record a debate between teachers over what grounds were sufficient for divorce. Matthew 19:3–9 gives the fuller version of Jesus' answer, going back to Genesis: “from the beginning it was not so” (19:8).
str: v. 31: the provision people knew: a certificate of divorce.
v. 32: Jesus' word, with its exception clause, and its effect on the wife and on the one who marries her.
kw: The legal document of dismissal in Deuteronomy 24. In that society only the husband normally issued it, which left the woman in the weaker position. Jesus' teaching protects her as well as the bond.
A broad word for sexual wrongdoing, found in the exception clause here and in 19:9. Its exact meaning in these verses is debated; see the question below.
vv: It was also said, ‘Whoever divorces his wife, let him give her a certificate of divorce.’
Jesus does not deny that Moses said this. In 19:8 he explains that it was allowed because of hardness of heart, and was never the plan.
But I say to you that anyone who divorces his wife, except on the ground of unchastity, causes her to commit adultery;

A dismissed woman of that time would usually have had to remarry to live. Jesus says the man who dismisses her bears responsibility for what follows. He puts the weight on the one who holds the power.
ch: The Church holds that Jesus taught plainly the original meaning of marriage, and that the permission given by Moses was a concession to the hardness of hearts (CCC 1614). A valid marriage between the baptized, once consummated, cannot be dissolved by any human power (CCC 1640). The Catechism also says that those who follow this teaching are not left on their own: by coming to Christ they receive the strength to live marriage in the new way of the Kingdom (CCC 1615).

qa: What does “except on the ground of unchastity” mean? Does Jesus allow divorce after all?

Catholic scholars give two main explanations. One is that porneia here means a union that was unlawful from the start, such as a marriage within the degrees of kinship forbidden in Leviticus 18; such a union is not a true marriage to begin with. The other, found in St Jerome and many later writers, is that a spouse may separate in such a case but not marry another. The Church's teaching does not depend on settling this. She holds that a valid, consummated sacramental marriage cannot be dissolved (CCC 1640). She allows separation when living together has become practically impossible (CCC 1649), and a tribunal may declare after examination that a marriage was never valid (CCC 1629). Those who have divorced and remarried civilly remain part of the Church, and she asks that they be cared for with attentive concern (CCC 1650–1651).
rite: In the Syriac marriage service the couple are crowned, and the Catechism notes that in the Eastern traditions the priest's blessing is itself necessary for the sacrament (CCC 1623). The crown of a Christian marriage is not an award for a happy home. It belongs to the one who has learned to give his or her life for another, and so it stands close to the crown of the martyrs.
study: Ephesians 5:21 comes before all the instructions. How would my home change if each of us began from “be subject to one another”?
Jesus protects the person with less power in Matthew 5:32. Who is in that weaker place in the marriages and families I know, and what can I do for them?

lead: In this week after Kohne Sunday the Church is still thinking of those who led her. Hebrews tells a tired community to remember its leaders, to hold on to the Christ who does not change, and to offer the sacrifices of praise and of sharing. John takes us into the Upper Room, where Jesus comforts frightened disciples and answers the question of the way. St Thomas the Apostle asks the question; St Thomas Aquinas, remembered today, gave his life to its answer.

r.h: Outside the camp, with the one who does not change
set: Hebrews calls itself a “word of exhortation” (13:22). It is a sermon for Christians, probably of Jewish background, who were growing tired. Its author is not named. Chapter 13 gathers its last practical counsels.

Verses 11–13 draw on the Day of Atonement: the bodies of the animals whose blood was carried into the sanctuary were burned outside the camp (Leviticus 16:27). The writer sees in this a sign of Jesus, who died outside the walls of Jerusalem (compare John 19:20). His point is to call Christians to Christ, not to speak against Israel's worship, which he sees as a shadow pointing forward (10:1).
str: vv. 7–8: remember your leaders; Christ remains the same.
vv. 9–10: do not be led astray by strange teachings; we have an altar.
vv. 11–14: Jesus outside the gate; let us go to him; we have no lasting city.
vv. 15–16: the two sacrifices that please God: praise and sharing.
kw: Those who go ahead of others. The word appears again at 13:17 and 13:24. In verse 7 the leaders seem to be those who have already died, since the people are told to consider the outcome of their lives. It is a fitting word for the week of Kohne.

“We have an altar” (v. 10). Commentators differ on what this means here: many take it as the Cross, and many Catholic writers also hear the Eucharistic table. The text does not settle it, and the two are not rivals, because the Eucharist makes present the one sacrifice of the Cross.
An Old Testament expression (see Psalm 50:14, 23). “The fruit of lips” comes from Hosea 14:2. The Catechism names “sacrifice of praise” among the names of the Eucharist, citing this verse (CCC 1330).
vv: Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever.
It stands between the memory of leaders who have gone and the warning against new teachings. Leaders die and fashions change. The one they preached does not.
Let us then go to him outside the camp and bear the abuse he endured.
To be with Christ may mean leaving the safe place. Holiness is found not by keeping away from the place of shame, but by going where he went.
Do not neglect to do good and to share what you have, for such sacrifices are pleasing to God.
Worship and sharing are named with the same word, sacrifice. The hand that gives is doing what the lips do at the altar.
ch: The Catechism uses this passage when it lists the names of the Eucharist (CCC 1330). It also teaches that the Eucharist is the sacrifice of the whole Church, and that the lives of the faithful, their praise, sufferings, prayer and work are joined to Christ's offering and gain a new value (CCC 1368). Every Holy Qurbono joins the two things the reading holds together: praise of God and care for the neighbour.

r.h: I am the way, and the truth, and the life
set: We are at the supper on the night before Jesus died. He has washed the disciples' feet (13:1–20). Judas has gone out into the night (13:30), Jesus has said that he is leaving them (13:33), and Peter has just been told that he will deny him (13:38). Chapters 14–17 are often called the Farewell Discourse. The fear in the room is real, and these words answer it.
str: v. 1: the command not to be troubled, and the call to believe.
vv. 2–4: the Father's house and the promise to come again.
vv. 5–6: Thomas's question and Jesus' answer.
kw: A verb used of water being stirred (John 5:7). John also uses it of Jesus himself, before the tomb of Lazarus (11:33), facing his hour (12:27) and at the betrayal (13:21). The one who says “Do not let your hearts be troubled” knows what it is to be troubled.

From menein, to remain, a favourite word of John. The word occurs in the New Testament only here and at 14:23, where the Father and the Son make their home with the one who loves. The Latin mansiones gave the old English “mansions”, but the point is staying with God, not grand houses.
The first Christians were called people of “the Way” (Acts 9:2). Jesus does not only show a road. He says he is the road.
vv: Do not let your hearts be troubled. Believe in God, believe also in me.
“Your” is plural: he speaks to the whole frightened group. The second part puts faith in Jesus beside faith in God, which is a large claim made on a very dark night.
And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and will take you to myself, so that where I am, there you may be also.
Heaven is described here not as a place first but as being with him. The Catechism takes this up: to live in heaven is to be with Christ (CCC 1025).
I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.
Thomas asked an honest question, and the Lord does not scold him. He answers about himself. Truth and life here are not ideas but a person.
ch: Left to its own powers, humanity has no access to the Father's house, says the Catechism, and only Christ can open it (CCC 661). St Thomas Aquinas, in his commentary on John, says that Christ is both the way and the goal: the way in his humanity, the goal in his divinity (in substance). The Second Vatican Council quotes this verse when it says that the Church must always proclaim Christ, even as she respects whatever is true and holy in other religions (Nostra Aetate 2).

qa: If no one comes to the Father except through Jesus, what happens to people who never knew him?

The Church holds both truths. All salvation comes through Christ. Yet those who, through no fault of their own, do not know the Gospel, but seek God with a sincere heart and try by grace to do his will, may also reach eternal salvation (Lumen Gentium 16; CCC 847). They too are saved through Christ, even without knowing his name, and this does not take away the Church's duty to proclaim him (CCC 848).
rite: Thomas is the Apostle whom the St Thomas Christians of India honour as their father in faith, and here he is the one who dares to say “we do not know”. St Thomas Aquinas (died 1274), Doctor of the Church, is remembered today in our calendar. In this week of Kohne we may thank God for the priests who first showed us the way, and imitate their faith as Hebrews asks.
study: Hebrews 13:7 asks me to remember those who spoke the word of God to me. Whom do I remember, and what in their faith can I imitate this week?
Thomas says plainly that he does not know the way. What is the honest question I need to bring to the Lord?

lead: Today's readings speak of giving oneself away. Paul asks Christians to offer their bodies as a living sacrifice, and to use their different gifts as members of one body. In John, Jesus answers some visiting Greeks by speaking of a grain of wheat that must die to bear fruit. Mar Ignatius of Antioch, remembered today, took up that same picture of wheat on his way to martyrdom.

r.h: A living sacrifice, one body
set: Paul wrote to the Christians of Rome, probably from Corinth about AD 57, before a visit he hoped to make. For eleven chapters he has set out what God has done in Christ. Chapter 12 opens with “therefore”: now he says how to live in response. Everything Paul asks in these chapters rests on “the mercies of God” already shown.
str: vv. 1–2: the offering of the body and the renewal of the mind.
v. 3: a warning against thinking too highly of oneself.
vv. 4–5: one body, many members.
vv. 6–8: seven gifts named, each to be used in its own way.
kw: Latreia is the word for temple service. Logikē can mean spiritual, reasonable or true to the mind, and translators find it hard to carry in one word. Paul means a worship that takes in the person's whole life and understanding.
The same verb is used of the Lord at the Transfiguration (Matthew 17:2; Mark 9:2). It is in the present tense and the passive, an ongoing change that God works in us.
Gifts of grace, from charis, grace. They are given not for the honour of the one who has them but for the body. The list is not only of rare wonders: it includes teaching, giving and showing mercy.
vv: to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God,
The animal on the altar died once. The Christian offering lives and goes on offering, in the body, in the ordinary work of each day.
Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your minds,
Two pressures are named: one from outside, which presses us into a mould, and one from within, as God renews how we think.
so we, who are many, are one body in Christ, and individually we are members one of another.
He does not only say that we belong to Christ. We belong to each other, so that another person's gift is mine, and my gift is his.
ch: The Catechism quotes Romans 12:1 when it says that the moral life is spiritual worship, and that Christian action finds its nourishment in the liturgy and the sacraments (CCC 2031). It quotes verses 6–8 when it speaks of the special graces given for the common good (CCC 2004). At the Holy Qurbono our lives are joined to Christ's offering (CCC 1368), and in that sense we carry our bodies to the altar and carry the altar home.

r.h: Unless a grain of wheat falls
set: This is the Passover of Jesus' death, just after his entry into Jerusalem. The Pharisees have said, “Look, the world has gone after him!” (12:19), and at once John shows us some of that world: Greeks who had come up to worship. They were probably Gentiles drawn to the God of Israel. They approach Philip, and Philip and Andrew both carry Greek names, which may be why they turn to them. John does not tell us whether the Greeks ever met Jesus; his answer goes beyond them.
str: vv. 20–22: the Greeks' request passes from Philip to Andrew to Jesus.
v. 23: the hour has come.
v. 24: the grain of wheat.
vv. 25–26: what this means for the one who follows.
kw: Up to now John has said that Jesus' hour had not yet come (2:4; 7:30; 8:20). Here, when Gentiles come seeking him, for the first time he says that it has. In John the hour means his death and his glorifying together.
In John the glory of Jesus is seen first in the Cross, where the love of God is shown fully. There is no other glory that comes before it.
In verse 25 this is a Semitic way of speaking about preferring one thing to another; see the question below.
vv: Sir, we wish to see Jesus.
It is the desire of every age. Jesus answers by pointing to the Cross: this is where he will be seen.
unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains just a single grain; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.

The picture answers the Greeks. Jesus alone in Jerusalem could reach only a few; after his death the fruit reaches every nation, as he says a little later: “I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself” (12:32).
Whoever serves me must follow me, and where I am, there will my servant be also.
The same law holds for the disciple as for the Master. The promise at the end of the verse is that the Father himself will honour such a servant.
ch: Tertullian's saying that the blood of martyrs is the seed of Christians, quoted by the Catechism (CCC 852), is this verse lived in the Church's history. The Catechism calls martyrdom the supreme witness to the truth of the faith, and among its examples it quotes the words of Mar Ignatius, who said that it was better for him to die in Christ Jesus than to reign over the ends of the earth (CCC 2473–2474).

qa: Does Jesus really want us to hate our own life?

“Hate” here is a Semitic way of speaking that means to put one thing clearly below another. Compare Luke 14:26 with Matthew 10:37, where the same teaching is given as loving “more than”. Jesus does not ask for contempt of the life God gave. He asks that it never be held on to at the price of following him.
rite: Our Church remembers today Mar Ignatius, called Noorono, the fiery one, bishop of Antioch, the see of the Syriac tradition. Taken under guard to Rome in the reign of Trajan, he wrote letters to the Churches on the way. To the Romans he said that he was God's wheat, to be ground by the teeth of wild beasts so as to become pure bread of Christ (in substance; To the Romans 4). He called the Eucharist the medicine of immortality (To the Ephesians 20; CCC 1405). The Gospel of the grain and the Holy Qurbono meet in him. We also pray today for Joshua Mar Ignathios on his name day.
study: Paul says the offering of the body is true worship. What in my ordinary day could I consciously offer at the next Holy Qurbono?
“We wish to see Jesus.” When people look at my family or my parish, what do they see of him?

lead: On this Saturday before the Lord's Day, both readings ask for a look within. Paul turns the Corinthians' testing of him back on themselves: examine yourselves. Jesus says that a tree is known by its fruit and that the mouth speaks from what fills the heart. Mar Aphrahat, the Persian Sage remembered today, taught that faith is a house that good works must build.

r.h: Test yourselves
set: Chapters 10–13 are the sharpest part of the letter. Rival teachers, whom Paul calls “super-apostles” (11:5; 12:11), had been questioning his authority, and some in Corinth wanted proof that Christ was speaking through him (13:3). Paul is about to come for a third visit (13:1). These verses come near the end of his defence, and he turns it into a pastoral appeal.
str: v. 5: examine yourselves; Christ is in you.
v. 6: Paul's hope that they will see that he has not failed.
v. 7: his prayer: that they do right, even if he seems to fail.
v. 8: the principle: nothing against the truth.
kw: The word for testing metal or coin to see whether it is genuine. A coin that fails is adokimos. The Corinthians have been testing Paul; he asks what the test would show of them. In Greek, the word “yourselves” comes first and is repeated, so that the stress falls on it.
For Paul this is not only a correct statement. It is the Gospel itself and what agrees with it.
vv: Examine yourselves to see whether you are living in the faith. Test yourselves. Do you not realize that Jesus Christ is in you?
The examination is not a search only for what is wrong. Its first discovery is that Christ is present. Paul speaks in the same way of himself: “it is Christ who lives in me” (Galatians 2:20).
But we pray to God that you may not do anything wrong
Here is the heart of a pastor. He prays that they will do what is right even if it makes him look like a failure, for it is their good he wants, not his own reputation.
For we cannot do anything against the truth, but only for the truth.
Even when he is defending himself, Paul will not win by bending the truth. In a quarrel, this is the hardest rule to keep.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the sacrament of Penance should be prepared for by an examination of conscience made in the light of the word of God (CCC 1454). St Paul uses the same word to the Corinthians about coming to the Eucharist: “Examine yourselves, and only then eat of the bread and drink of the cup” (1 Corinthians 11:28; CCC 1385). A Saturday evening is a good hour for it, before the Holy Qurbono of the Lord's Day.

r.h: From the abundance of the heart
set: Jesus has just healed a man who was blind and mute, and some Pharisees say that he drives out demons by the ruler of the demons (12:22–24). He answers them and warns about blasphemy against the Holy Spirit (12:31–32). Today's words follow directly, so they first concern these particular opponents and what they said about the work of the Spirit. The Pharisees were not all of one mind, and many scholars think that Matthew's sharp tone also reflects the disputes of his own day. The teaching itself is for every disciple.
str: v. 33: the tree and its fruit.
vv. 34–35: the heart and the mouth, the treasure and what comes from it.
vv. 36–37: the account to be given for words.
kw: What overflows. Speech is what spills over when the heart is full. Under pressure, a person's words show what was stored.
The word can mean both what is stored and the place of storing. See 6:21: “where your treasure is, there your heart will be also”.
Argos means idle or not working. It is a word that does no good work, spoken without thought.
vv: for the tree is known by its fruit.
Those who called his good work evil are told to look at the fruit: a man has been healed. The same test applies to us (7:16).
You brood of vipers! How can you speak good things, when you are evil? For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.
John the Baptist used the same harsh words (3:7). They are a prophet's warning to those who should have known better, not a description of a people.
I tell you, on the day of judgment you will have to give an account for every careless word you utter;
Words are not small things. James says the same at length (James 3:2–10).
ch: The Catechism says that the heart is the seat of moral personality, and that sin has its root there, as charity also does (CCC 2517, 1853). It warns against rash judgment, detraction and calumny as sins of the tongue against the truth and against a neighbour's good name (CCC 2477). Changing the words alone will not do. The Lord asks for a change in the tree.

qa: Must I really answer for every careless word? Who could survive that?

Jesus is not trying to frighten people into silence. He is saying that words matter because they show the heart, and that God takes us seriously. The same Lord forgives those who come to him, and the sacrament of Penance is there for the sins of the tongue as for others. James says that all of us make many mistakes (3:2). The right answer to this saying is not fear but an examination of conscience, and a heart more often filled with good.
rite: The Syriac tradition remembers today Mar Jacob Aphrahat, the Persian Sage, who lived in the Persian Empire in the fourth century and is the earliest Syriac Father whose writings have come down to us. His Demonstrations open with one on faith, which he compares to a house built on the rock who is Christ, and he says that the house must be raised with works such as pure fasting, pure prayer, love and almsgiving (in substance). The tree and its fruit is his teaching too.
study: Paul says the first thing to look for is that Christ is in me. How would this change the way I make my examination of conscience tonight?
Thinking back over this week's words, what do they tell me about what is filling my heart?

lead: Last Sunday the Church remembered her departed priests. Today, Aneede Sunday, she remembers all the faithful departed, and next Sunday the Great Fast begins. So before the road to Easter opens, the Church gathers her dead and reads about what death is, and what it is not.

The lectionary gives many readings. The Evening Gospel is the judgment of the nations, where the king says, “just as you did it to one of the least of these who are members of my family, you did it to me” (Matthew 25:40). The Old Testament lessons look at death from several sides. Jacob “breathed his last, and was gathered to his people” (Genesis 49:33). Sirach tells us, “Do not fear death’s decree for you” (Sirach 41:3). Hezekiah, spared from death, sings to God, “you have cast all my sins behind your back” (Isaiah 38:17). The Catholic Epistle looks ahead to “new heavens and a new earth, where righteousness is at home” (2 Peter 3:13).

Three readings are studied here. In 2 Maccabees, Judas and his men pray and offer sacrifice for their dead. In 1 Thessalonians, Paul writes to Christians who are grieving, so that their grief may have hope in it. In John, Jesus says that the dead will hear his voice. The key words of this Sunday are sleep, hope and voice.

r.h: Prayer for those who have fallen
set: Of the Old Testament lessons this one stands closest to the Gospel, since it rests its action on the hope of the resurrection. Second Maccabees was written in Greek, and presents itself as a summary of a five-volume history by Jason of Cyrene (2:23). It tells of the Jews' struggle in the second century BC, when the Seleucid king Antiochus IV tried to force Greek worship on them and profaned the Temple, and of how Judas Maccabeus and his followers recovered and rededicated it (10:1–8).

Chapter 7 of the same book has the martyrdom of a mother and her seven sons, who die confessing that “the King of the universe will raise us up” (7:9). So this is a book in which the resurrection is already a living faith. Today's passage comes after a battle against Gorgias, the governor of Idumea (12:32–37).
str: v. 38: the army keeps the sabbath at Adullam.
vv. 39–40: gathering the dead, they find the tokens of idols under their tunics.
vv. 41–42: they bless God and pray that the sin be blotted out; Judas warns the living.
v. 43a: the collection, sent to Jerusalem for a sin offering.
vv. 43b–45: the author's own comment: this was done with the resurrection in mind.
kw: Amulets dedicated to the gods of Jamnia, a city on the coast. Deuteronomy 7:25 forbade the Israelites to take such things. These men had fought for the Lord while keeping a charm against the day of danger.
Verse 43 gives this as the reason for Judas's action. It is one of the clearest statements of resurrection faith in the Old Testament, along with Daniel 12:2.
In v. 45, “those who fall asleep in godliness”. This is the word Paul uses in today's Epistle, so that the two readings speak the same language of the dead.
The word for the removal of sin. The dead are named as those who can still be helped, and that help comes from God through the prayer and offering of the living.
vv: So they all blessed the ways of the Lord, the righteous judge, who reveals the things that are hidden;
Their first reaction to finding their brothers' sin is to praise God's justice. Their second is not to condemn the dead, but to pray for them.
He also took up a collection, man by man, to the amount of two thousand drachmas of silver, and sent it to Jerusalem to provide for a sin offering.

Soldiers give their money for the sake of comrades who have been shown to be sinners. Many scholars think that Judas himself may have aimed first at protecting the army from guilt, as in the story of Achan (Joshua 7), and that the author draws out the deeper meaning in the comment that follows.
For if he were not expecting that those who had fallen would rise again, it would have been superfluous and foolish to pray for the dead.
The reasoning is simple, and it is ours. Prayer for the dead makes sense only if they are alive to God.
Therefore he made atonement for the dead, so that they might be delivered from their sin.
This is the verse the Catechism quotes (CCC 1032).
ch: The Catechism cites this verse in its teaching on the final purification, and goes on: “From the beginning the Church has honored the memory of the dead and offered prayers in suffrage for them, above all the Eucharistic sacrifice” (CCC 1032). In the same place it quotes St John Chrysostom, who says that if Job's sons were purified by their father's sacrifice, we should not doubt that our offerings for the dead bring them some consolation (Homilies on 1 Corinthians 41). St Augustine records the request of his mother, St Monica, as she was dying, that wherever they were they should remember her at the altar of the Lord (Confessions IX; CCC 1371). The Church also commends almsgiving and works of penance for the dead (CCC 1032), so Judas's collection has many descendants.

r.h: Grief with hope
set: This is very likely the oldest writing in the New Testament, sent by Paul about AD 50 or 51, probably from Corinth. Paul had founded the Church at Thessalonica but had been forced to leave soon after (Acts 17:1–10). Timothy has now brought him news (3:6). The young Church is firm, but some of its members have died, and those who remain are troubled: what about those who have died before the Lord's coming? Will they miss it?
