Paul does not rebuke their grief. He teaches them what to do with it. “Others” in verse 13 are those who do not share the Christian hope; he is not mocking their sorrow, for he knows the weight of it, but he wants his people to have something more.
str: v. 13: the reason for writing: that they may not grieve without hope.
v. 14: the creed: Jesus died and rose, so God will bring those who have died.
v. 15: those still alive have no advantage.
vv. 16–17: the coming of the Lord, told in the images of the Bible.
v. 18: the purpose of it all: encourage one another.
kw: Paul's word for the dead in vv. 13–15. The NRSV has “those who have died” and the POC keeps “those who have fallen asleep”. Our word cemetery comes from koimētērion, a place of sleeping. It does not mean that the dead are unconscious: Paul can also say that he wants “to depart and be with Christ” (Philippians 1:23). It is the language of one who expects to see someone wake.
The word used for the arrival of a king or high official to a city. In verse 15 it refers to the coming of the Lord.

The word used when the leading people of a city went out to greet an arriving dignitary and escort him in. This may be what Paul has in mind in verse 17: the Church goes out to meet the Lord and returns with him. Matthew 25:6 uses the same word for going out to meet the bridegroom.
vv: so that you may not grieve as others do who have no hope.
He does not say “so that you may not grieve”. Jesus himself wept at the tomb of a friend (John 11:35). The difference is in the kind of grief.
For since we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so, through Jesus, God will bring with him those who have died.
This is the argument in one verse. Paul does not reason from the human soul but from what happened to Jesus, and those who belong to him share it.
Then we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up in the clouds together with them to meet the Lord in the air; and so we will be with the Lord forever.

The word to hold on to is “together”. The living and the dead are not parted in Christ. Paul's “we” may suggest that he hoped to be alive at that day, but he goes on to say that the day will come like a thief in the night (5:2), and no one knows it (compare Matthew 24:36).
Therefore encourage one another with these words.
Doctrine is for comfort. Paul expects this teaching to be spoken at the bedside and at the grave.
ch: The Catechism, quoting Philippians and this verse among others, says that “to live in heaven is to be with Christ” (CCC 1025). Because of Christ, Christian death has a positive meaning (CCC 1010). When the Catechism explains the Christian funeral, it quotes St Symeon of Thessalonica: even in death we are not separated from one another, for we all run the same course and shall find one another again in the same place (CCC 1690). St Symeon, a bishop of the city to which this letter was written, was saying the same thing many centuries later.

r.h: The dead will hear his voice
set: Jesus has healed a man at the pool of Beth-zatha on the sabbath (5:1–9). When he is challenged, he replies, “My Father is still working, and I also am working” (5:17), and “the Jews” seek to kill him for making himself equal to God (5:18). In John this phrase often means the religious authorities who opposed him, not the Jewish people, to whom Jesus and his first disciples belonged (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597). Today's passage is his answer.

Later Jewish writings show the question was familiar: if God rested on the sabbath, how is it that he continues to give life and to judge? Those two works are God's own (Deuteronomy 32:39). Jesus now says that the Father has given both to the Son. Many scholars hear behind vv. 19–20 an everyday picture: a son learning his father's trade by watching him.
str: vv. 19–20: the Son does what he sees the Father doing.
vv. 21–23: two works given to the Son: giving life and judging.
vv. 24–25: already now: whoever hears has passed from death to life.
vv. 26–27: why: life in himself, and authority as Son of Man.
vv. 28–29: still to come: all in their graves will hear his voice.
kw: The word used of God raising the dead (Romans 4:17). In v. 21 it is what the Father does, and also what the Son does for whomever he wishes.
This word recurs four times in the passage (vv. 22, 24, 27, 29). It can mean both a decision and condemnation; the word in v. 29 translated “condemnation” is the same one.
“The hour is coming, and is now here” (v. 25), but in v. 28 only “the hour is coming”. The change is deliberate: there is a life that begins now, and a resurrection of the body that is still to come.
vv: Very truly, I tell you, anyone who hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and does not come under judgment, but has passed from death to life.
The verb is “has”, not “will have”. Eternal life starts at the font, not at the funeral.
the hour is coming, and is now here, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live.

“The dead” here are first of all those dead in spirit who are given life by his word. St Augustine distinguishes the two resurrections in this passage: of the soul now, and of the body at the end (in substance; City of God XX).
all who are in their graves will hear his voice

This is plainly the bodily resurrection. The word for grave recalls a memorial tomb, a place of remembrance. No one in any grave is out of reach of that voice. Lazarus has not yet been called out (11:43), but John has prepared us.
those who have done good, to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil, to the resurrection of condemnation.

This echoes Daniel 12:2. It stands beside v. 24, and the two need each other: faith is not a replacement for good deeds, and the works of faith show what we have heard. The Evening Gospel of the judgment of the nations says the same.
ch: The Catechism quotes vv. 28–29 when it teaches that the resurrection of all the dead will come before the Last Judgment (CCC 1038). It teaches that the full right to pass definitive judgment belongs to Christ as Redeemer, as the Father has given “all judgment to the Son” (CCC 679). It also holds both sides of the “now” and the “not yet”: Christ will raise us on the last day, and yet in a certain way we have already risen with him (CCC 1002). The prayer of the Church over her dead is said in this light. They hear a voice that has already spoken to them at their baptism.

qa: Some Bibles do not have 2 Maccabees. Why does the Church use it to support prayer for the dead?

The Catholic Church counts 2 Maccabees in the canon of Scripture (CCC 120), and so do the Orthodox Churches; the Churches of the Reformation do not, which is why some Bibles leave it out. The book is not the only ground for the practice. Even apart from its inspired status, it shows that faithful Jews were praying for their dead before Christ, as Jewish people still do in their own prayers for the departed today. From the beginning Christians did the same (CCC 958, 1032), and the inscriptions and liturgies of the early Church bear witness to it.
Is “Purgatory” only a Latin idea? Does our Syriac tradition believe it?

The word comes from the Latin tradition, and the Catechism uses it for the final purification of the elect (CCC 1030–1031). The Syriac prayers for the dead do not usually use that word or build a theory around it; they ask mercy and rest for the departed, and offer the Holy Qurbono for them. The faith underneath is one: those who die in God's friendship but are not yet fully purified can be helped by the prayers of the Church. The Council of Florence, which met with Eastern bishops, taught this, while leaving aside the fiery images found in some Western preaching.
Does 1 Thessalonians 4:17 teach a “rapture”, with Christians secretly taken away from the earth?

No. Some modern preachers have read it so, but the Church does not. The passage is about the Lord's public coming, announced with “the sound of God's trumpet” (4:16). Paul's point is that the living and the dead will be with him together. His images come from the Bible's own language of God's coming, and the Catechism teaches the coming of Christ in glory and the final judgment, not a secret removal (CCC 1001, 1038).
rite: Aneede means “the departed” in Syriac. In the Malankara calendar, the Sunday of the departed priests (Kohne) and this Sunday of all the departed stand just before the Great Fast, as if the Church wants all her members with her as she goes up to Easter. In every Holy Qurbono the Thubden names the faithful departed. Today many families will also go to the graves of their own. It is good to bring the children, to say the names of those we never met, and to tell them that those we pray for are not forgotten: the Son's voice reaches them. It is also good to do what the Evening Gospel asks in their memory: to feed someone who is hungry, as Judas's soldiers gave what they had.
study: Judas's soldiers paid for the prayers for men who had sinned. For whom among my own dead should I pray most, and what could I offer for them besides words?
Paul does not forbid grief, only grief without hope. How do I speak of death to a grieving person, and what would “encourage one another with these words” sound like?
John 5:24 says that eternal life has begun. What in my life shows that I have heard his word and have “passed from death to life”?
As the Great Fast comes near, what do I want to have done by the time the Son's voice calls me?
